title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Replace combinational DIV/REM in ALU with a shared iterative divider (EX stall) and a single shared multiplier
motivation:
The Gowin timing report puts the baseline at 5.44 MHz with a 199.8 ns worst
path of 150-156 logic cells running MEM/WB.rd -> forward_unit -> EX operand
mux -> alu -> EX/MEM.alu_result (absorbed into the dmem BSRAM address).
That depth is the combinational 32-bit signed/unsigned `/` and `%` in
alu.sv: four separate 32-iteration restoring-divide cascades synthesised as
pure LUT logic. They account for most of the 12.3K LUT4 and essentially the
whole critical path; every other path in the core (32-bit adder, shifter,
DSP multiplier, branch compare, forwarding) is a small fraction of 200 ns.
CoreMark (2K, -O3, rv32im) contains no divisions in its timed region: the
list, matrix and state kernels use only +, *, shifts and CRC; compiler
div-by-constant is strength-reduced to MULH. Divides only occur in setup /
printf, outside the 0x10000100..0x10000104 markers. So a divider that takes
~34 cycles costs ~0 iterations/cycle but removes the single path that sets
Fmax. Fitness = iter/cycle x Fmax, so this is almost a pure Fmax win. The
new critical path becomes the DSP multiplier / forwarding path (est. 25-45
ns, i.e. 20-40 MHz), a 4-7x gain, far above the 4.6% acceptance bar.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
(1) Move DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU out of the combinational ALU into a new small
iterative radix-2 divider module (rtl/divider.sv) used by the EX stage as a
multi-cycle operation. (2) Replace the three 64-bit products in alu.sv with
ONE 33x33 signed multiplier whose operand sign-extension bits are chosen by
op (smaller, shallower LUT/DSP footprint; results bit-identical).

Divider (rtl/divider.sv), clocked. Inputs: clock, reset, start, op[1:0]
(is_signed, is_rem), a, b. Outputs: busy, result[31:0]. On `start` latch
operands, compute magnitudes (negate if signed and negative), run 32
iterations of shift-subtract on a {remainder[32:0], quotient[31:0]} shift
register (one 33-bit subtract + mux per cycle, ~10 ns), then apply sign
fix-up (quotient negated if signs differ, remainder takes dividend's sign)
in the final cycle or a 33rd cycle, and register `result`. Special cases
keep the exact existing semantics: b==0 -> DIV/DIVU = 0xFFFFFFFF,
REM/REMU = a (skip the sign fix-up for b==0); INT_MIN / -1 -> DIV =
0x80000000, REM = 0 (falls out naturally from |INT_MIN| / 1 with sign
fix-up, but must be tested).

EX-stage integration (rtl/ex_stage.sv, rtl/hazard_unit.sv, rtl/core.sv):
  * ex_is_div = in.valid && alu_op in {ALU_DIV, ALU_DIVU, ALU_REM, ALU_REMU}.
  * New small FSM in ex_stage: div_run_q (iterating) and div_done_q (result
    ready for the instruction currently in EX). ex_busy = ex_is_div &&
    !div_done_q. On the first cycle ex_busy is seen with div_run_q==0, pulse
    `start` capturing the POST-FORWARD rs1/rs2 (the forwarding sources
    disappear while the pipe drains, so operands MUST be latched at start;
    also latch them into the EX/MEM rs1_val/rs2_val fields so RVFI
    rs1_rdata/rs2_rdata stay correct). When the divider finishes set
    div_done_q; clear div_done_q on the cycle the EX/MEM register actually
    captures the instruction (i.e. !stall), NOT earlier, so a dmem stall
    that holds EX/MEM while the div is done keeps the result valid.
  * alu_result mux: ex_is_div ? div_result : alu_result (this feeds the
    existing `reg_q.alu_result` path; JAL/JALR override is unaffected).
  * While ex_busy && !stall (stall = dmem stall) the EX/MEM register
    captures a bubble (`reg_q <= '0`, valid=0, reg_write=0, mem ops=0), so
    the older instruction drains MEM -> WB normally and the div is not
    duplicated. dmem stall keeps priority (EX/MEM holds); the divider FSM
    runs independently of dmem stall because its operands are latched.
  * hazard_unit gets an `ex_busy` input: stall_if |= ex_busy, stall_id |=
    ex_busy (holds ID/EX and PC; the wrong-fetched imem word is simply
    refetched, same as the existing load-use stall). flush_id/flush_if need
    no change (a div cannot redirect and is not a load, so load_use_hazard
    is 0 while it sits in EX). redirect is 0 for div ops, so there is no
    redirect-vs-stall priority issue.
  * Under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS: ex_busy = 0 and the existing ALTOPS
    XOR stand-ins in alu.sv for DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU remain the result source
    (div_result mux disabled), so the per-iteration formal gate is
    unchanged and still fast; riscv-formal liveness/unique are unaffected.
    The real (non-ALTOPS) alu.sv branch just drops the four DIV/REM arms
    (default 0) and the `/` `%` operators entirely.

Single multiplier in alu.sv (non-ALTOPS branch): sa = (op != ALU_MULHU) &
a[31]; sb = (op == ALU_MULH) & b[31]; prod = $signed({sa,a}) * $signed({sb,b})
(66-bit); MUL = prod[31:0]; MULH/MULHU/MULHSU = prod[63:32]. This replaces
mul_ss/mul_uu/mul_su so one DSP-mapped multiplier is built instead of three
and the output mux shrinks. ALU port list is unchanged, so test_alu's
non-divide vectors still apply bit-for-bit.

Tests (allowed under test/): move every DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU vector (including
/0, INT_MIN/-1, negative operands, remainder-sign cases) out of
test_alu.py (the ALU now returns 0 for those ops in the real build) into a
new test_divider.py that drives divider.sv with start/busy/result and
checks ~34 cycle latency plus several hundred random vectors against a
Python RV32M reference model. Add one test_pipeline case that runs a
dependent sequence (producer ALU/load -> DIV -> consumer using the result,
plus a store/load in flight) to cover forwarding into a div and dmem-stall
overlap. This preserves invariant 5b coverage of divide arithmetic.

Why this is the best micro_opt angle: it deletes the one structure that
sets Fmax (~5 ns/level x ~40 levels of divider) at ~zero cycle cost on
CoreMark, needs no change to the I/O contract or RVFI discipline (rvfi_order
advances only on valid retire; bubbles have valid=0), and shrinks LUT4 by
several thousand (helping place-and-route).

title: Replace combinational mul/div in ALU with multi-cycle EX-stage muldiv unit
motivation:
The baseline scores Fmax 5.442 MHz with a 199.8 ns critical path of ~156 logic
cells that runs through cpu/u_fwd -> u_ex -> u_ex/u_alu. That is the 32-bit
combinational `/` and `%` array dividers (plus three separate 32x32 `*`
products) that alu.sv builds into the single-cycle EX stage. Every other path in
this 5-stage core (forward mux -> adder/comparator -> redirect -> PC mux) is
roughly 10-15 ns. Fitness is iter/cycle x Fmax, so the divider alone caps the
score at ~5 MHz, about 10x below what the rest of the pipeline can clock.
CoreMark's timed region has almost no divides and only a few thousand
multiplies (matrix kernels) out of ~449k cycles per iteration, so cycles spent
on a slow M unit cost under ~3% IPC, while the Fmax gain is several-fold.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move all M-extension arithmetic out of the combinational ALU into a new
sequential `muldiv` unit that lives alongside the EX stage and stalls the front
of the pipeline while it works (the same hold mechanism the dmem stall already
uses). The ALU keeps only the single-cycle ops.

Unit design (rtl/muldiv.sv):
* Operands are latched on the first EX cycle of an M op from the already-forwarded
  rs1/rs2, so later forwarding changes do not matter.
* One shared 33x33 signed multiplier handles MUL/MULH/MULHU/MULHSU (a_ext =
  {a[31]&signed_a, a}, same for b). It is pipelined: cycle 1 latches the operands;
  cycle 2 computes four 17x17-or-narrower partial products (each fits one Gowin
  18x18 DSP) into registers; cycle 3 sums them into a registered 64-bit product;
  then the result is selected by op. About 3-4 cycles per multiply. This leaves
  only reg -> DSP -> reg and one 64-bit add per cycle, instead of the
  forward-mux -> 3 multipliers -> result-mux chain in the baseline.
* DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU use a 1-bit/cycle restoring divider on |a|, |b| (33-bit
  subtract + mux per cycle, ~34 cycles). Sign fix-up on quotient and remainder at
  the end. Special cases are handled explicitly to match the current alu.sv: b==0
  gives q=0xFFFFFFFF and r=a, and INT_MIN/-1 gives q=INT_MIN and r=0 (the abs-based
  path already yields that for the overflow case).
* Interface: `busy` (M op in EX and not yet done) and a registered `done`
  flag. While `busy`, ID/EX, the PC and IF hold (hazard_unit adds `ex_busy` to
  stall_if and stall_id, and forces flush_id low). EX/MEM captures a bubble
  (`reg_q <= '0`) each busy cycle, so no false forwarding or double retire. On the
  cycle `done` is high, the M result goes into EX/MEM.alu_result like any ALU
  result and ID/EX advances. The unit's FSM only advances when !stall_ex_mem
  (dmem stall). If a dmem stall lands on the done cycle, EX/MEM just holds and
  `done` stays set.
* RVFI correctness: on the done cycle EX/MEM.rs1_val, rs2_val and write_data must
  be the latched operands, not the live forward mux output, since the producer may
  have retired to the regfile in the meantime. This mux only feeds RVFI, which
  synthesis prunes from the timed netlist, so it is off the critical path.
* Formal/ALTOPS: under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` keep the existing combinational
  XOR-of-add/sub substitutes in alu.sv and force `is_muldiv=0` in ex_stage, so the
  formal view is unchanged. The real arithmetic lives in muldiv.sv and is
  checked by cosim, which diffs each retired MUL/DIV/REM against the Python ISS,
  and by a new cocotb test.
* alu.sv gains `parameter bit HAS_MULDIV = 1` (default 1 keeps the existing
  test_alu.py valid as a golden model). ex_stage instantiates
  `alu #(.HAS_MULDIV(0))` so the mul/div logic is not in the synthesized core.

Expected result: the 200 ns path disappears. The new worst path should be the
forward mux -> adder/comparator -> redirect -> PC/imem address (~15-25 ns) or
the DSP stage, giving Fmax in the tens of MHz. LUT4 count should also fall a lot
(one shared 33x33 multiplier and a small iterative divider replace 3 multipliers
and 2 array dividers). The IPC cost is roughly 2-3 extra cycles per mul and ~34
per div, on the order of 2-3% of CoreMark cycles.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-002-r1s1 (improvement, +839.85%): Fmax was capped at ~5 MHz by the combinational 32-bit `/`/`%` dividers and three `*` products in the single-cycle EX ALU (~200 ns vs ~10-15 ns for the rest of the pipeline), and since CoreMark's timed region has few M ops, moving them into a multi-cycle `muldiv` unit that stalls the front end through the existing hazard_unit hold path (with a `HAS_MULDIV` alu parameter and ALTOPS left intact for riscv-formal) traded ~3% IPC for a several-fold Fmax gain, so check for rarely-executed arithmetic on the critical path before tuning anything else.

title: IF-stage predecode predictor: early JAL, BTFN-agree 2-bit BHT, mispredict-only EX redirect
motivation:
The baseline resolves every branch/jump in EX and implicitly predicts
not-taken, so every taken branch, JAL and JALR costs a one-cycle bubble
(flush_if kills the instruction fetched behind it and the PC reloads one
cycle late). Measured on the CoreMark cosim trace (10 iterations, 2K,
istall+dstall): 532k dynamic branches (296k taken: 236k backward-taken,
60k forward-taken), 49.6k JAL, 13.8k JALR = ~359k redirect bubbles out of
4.49M cycles (8%). The critical path (200 ns, Fmax 5.4 MHz) is the
combinational multiplier/divider in the ALU, so logic added in the IF /
branch-resolve cone has >150 ns of free slack and cannot move Fmax; only
cycles per CoreMark iteration change.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add an early-redirect predictor in the IF stage that predecodes the
fetched word (imem_data) combinationally and needs NO target storage
(target = pc + Jimm / Bimm computed by one 32-bit adder):
  - JAL: always predicted taken, target pc+Jimm  -> 0-bubble JAL.
  - Conditional branch (funct3 not 2/3): direction predicted from a small
    "agree-with-BTFN" 2-bit BHT (256 entries, index pc[9:2]). Counter
    state d (stored in a 256x2 array, reset/initial value 0 = strongly
    agree): predict taken iff (imm[31]  XOR  d[1]), i.e. d<2 follows
    backward-taken/forward-not-taken and d>=2 flips it. Update at EX
    (only when in.valid && is_branch && !stall_ex_mem): agree =
    (branch_taken == in.imm[31]); d <- agree ? (d==0?0:d-1) : (d==3?3:d+1);
    write index in.pc[9:2]. The 2-bit read value is carried in ID/EX
    (`pred_ctr`) so the table has ONE async read port (IF) and ONE write
    port (EX), mappable to LUT-RAM; no reset loop is required because
    correctness never depends on predictor state (EX verifies).
  - JALR and everything else: not predicted (fall through), still
    redirects from EX.
Predicted-taken sets next_pc = pred_target (only when the fetched word is
valid: !(flush||redirect), imem_ready, !stall) and sets a `pred_taken`
bit carried in if_id_t -> id_ex_t. EX computes the real outcome exactly
as today but `redirect` now fires only on MISPREDICT:
actual_taken_eff = (branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault;
redirect = (actual_taken_eff != in.pred_taken);
redirect_target = actual_taken_eff ? (is_jump ? jump_target : branch_target)
                                   : in.pc + 4.
For JAL/branches the predicted and actual targets are both pc+imm so no
target compare is needed. The RVFI pc_wdata (reg_q.pc_next) logic is left
untouched (computed from the resolved outcome only), so riscv-formal
pc_fwd / unique / liveness stay valid; predictor state only affects
timing, never architectural results. Under dmem stall the EX instruction
and IF PC are both held, so the prediction is simply recomputed; the BHT
write is gated by !stall_ex_mem so a held branch trains once.
Evidence: the STATIC half (JAL + BTFN, no table) was prototyped in the
cosim: 4,491,485 -> 4,259,699 bracketed cycles (+5.4% iter/cycle), CRCs
and "Correct operation validated" intact. Replaying the measured branch
trace through the agree-BHT gives 111,790 -> ~40,000 branch mispredicts
at 256 entries (another ~72k cycles, ~+1.7%), so the full design should
land near +7% cycles-wise (4.19M cycles). Implement the static half first,
confirm cosim, then add the BHT. Non-goals: BTB, RAS/JALR prediction (only
~0.3% available), gshare (trace showed history hurts on CoreMark).

changes.description: Add `pred_taken` (1 bit) to if_id_t and id_ex_t, and `pred_ctr` (2 bits, the BHT disagree-counter read at IF) to if_id_t and id_ex_t.

Predecode imem_data: JAL (opcode 1101111) and conditional branch (1100011, funct3[2:1] valid). Compute pred_target = pc + (is_jal ? Jimm : Bimm). lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-003-r1s2 (regression, +3.38%): The IF-stage predecode predictor (JAL + agree-BHT BTFN, mispredict-only EX redirect) was cycle-only and earned just +3.38% on the old 5.4 MHz baseline (vs +7% projected, +5.4% cycles from the static half alone), so it scored as a regression against the post-muldiv baseline (113.91); because that baseline's critical path now runs through u_if/u_ex/u_hazard (the redirect/flush cone), the "IF/branch logic has >150 ns free slack" premise is gone and any early-redirect predictor must be re-evaluated for Fmax loss (predecode + pc+imm adder + pred_taken compare feeding next_pc/flush), not just cycles.

title: Cut redirect out of the IF/ID kill mux and narrow ID/EX flush/stall fanout to ctrl+valid
motivation:
After the muldiv change the Gowin critical path is 24.2 ns / 20 logic levels with
module sequence u_id -> u_ex -> u_if -> u_hazard -> u_id (endpoint id_ex.rs2_val_29).
That is the redirect cone: ID/EX regs -> forward mux -> branch compare -> `redirect`
(u_ex) -> if_stage `out.instr = (flush||redirect) ? NOP : imem_data` (u_if) ->
hazard_unit `load_use_hazard` compares the *masked* instr[19:15]/[24:20] against
id_ex_rd and drives stall_id / flush_id / stall_if (u_hazard) -> CE and sync-reset
pins of ~200 ID/EX flops (u_id). So a late EX-resolved signal goes through a 32-bit
mux, a 5-bit equality compare, an OR tree and then a very high-fanout net before it
reaches any flop. Every one of those stages is redundant: `flush_id` already clears
the whole ID/EX register on redirect (unless dmem_stall/ex_busy hold it, in which
case the captured value is discarded anyway), and PC already gives redirect priority
over stall. The ID/EX *data* fields (pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, rd, rs?_addr, instr)
also do not need a synchronous clear at all: every consumer is gated by ctrl.* or
valid, which are the only bits that must read 0 for a bubble. Removing the wide
reset/flush from ~200 flops removes a 200-fanout net from the critical cone.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Four small, behaviour-preserving edits that shorten the redirect -> ID/EX path
without touching IPC (cycle count must be bit-identical on CoreMark):

1. if_stage.sv: drop `redirect` from the IF/ID kill. `out.instr = flush ? NOP :
   imem_data; out.valid = !flush;` where flush is now imem_stall only (early signal
   from the stall LFSR flop). The wrong-path instruction is still discarded because
   hazard_unit's flush_id (which includes redirect) clears ID/EX on the same edge, and
   when dmem_stall holds ID/EX the fetched word is never captured. Simplify
   `next_pc` to `pc + 4` (redirect already has priority in the always_ff chain).
2. hazard_unit.sv: `flush_if = imem_stall` (no redirect term). load_use_hazard now
   sees imem_data[19:15]/[24:20] unconditionally of redirect, so it no longer depends
   on EX. When redirect=1 and load_use fires spuriously, stall_if is overridden by the
   PC redirect priority and flush_id is already 1, so behaviour is unchanged; redirect
   and ex_busy are mutually exclusive (an M op is not a branch).
3. id_stage.sv: split the ID/EX register. Control + valid (ctrl_t, valid: ~23 flops)
   keep `if (reset||flush) clear; else if (!stall) capture`. All data fields (pc,
   rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, rd, rs1_addr, rs2_addr, instr) lose reset/flush and get
   capture-enable `!hold` where hold = dmem_stall || ex_busy (new input
   `hold_data`, from hazard_unit, built only from registered/early signals). On a
   load-use cycle ctrl/valid are cleared (bubble) while data flops simply recapture
   the same IF/ID instruction, which is replayed next cycle anyway because PC holds.
   Bubbles with stale data are harmless: forward_unit is gated by ctrl.reg_write,
   mem_stage by ctrl.mem_read/mem_write, ex_stage redirect by ctrl.is_branch/is_jump,
   muldiv req by valid, wb by valid, RVFI by valid.
4. (optional, same spirit) ex_stage.sv: share one 33-bit comparator for BLT/BGE/BLTU/BGEU
   (`{signed & rs1[31], rs1} < {signed & rs2[31], rs2}`) instead of separate signed and
   unsigned compares, and compute `branch_target[1:0]` / `jump_target[1:0]` misalign
   checks from the low two bits of the adders only.

Expected effect: the redirect cone loses the instr mux, the hazard compare and the
200-flop reset/CE net (about 6-8 logic levels and one large routed net), so the
critical path should fall from ~24 ns toward ~17-20 ns (new limiter probably EX
forward -> compare -> PC D, or MEM/WB forward -> ALU -> EX/MEM), with no cycle
change and fewer FFs/LUTs. riscv-formal is unaffected (all RVFI-visible state is
gated by valid; the decoder default-illegal and trap discipline are untouched).

title: Decouple EX redirect cone from IF/ID: drop redirect from IF NOP mux and load-use path, flush only ID/EX control bits
motivation:
Measured with `make timing TARGET=bench` on the current champion (Fmax 52.9-54.4 MHz):
the worst path is 24.19 ns arrival / 18.9 ns of data delay, 20 levels, and
~10 ns of it is a TAIL that follows the branch comparator, not arithmetic:
  regfile BSRAM DO (7.6) -> ID/EX bypass LUT -> 3 fwd-mux LUTs (11.5)
  -> 32-bit compare carry chain (14.2) -> branch_taken/redirect (16.0..16.7)
  -> u_if instr-NOP select `flush_if = redirect|imem_stall` (fanout 102, 17.8)
  -> muxed instr[24:20] (rs2_addr) -> u_hazard load-use 5-bit compare chain (20.5)
  -> stall/flush_id LUTs (22.4) -> ID/EX sync RESET net (fanout 33 x ~7, 24.2).
So `redirect`, the latest-arriving signal in the core, is serialised in front of
the IF NOP mux, the load-use comparators and then the wide ID/EX reset net.
None of that serialisation is architecturally needed:
(a) a redirect only fires when a branch/jump is in EX, and that instruction
has mem_read=0, so load_use_hazard and redirect are mutually exclusive; and
(b) whenever redirect fires without a dmem stall, flush_id already clears
ID/EX, so whatever IF presented to ID that cycle is discarded anyway (under a
dmem stall ID/EX holds and also ignores it; ex_busy and redirect are exclusive
because an M op in EX is not a branch/jump).
The NOP substitution on `redirect` is therefore dead weight on the critical path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Structural re-wiring of the front end so the late EX redirect only drives
(1) the PC next-state mux and (2) a small set of ID/EX kill bits, in parallel
with -- not in series in front of -- decode, regfile address, and hazard detect:
1. if_stage: out.instr = imem_stall ? NOP : imem_data and out.valid = !imem_stall,
   where the select is the early `!io_imemReady` only (stall-generator flop).
   `redirect` is removed from the instr/valid mux. PC update keeps
   redirect > stall > pc+4 priority. A wrong-path instruction in IF during a
   redirect cycle is never captured: flush_id clears ID/EX (no dmem stall) or
   ID/EX holds (dmem stall).
2. hazard_unit: flush_if = imem_stall only (no redirect). load_use is computed
   from the raw fetched rs fields, which no longer depend on redirect.
   flush_id = (load_use | redirect) & ~dmem_stall & ~ex_busy stays, and is now
   the only consumer of redirect besides the PC mux.
3. id_stage ID/EX register: split into kill bits (valid, ctrl.is_branch,
   is_jump, mem_read, mem_write, reg_write, is_illegal) that take the
   synchronous flush|reset, and the wide data fields (pc, rs1_val, rs2_val,
   imm, instr, rd, rs1/rs2 addr, alu_op/alu_src/branch_op/width/sext/other
   ctrl) that load on !stall and clear only on global reset. This takes ~170
   flops off the `redirect -> flush_id -> RESET` high-fanout net (~200 -> ~25
   loads), cutting the 1.2 ns reset-net route plus the extra reset-merge LUT
   level. RVFI reads data fields only when valid=1, so stale data on a bubble
   is unobservable; forwarding, hazard, redirect and ex_busy (req includes
   in.valid) all key off the cleared kill bits.
Expected effect: the critical redirect cone becomes ID/EX/BSRAM -> fwd mux ->
compare -> redirect -> {PC D-mux/CE, ~25 kill-bit flops}, removing the
NOP-mux (fanout 102) -> rs-addr -> hazard-compare -> reset-merge tail,
roughly 4-5 ns of the 18.9 ns data delay. The next limiters (redirect -> PC
mux, fwd-mux -> ALU -> EX/MEM/dmem BSRAM address) sit within a couple of ns of
that, so the realistic gain is ~15-20% Fmax. Retirement behaviour is
bit-identical (same cycle count), so the whole gain is Fmax; ALTOPS/formal
views are unchanged.

title: pc-indexed BTB + RAS in IF, mispredict-only registered EX redirect (cuts redirect cone)
motivation:
The post-muldiv critical path (24.2 ns, 50 cells) is the redirect cone:
ID/EX regs -> EX forward mux -> 32-bit branch compare / pc+imm -> `redirect`
-> if_stage `instr` NOP-gating -> hazard_unit load-use compare -> flush/stall
-> ID/EX register inputs (modules on the path: u_id > u_ex > u_if > u_hazard
> u_id). All other logic (ALU, muldiv, dmem load align) is ~10-15 ns. Taken
branches/jumps cost a flat 1-cycle penalty today (~14% of CoreMark
instructions are taken CTIs), and the previous predictor attempt
(hyp-003-r1s2) failed because its predecode + adder + compare logic sat
*inside* that cone (imem_data -> decode -> pc+imm -> next_pc/flush) and cost
Fmax. The way out is a predictor whose lookup depends only on the registered
PC (not on imem_data), and that lets the EX redirect be *registered*, so the
EX compare no longer fans out combinationally into the fetch/hazard logic.

ID/EX regs -> EX forward mux -> 32-bit branch compare / pc+imm -> `redirect`
-> if_stage `instr` NOP-gating -> hazard_unit load-use compare -> flush/stall
-> ID/EX register inputs (modules on the path: u_id > u_ex > u_if > u_hazard
> u_id). All other logic (ALU, muldiv, dmem load align) is ~10-15 ns. Taken

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small pc-indexed branch target buffer (BTB) in IF, verify every
prediction in EX against the actual next-PC, and register the (now rare)
mispredict redirect, so the cone ends at a flop instead of crossing
u_if/u_hazard/u_id.

1. New rtl/btb.sv: 16-entry direct-mapped, index = pc[5:2]. Per entry:
   valid flop (reset to 0), tag = pc[19:6] (14b), target = next_pc[19:2]
   (18b), 2-bit saturating counter. Tag+target (32b) and counter (2b) live
   in two small async-read/sync-write arrays (infer Gowin RAM16 LUT-RAM; the
   valid bits are plain flops). Lookup is purely a function of the `pc`
   register: hit = valid[idx] && tag == pc[19:6]; pred_taken = hit && ctr[1];
   pred_npc = {12'b0, target, 2'b00}. ~7-8 ns, no imem_data dependence.
2. if_stage: next_pc = redir_q ? redir_target_q : pred_taken ? pred_npc :
   pc + 4 (redir_q overrides stall exactly like today's `redirect`). Emit
   pred_taken, pred_npc[19:2], pred_hit, pred_ctr in the if_id_t bundle and
   carry them through ID/EX (new fields in core_pkg.sv if_id_t / id_ex_t).
   flush_if = redir_q || imem_stall (redir_q is a flop, so the old
   redirect -> instr-NOP-gating -> load-use compare hop disappears).
3. ex_stage verifies ALL instructions, not just branches: compute the true
   next PC (the existing pc_next expression, including the misalign-trap
   fallback to pc+4) and the predicted next PC (pred_taken ? {12'b0,
   pred_npc, 2'b0} : pc+4). mispredict = in.valid && !redir_q && (actual_npc
   != predicted_npc). This makes the predictor safe against aliased/stale
   BTB hits, non-branch instructions, JALR, and the formal flow's
   unconstrained symbolic imem (a BTB hit on an instruction that is not the
   branch that was learned just yields a mispredict and a redirect to
   the correct address). Compute the two compares (target vs pred, pc+4 vs
   pred) in parallel from early signals and select with the late
   branch_taken so the only late signal is a 2:1 select.
4. Registered redirect: when (mispredict && !stall && !ex_busy) set
   redir_q <= 1 and redir_target_q <= actual_npc (the branch advances to
   EX/MEM that same edge). In the redir_q cycle: the wrong-path instruction
   sitting in EX is killed (ex_valid = in.valid && !redir_q gates muldiv
   `req`, ex_busy, mispredict/BTB-update, and EX/MEM takes a bubble `'0`),
   the instruction being fetched is NOP'd (flush_if), ID/EX is flushed
   (flush_id; hazard_unit's `redirect` input is now redir_q), and pc <=
   redir_target_q. dmem_stall cannot coincide with redir_q because the
   instruction in EX/MEM that cycle is the branch/jump itself (not a mem
   op), and while a branch is held in EX by dmem_stall redir_q stays 0 and
   the check is re-evaluated until it advances. RVFI is unchanged: only
   correct-path instructions ever reach MEM/WB with valid=1, and pc_next is
   still the architectural next PC.
5. Training in EX when a direct branch (is_branch) or JAL (is_jump &&
   !is_jalr) advances out of EX (valid, !stall, !ex_busy, !redir_q, not a
   misalign trap): taken -> write tag/target arrays (target =
   branch_target[19:2]), set valid, counter = hit ? sat_inc(pred_ctr) :
   (JAL ? 3 : 2); not taken and pred_hit -> counter = sat_dec(pred_ctr),
   no tag/target write. Using the pred_hit/pred_ctr carried from fetch
   avoids a second read port. JALR is not trained into the direct-branch
   entries.
6. Optional second step (only after step 1-5 pass cosim/formal and timing):
   add a 4-entry return-address stack so `ret` (JALR x0,x1,0) stops paying
   the now-2-cycle indirect penalty: one extra BTB bit `is_ret`, set when a
   JALR with rs1==x1, rd==x0 resolves; at fetch, hit&&is_ret selects the
   RAS top as pred_npc; push pc+4 non-speculatively when a JAL/JALR with
   rd==x1 advances out of EX, pop when an `is_ret` JALR advances. Stale RAS
   tops are harmless because of the EX verification.

Expected effect: (a) Fmax: the 24.2 ns redirect cone (EX compare -> u_if ->
u_hazard -> ID/EX control) is cut at redir_q; the new longest paths are
ID/EX -> fwd mux -> {adder/compare} -> redir_q D (~10-13 ns) and the
unchanged ALU / load-align paths, so Fmax should move from ~54 MHz toward
~70-80 MHz (limited by whatever the next-worst path is, likely the regfile
read -> ID/EX or the 32-bit EX adder/shifter). (b) Cycles: taken
branches/JAL that hit the BTB drop from 1-cycle to 0-cycle penalty, but
mispredicts and JALR rise from 1 to 2 cycles; with 2-bit counters and a
16-entry BTB (plus the RAS) the net is estimated at -3..-6% cycles
(previous static JAL+BTFN predictor gave -6.7% cycles at a 1-cycle
penalty). Area +~250 LUT4 / ~50 FF (RAM16 arrays), well inside budget.
Risk: if another path (regfile read, ALU) is already within ~2 ns of the
redirect cone, the Fmax gain is capped; cycles are then roughly neutral
and the hypothesis would not clear the +4.6% bar.

title: Late-operand-last EX forwarding: ID-precomputed registered selects + pre-muxed WB data
motivation:
Gowin's report for the champion (make timing, path 1, 22.88 ns arrival, ~17.6 ns
after the BSRAM clock) shows where the time goes. The ID/EX rs1_val register
is absorbed into the regfile BSRAM (tC2Q 2.26 ns), then the data goes through
the regfile write-first bypass LUT (id_ex_w.rs1_val_*_s14), then THREE LUT
levels of the EX forward mux (u_ex/rs1_*_s9 -> s8 -> s7, ~3.9 ns with routing),
then the alu_a = is_auipc ? pc : rs1 LUT, and only then the ALU + result mux
(8 levels) into the dmem BSRAM address. The same ~7 ns operand prefix feeds the
co-critical cone ending at redir_target_q (path 3, 22.87 ns: branch compare /
jalr sum -> pc_next_w). A 3:1 forward mux should cost one LUT on the late
operand, not three: the select signals (5-bit rd/rs compares against EX/MEM and
MEM/WB, then priority) are computed combinationally in EX from ID/EX.rs?_addr,
ex_mem.rd and mem_wb.rd, so they arrive about as late as the BSRAM data and the
mapper chains the late operand through the select logic. Every EX-stage cone
starts with this prefix, so shortening it shifts all of them at once, at
identical cycle counts.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure forwarding so the only late signal (the regfile/ID-EX value) goes
through a single 2:1 LUT, with everything else precomputed from flops:

1. ID-time registered selects (id_stage.sv, core_pkg.sv id_ex_t, forward_unit.sv).
   In ID, compare the instruction's rs1/rs2 fields with the instruction ahead:
     p1_rsN = id_ex.ctrl.reg_write && id_ex.rd != 0 && id_ex.rd == rsN_field
              (the producer now in EX; at EX time it sits in EX/MEM)
     p2_rsN = ex_mem.ctrl.reg_write && ex_mem.rd != 0 && ex_mem.rd == rsN_field
              (the producer now in MEM; at EX time it sits in MEM/WB)
   and latch p1_rs1, p2_rs1, p1_rs2, p2_rs2 as 4 new ID/EX flops (cleared by
   the existing reset/flush bubble; held with the rest of ID/EX on stall). The
   ID/EX register only captures when the pipeline shifts (stall_id/ex_busy
   hold it, flush_id bubbles it), so "producer in EX at ID time" == "producer
   in EX/MEM on the consumer's first EX cycle", and it stays equivalent while
   the consumer is held in EX because EX/MEM and the retained MEM/WB fields are
   held too. The compares now end in a flop and the EX-time compare cone
   (forward_unit's 4 five-bit comparators) is removed from EX.
2. Trap-safe gating from early flops. The old logic used the EX/MEM and MEM/WB
   ctrl.reg_write AFTER the EX misalign-jump/branch and MEM misalign-access
   clears. Keep that: in EX, s1 = p1_rsN & ex_mem.ctrl.reg_write;
   s2 = p2_rsN & mem_wb.ctrl.reg_write & ~s1; (p2 is deliberately not masked by
   p1 at ID time so a trapped younger producer falls back to the older one,
   exactly as the old priority chain did). hit = s1 | s2 is 2 early LUT levels
   from flops.
3. Single late LUT. In ex_stage.sv write the operand as
     early = s1 ? fwd_ex_mem : fwd_mem_wb;     // both from flops
     rsN   = hit ? early : in.rsN_val;          // in.rsN_val is the late BSRAM+bypass value
   so the late path is bypass LUT -> one mux LUT (was bypass -> 3 LUTs).
4. Pre-mux the WB data (mem_stage.sv, core_pkg.sv mem_wb_t, wb_stage.sv). Store
   wb_data = ctrl.mem_to_reg ? load_data : alu_result in MEM/WB instead of
   separate read_data/alu_result and mux in WB. wb_w_data (regfile write data,
   MEM/WB forward source and RVFI rd_wdata) becomes a flop output, removing
   one LUT level from the `early` side of the forward mux and from the
   regfile write path. Misalign-trap clearing of reg_write stays as is.
5. Fold the ALU operand selects into the early side (ex_stage.sv). The
   decoded ctrl bits is_auipc and alu_src are already ID/EX flops, so no new
   state is needed:
     a_early = is_auipc ? in.pc  : early;   a_sel = is_auipc | hitA
     b_early = alu_src  ? in.imm : early;   b_sel = alu_src  | hitB
     alu_a   = a_sel ? a_early : in.rs1_val
     alu_b   = b_sel ? b_early : in.rs2_val
   is_auipc / alu_src must win over a register-name match (AUIPC/LUI/I-type
   encodings carry rs1/rs2 field bits that can spuriously compare equal), which
   the nesting above guarantees. alu_b gets its own mux next to the plain rs2
   mux that still feeds store write_data / branch compare / RVFI (~64 extra
   LUTs, ample headroom). The late value then reaches the ALU through one LUT
   instead of forward-mux (3 LUTs) + operand-mux (1 LUT).
Branch compare, JALR sum, mispredict check, BTB training, redirect and RVFI
keep using the registered rs1/rs2 outputs of step 3, so architectural
behaviour and cycle counts are bit-identical (cosim, cocotb and riscv-formal
should all pass unchanged). The riscv-formal wrapper (symbolic imem) exercises
the compare/priority/trap corner cases, which is why step 2 keeps the exact
reg_write gating.
Expected: late operand reaches the ALU 3 LUT levels earlier (~3.5-4 ns of the
17.6 ns budget on path 1 and ~2.5 ns on the pc_next_w cone), tempered by the
next co-critical cones (ALU result mux -> dmem address, BTB/redirect target),
so ~+8% Fmax at the same IPC.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-001-r3s0 (regression, +5.29%): Registering the forwarding selects at ID (4 `p?_rs?` ID/EX flops gated in EX by post-trap `reg_write`, pre-muxed MEM/WB `wb_data`, ALU-operand selects folded onto the early side so the late BSRAM/bypass operand crosses one 2:1 LUT instead of four) is cycle-identical but bought only ~0.8 ns (61.35 -> ~64.6 MHz) of the ~3.5-4 ns that counting removed LUT levels predicted, so LUT-level arithmetic on the shared EX operand prefix overestimates Fmax gain while the ALU-result -> dmem-BSRAM-address and BTB/redirect-target cones sit right behind it; after r2s1 this is the second single-cone trim capped at ~5-7%, so budget gains from the next co-critical cone, not from the cone just shortened.

title: Move the register file out of BSRAM into 16-deep LUT-RAM banks so EX paths start at a flop
motivation:
`make timing` on the current champion (place option 0: 56.9 MHz, 22.88 ns,
14 cells) shows that EVERY one of the top-5 worst paths launches from the
register-file BSRAM (`cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s`, 6 BSRAM total = 4 dmem + 2
regfile read-port copies): regs BSRAM -> u_id -> forward mux (u_ex) -> ALU
(u_alu) -> dmem BSRAM address, and regs BSRAM -> u_ex/u_btb compare ->
redir_target_q (38 cells). Gowin inferred the 32x32 `regs` array (async
read in the source) as BSRAM with the ID/EX read register absorbed into the
RAM, so the whole EX cycle begins with a BSRAM clock-to-output (several ns,
vs ~0.5 ns for a fabric flop) instead of a flop. The 16-entry BTB arrays in
btb.sv, coded the same way, were inferred as LUT-RAM (17 LUT-RAM in the
report), so the inference rule is size/shape driven and can be steered
structurally. The earlier lessons ("regfile BSRAM -> fwd mux -> ALU -> dmem
BSRAM address is co-critical") are consistent: cutting the redirect cone
alone is capped by this head-of-path cost.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Re-implement reg_file.sv so Gowin cannot map it to BSRAM, keeping the same
port-level behaviour (two async read ports, write-first bypass, x0 = 0), and
keep the explicit ID/EX flops in id_stage as the only register boundary.

Primary form (proven inference pattern, same style as btb.sv): split the
file into four 16 x 32 arrays - {rs1 port, rs2 port} x {regs 0-15, regs
16-31}. Each is written with the same WB data under
`if (w_en && w_addr[4] == BANK) arr[w_addr[3:0]] <= w_data;` (no reset, plain
async read `assign rd = arr[addr[3:0]]`), which is the shape that produced
LUT-RAM (RAM16S4) for the BTB; the read value is then selected with
`rs_addr[4]`, zeroed for x0, and write-first-bypassed from WB exactly as
today. 4 x 8 RAM16S4 cells ~ +130 LUT4, well inside budget. The reset loop
is dropped (it is what prevents RAM inference; LUT-RAM powers up as 0 and
riscv-formal's register checks are insensitive to the initial register
contents - confirm with `make formal`). Fallback if Gowin still infers
BSRAM: write the registers as 31 explicit 32-bit flop vectors via a
generate loop (keep the sync reset) with a mux-tree read, or add
`(* syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram" *)` / `"registers"` on the arrays.

Effect: ID/EX.rs1_val / rs2_val become ordinary fabric flops (tco ~0.5 ns)
and the async LUT-RAM read sits in the ID stage where there is large slack
(instruction address comes from the imem data, read + bypass ~6 ns). The EX
cone (forward mux -> ALU/adder -> EX/MEM address or redir_target_q) loses
the BSRAM clock-to-out from its head. Pipeline structure, hazards, BTB and
cycle counts are unchanged, so iter/cycle is identical and the gain is
pure Fmax: roughly 2-4 ns removed from the 22.9 ns path, i.e. +10-17% Fmax,
limited afterwards by MEM/WB -> wb mux -> forward mux -> ALU -> dmem
address (flop-launched, 14 levels) which is the next-worst cone.

changes.description: Replace the 32x32 reset-looped array (inferred as BSRAM with an absorbed read register) with four 16x32 async-read / sync-write arrays (two read-port copies x two banks selected by addr[4]), no reset on the arrays, read-bank mux + x0 zero + write-first bypass unchanged at the port level. Fallback: 31 explicit flop registers via generate, or a syn_ramstyle attribute, if Gowin still maps it to BSRAM.

No functional change expected; confirm ID/EX rs1_val/rs2_val remain plain registers (stall/flush) fed by the async regfile read, and add a comment that the regfile read is intentionally combinational in ID.

title: BTB-driven decoupled fetch queue: predicted fetch runs ahead of ID, hides imem stalls behind downstream stalls
motivation:
I profiled the champion on the CoreMark ISS trace (2.94M retired instrs,
built from bench/programs/coremark.elf) with a Python model of the
predictor and a cycle-level model of this exact pipeline (random 22%
imem/dmem stalls, load-use, 3/35-cycle muldiv, registered 2-cycle
mispredict). The cycle model reproduces the real CPI (1.57 vs 1.56 from
4.579M cycles), so its deltas are trustworthy.

Finding 1 -- pure predictor work is capped. The champion BTB has ~82k
mispredicts in 2.94M instrs (54.7k cond. branches, 13.8k returns, 13.5k
JAL, 21 other JALR). At 2 cycles each that is 164k cycles = 3.6% of all
cycles, so even a PERFECT predictor (bigger BTB, RAS, gshare...) is worth
< 3.6%, below the 4.6% acceptance bar. A 64-entry 2-way BTB + RAS only
saves ~1.6% in the model. Predictor-only ideas cannot win this round.

Finding 2 -- the real front-end loss is that imem stalls are *serial*
with every other stall. Today fetch is lock-stepped with ID: the IF/ID
payload is the combinational imem_data of the pc register and pc holds on
load-use / dmem stall / muldiv busy, so after each such stall the same
instruction is re-fetched and again has a 22% chance of an imem bubble.
imem bubbles alone are ~0.28 cycles/instr (~18% of all cycles) and are
never overlapped with the ~0.7M cycles of dmem/load-use/muldiv/mispredict
stalls. A queue between the (predicted) fetch pc and ID lets fetch keep
running ahead during those stalls so the next instruction is already
waiting. Ideal bound: cycles >= instrs/0.78 = 3.77M vs 4.58M now.

Cycle-model result (same trace, same stall statistics, BTB unchanged):
queue depth 0 (today) = 1.571 CPI; depth 1 = 1.538 (-2.1%); depth 2 =
1.474 (-6.1%); depth 3 = 1.453 (-7.5%); depth 4 = 1.448 (-7.8% cycles,
~+8.5% fitness at constant Fmax).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Turn the predicted fetch into a decoupled, BTB-driven fetch queue
(prediction-ahead front end). The BTB lookup, EX verification and the
registered redirect (redir_q / redir_target_q) stay exactly as in the
champion; only the IF->ID handoff changes.

1. New rtl/fetch_queue.sv (or inside if_stage.sv): 4-entry circular
   buffer with 2-bit wr_ptr/rd_ptr and a 3-bit count (reset to 0; data
   array needs no reset, plain flops or LUT-RAM). Entry = {pc[31:2],
   instr[31:0], pred_taken, pred_npc[19:2], pred_hit, pred_ctr[1:0]} --
   i.e. the existing if_id_t payload, so EX still verifies each
   instruction against ITS OWN prediction (verify-everything is
   unchanged, so stale/wrong-path/aliased entries remain safe).
2. Fetch side (fpc = the register driving io_imemAddr, BTB indexed by
   fpc as today):
      fire = io_imemReady && !redir_q && (count != 4)
   (deliberately NOT dependent on stall_id / load-use / hazards, so the
   hazard compare no longer feeds the pc register at all). On fire:
   write {fpc, imem_data, btb pred fields} at wr_ptr, wr_ptr++, and
      fpc <= pred_taken ? {pred_target,2'b00} : fpc + 4.
   On redir_q: fpc <= redir_target_q, wr_ptr = rd_ptr = count = 0 (whole
   queue is wrong-path, drop it), the in-flight fetch is dropped (fire is
   gated by !redir_q). redir_q overrides everything exactly like the
   current `redirect` does.
3. Decode side with zero-latency bypass (REQUIRED -- no extra cycle on
   the mispredict path): head = (count != 0) ? q[rd_ptr] : {incoming
   fetch entry}; head_valid = (count != 0 || io_imemReady) && !redir_q.
   if_id_t out = head with instr forced to 0x00000013 and valid = 0 when
   !head_valid (same NOP-gating as flush_if today, so the hazard unit
   never sees garbage rs1/rs2 and bubbles carry harmless ctrl).
   consume = head_valid && !stall_id; rd_ptr += consume; count_next =
   count + fire - consume. The bypass case (count==0, fire, consume) is
   handled naturally: the entry is written and popped in the same cycle
   (count unchanged); write data is unconditional on fire so the stall_id
   cone only drives the 2-bit pointers/count, not the data flops.
4. hazard_unit: stall_if is no longer a pc stall -- remove it from
   if_stage; the hazard unit keeps stall_id = dmem_stall || load_use ||
   ex_busy, flush_id = (load_use || redirect) && !dmem_stall && !ex_busy,
   stall_ex_mem, hold_mem_wb unchanged. load_use is evaluated on
   head.instr[19:15]/[24:20] (queue head or bypass). imem_stall now only
   means "no incoming instruction while the queue is empty" and is folded
   into head_valid.
5. ID/EX, EX, MEM, WB, forwarding, BTB, RVFI plumbing: unchanged. The
   RVFI pc/insn/order fields come from the ID payload as today, so
   formal's unique/pc_fwd/causal checks see the same retirement stream.
   Check formal/wrapper_si.sv for any assumption tying imem_data to the
   *current* address (stability while !ready); the queue stores the data
   captured at fetch time, which is what the pipeline retires.

Timing: the pc update cone gets shorter (no stall_if), the BTB lookup
cone is untouched, and the added logic on the ID path is one 4:1/2:1
mux level (queue head vs bypass) in front of decode/regfile-address,
an ID path with large slack (critical path remains regfile BSRAM -> fwd
mux -> ALU -> dmem address, ~22.9 ns, which this change does not touch).
Cost ~ 4 x 86 flops (~350 FF) + ~150 LUT, well inside the 10k LUT budget.

If depth 4 hurts Fmax or area the implementer may fall back to depth 2
(model: -6.1% cycles) -- keep the circular-buffer structure and just
change the depth/pointer width. Do NOT add a registered IF/ID stage
without the bypass: the model shows +1 cycle on every mispredict costs
~1.8% and cancels a quarter of the gain.

changes.description: New module: 4-entry circular fetch queue (2-bit wr/rd pointers, 3-bit count, entry = if_id_t payload). Inputs: fire + incoming entry, consume, flush (redir_q). Outputs: head entry (queue head or combinational bypass of the incoming entry when empty), head_valid, full. Data written unconditionally on fire; only pointers/count depend on consume.

Keep the fetch pc register (io_imemAddr) and BTB-predicted next_pc (pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4); pc now advances on fire = imem_ready && !redir_q && !queue_full instead of on !stall; redir_q still overrides with redir_target_q. Instantiate fetch_queue, emit its head as the IF->ID bundle with NOP-gating and valid = head_valid (replaces flush_if/imem_stall instr gating). Add consume input from the hazard/ID side.

Drop stall_if as a pc-hold (fetch no longer stalls on load-use/dmem/ex_busy); keep stall_id/flush_id/stall_ex_mem/hold_mem_wb semantics; compute consume = head_valid && !stall_id and export it; imem_stall no longer separately flushes (folded into head_valid).
Wire the new consume/head_valid/redirect signals between if_stage, hazard_unit and id_stage; imem address/ready ports and RVFI outputs unchanged.

Add fetch_queue.sv to the cocotb runner source list (after core_pkg.sv); relax any cycle-exact fetch/stall expectations, keep architectural-result checks, and add a directed test with random imem_ready toggling plus load-use/dmem stalls and a taken-branch mispredict to check no instruction is lost, duplicated, or executed from the wrong path after redir_q.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-003-r3s2 (improvement, +7.68%): With the BTB at ~82k mispredicts (~3.6% of cycles) so predictor-only work was capped below the acceptance bar, the remaining front-end loss was that fetch was lock-stepped with ID so every load-use/dmem/muldiv stall re-fetched the same pc and re-rolled the ~22% imem-bubble chance; a BTB-driven fetch queue that keeps fetching during those stalls (fire gated only on imem_ready/!redir_q/not-full, never on stall_id, with a zero-latency empty-queue bypass so the registered 2-cycle mispredict path gains no cycle, and per-entry predictions kept so EX still verifies everything) overlapped imem stalls with downstream stalls and landed on the ISS-trace cycle model's ~7-8% prediction, so when a stall source is ~18% of cycles and never overlapped with the others, decoupling it beats refining the predictor, and a cycle model replaying the CoreMark trace with the real stall statistics is a trustworthy way to size such a change before RTL.

title: EX cone trim: ID-registered forward selects, x0/bypass LUT removal, one-hot ALU result select with shared shifter
motivation:
I ran `make timing` on the current champion (59.7 MHz at placement option 0;
top five paths all land at 22.01-22.05 ns, i.e. the placer has equalised
them). Path 1 broken down (launch clock edge at 5.33 ns, so 16.7 ns of
logic):
  BSRAM regfile tC2Q                          2.26 ns
  2 post-BSRAM LUTs in u_id (write-first
    bypass + x0 gate: rs2_val_s14, s13)       2.47 ns
  2 EX forward-mux LUTs (rs2_s8, rs2_s7)      1.84 ns
  alu_b select LUT (fanout 79)                1.64 ns
  adder carry chain (to bit 7)                2.5  ns
  5 LUTs of ALU/result mux after the adder
    SUM (n1185_s13/s8/s3/s2, dmem_addr_c)     4.9  ns
  route to dmem BSRAM ADB[]                   1.2  ns
Paths 4 and 5 are the same prefix ending at the dmem address and at the BTB
valid/training flops, so the 5.8 ns operand prefix (BSRAM -> 5 LUTs -> ALU
input) is shared by every EX cone, and the ALU-result tail (5 LUTs after
the adder: an 11-way case on a 5-bit alu_op, then is_muldiv ? md :
is_jump ? pc+4 : alu in ex_stage) is the largest single removable block.
r3s0 (ID-registered forward selects) was cycle-identical and took Fmax
61.35 -> 64.6 MHz (+5.3%) but lost its round to the fetch queue, so that
gain was never banked on the current champion, and it did not touch the
ALU result tail or the two post-BSRAM bypass LUTs.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Cycle-identical Fmax work on the one cone that dominates every top path
(BSRAM -> operand -> ALU -> dmem address). Three parts, each independently
safe to fall back from:

1. Forwarding selects computed in ID (r3s0 recipe on the new champion). In
   id_stage compare the instruction's rs1/rs2 fields against id_ex.rd /
   reg_write (producer now in EX, in EX/MEM when the consumer reaches EX)
   and ex_mem.rd / reg_write (producer in MEM, in MEM/WB at EX); latch four
   flags p1_rs1/p2_rs1/p1_rs2/p2_rs2 in ID/EX (cleared by the existing flush
   bubble, held with ID/EX on stall; the fetch-queue head is only popped
   when ID/EX captures, so "producer position at ID time" equals "producer
   position on the consumer's first EX cycle"). In EX gate them with
   ex_mem.ctrl.reg_write / mem_wb.ctrl.reg_write (keeps the misalign-trap
   reg_write clearing exact, p2 not masked by p1 so a trapped younger
   producer falls back to the older one as today). The late BSRAM operand
   then crosses one LUT: rsN = hit ? (s1 ? ex_mem.alu_result : wb_data) :
   in.rsN_val. Pre-mux the WB data in mem_stage (store wb_data = mem_to_reg
   ? load_data : alu_result in MEM/WB) so the early side is flop-fed. Fold
   is_auipc / alu_src onto the early side for alu_a / alu_b so the late
   operand crosses one LUT into the ALU instead of fwd-mux (2) + alu_b (1).

2. Drop the regfile's x0 gate from the post-BSRAM path (reg_file.sv).
   regs[0] is never written (writes to x0 stay dropped and the reset clear
   loop is kept for formal, which asserts reset in step 0), so reading
   address 0 already returns 0; remove the `rs_addr == 0 ? 0` select. For
   safety carry a registered x0 flag in ID/EX (instr rs field == 0, from
   the early ID side) and fold it into the single late LUT of part 1:
   rsN = hit ? early : (x0 ? 0 : in.rsN_val) (4-input LUT). That removes one
   of the two post-BSRAM LUT levels (~1.2 ns on every EX cone).

3. ALU result tail. (a) Decode a registered one-hot result select in ID
   (sel_add_sub, sel_logic, sel_slt, sel_shift, sel_lui, sel_pc4,
   sel_md) as ID/EX ctrl flops. JAL/JALR's pc+4 (separate EX adder fed
   by in.pc) and the muldiv result become additional AND-OR terms, so
   ex_stage's is_muldiv/is_jump priority chain and the 11-way case
   collapse into: result = (sel_add & add_sum) | rest, where `rest` is the
   OR of the other terms, built in parallel from early operands. The late
   adder SUM then crosses one LUT instead of ~5. (b) One shared right
   shifter: SLL via bit-reversal of the operand in and out (wiring), SRA/SRL
   differ only in the fill bit; shifter data input is rs1 directly (shifts
   never use auipc), shamt = alu_b[4:0]. Replaces three barrel shifters so
   the shifter term arrives no later than the adder. (c) One add/sub carry
   chain (b XOR sub, cin = sub) with SLT/SLTU derived from its sign/carry
   instead of two additional comparator chains. The alu.sv op/a/b/out
   interface used by test_alu.py and the RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS arms stay
   intact (one-hot path is an EX-level wrapper; ALTOPS keeps the original
   case).

Expected: ~2-3 LUT levels off the shared operand prefix and ~3-4 off the
ALU tail on path 1 (~5 ns counted). Discounting for the r3s0 experience
(counted 3.5-4 ns, realised 0.8 ns because co-critical cones sat right
behind) a realised Fmax of ~65-67 MHz (+8-10%) at identical IPC is
projected; the BTB-training and pc_next_w cones share the same prefix and
move with it. cosim/cocotb/formal behaviour is unchanged by construction.

title: Split the EX cone: dedicated rs1+imm address register for dmem BSRAM, ID-precomputed branch target / pc+4 / mispredict-match bits
motivation:
The champion (144.27, 60.9 MHz, CPI 1.436 vs a front-end floor of ~1.28 =
1/0.78 imem delivery rate) is Fmax-limited, not cycle-limited: at most ~10%
is left on the IPC side, while Fmax is 60.9 MHz against a 135 MHz target.
The reported worst path in every recent run is the same one:
regfile BSRAM -> fwd mux -> ex_stage alu_a/alu_b mux -> alu (adder + 11-way
op mux) -> ex_stage `is_muldiv ? md_result : is_jump ? pc+4 : alu_result`
mux -> dmem BSRAM address pin (14-15 LUT levels, ~22 ns). The dmem BSRAM
absorbs the EX/MEM `alu_result` flop as its address register, so the ALU's
full result mux (shifter, SLT compare, logic, muldiv/link selects) sits in
front of a BSRAM address setup, even though a load/store address is just
rs1 + imm and only bits [12:2] reach the BSRAM. The next co-critical cones
(LESSONS r2s1 / r3s0: "single-cone trims cap at ~5-7% because the ALU ->
dmem-address and BTB/redirect-target cones sit right behind") are the
mispredict cone (fwd mux -> pc+imm 32-bit adder -> 32-bit != pred_full ->
select -> redir_q) and the redir_target_q data path (pc+imm / pc+4 /
jalr_sum -> pc_next_w). Trimming one at a time keeps hitting the other.
This hypothesis removes work from BOTH cones structurally, by moving
operand-independent arithmetic out of EX into the ID stage (which has
slack) and giving memory addressing its own datapath.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two structural separations; cycle behaviour is identical (CPI unchanged,
no new stalls, no new pipeline stage, formal/cosim semantics unchanged).

(1) Dedicated memory-address datapath. ex_stage already has a separate
adder `jalr_sum = rs1(fwd) + in.imm`. Reuse that exact sum as the load/store
effective address: add `mem_addr[31:0]` to ex_mem_t, loaded from `jalr_sum`
(full 32 bits so the oob check / RVFI aligned address are unchanged) under
the same hold/bubble rules as the other EX/MEM fields. mem_stage then uses
`in.mem_addr` (not `in.alu_result`) for dmem_addr, byte_mask, misalign
check, load-shift amount and aligned_addr. `alu_result` keeps feeding the
forward mux / write-back only. The dmem BSRAM address register is now
fed by fwd mux -> one 32-bit adder (only [12:2] matter for the BSRAM) with
no alu_a/alu_b operand mux, no shifter/SLT/logic result mux, no
muldiv/link select. That removes ~6-8 LUT levels from the worst
endpoint and drops the BSRAM-address setup penalty from the ALU path (the
ALU result now ends at an ordinary flop).

(2) ID-stage precompute of operand-independent EX arithmetic. In id_stage
(pc, imm, pred_taken/pred_npc are all flops/LUT-RAM outputs of the fetch
queue head, independent of the register file and forwarding) compute and
register into new id_ex_t fields:
  * btgt   = pc + imm            (branch / JAL target; replaces the EX adder
                                  `in.pc + in.imm`, used by branch_target,
                                  jump_target (JAL) and pc_next_w)
  * pc4    = pc + 4              (replaces the EX incrementer; used by
                                  pc_next_w, the JAL/JALR link value, mp_seq)
  * mp_seq  = (pc4  != pred_full_id)   where pred_full_id = pred_taken ?
              {pred_npc,2'b00} : pc4
  * mp_btgt = (btgt != pred_full_id)
In EX the mispredict logic becomes: mp_seq / mp_btgt are plain flop outputs;
only the JALR compare `({jalr_sum[31:1],0} != pred_full)` (fed by fwd mux +
the already-shared rs1+imm adder) and the late branch_taken 2:1 select
remain. The EX cone for redir_q is therefore fwd mux -> {32-bit eq/lt
compare -> select} or {adder -> 32-bit != -> select (JALR only)}, with the
pc+imm adder and its 32-bit compare removed, and redir_target_q's D input
loses the pc+imm / pc+4 adders (btgt, pc4 are flops). Misalign tests use
btgt[1:0] (= imm[1:0]) from the flop. If the ID path (queue-head LUT-RAM /
bypass -> imm_gen -> 32-bit add -> 32-bit != -> flop) proves deeper than
~14 levels, drop mp_seq/mp_btgt and register only btgt/pc4, doing the two
compares in EX against flops (still removes both adders from EX).

Cost: ~32 (mem_addr) + 32 (btgt) + 30 (pc4) + 2 FFs, no extra LUT-heavy
logic (the adders move, not duplicate; the pc+4 incrementer already exists
in IF/EX). LUT/FF budget is nowhere near the limit (2946/10000 LUT4).
RVFI is unaffected (pc_next/branch_target values are the same; mem_addr
still reported word aligned via aligned_addr from the registered address).
ALTOPS formal view unchanged: the ALU is untouched, only its consumers
change. No change to IO, nret, decoder or hazard/forward logic. The ID
precompute is purely a function of the queue head, so wrong-path/aliased
entries still only cost a redirect (EX verifies every instruction).

Expected result: the worst-path endpoint (BSRAM address) and the redirect
cone both get 5-8 levels shorter. Prior single-cone trims gave +5-7% Fmax;
trimming the two co-critical cones together should lift Fmax toward
~68-72 MHz (+12-18%) at unchanged CPI, with the ALU result -> flop path and
the fwd-select compare path becoming the new limiters.

title: 1-cycle mispredict (redirect-cycle fetch bypass) + 64-entry partial-tag BTB + fetch-predecoded RAS
motivation:
I replayed the CoreMark ISS trace (2.937M retired instrs, built from
bench/programs/coremark.elf, 532k cond. branches, 49.6k JAL, 13.8k JALR)
through a model of the champion BTB. It reproduces the ~82k mispredicts
(54.7k branch, 13.5k JAL, 13.8k JALR - returns are never trained so every
return mispredicts). Model results for the same trace: 64-entry
direct-mapped BTB -> 63.8k mispredicts (JAL 13.5k -> 6.6k, B 54.7k ->
43.5k); adding a return-address stack removes ~13k more (-> ~50.7k);
a 16-entry BTB shared with returns is WORSE (returns evict branches:
80.9k), so returns must not be allocated in the BTB. The remaining ~41k
conditional-branch mispredicts are data-dependent direction errors that
no BTB size fixes (256-entry 2-way still leaves 40.5k).
Every mispredict costs 2 cycles today: EX sets redir_q at t, redir_q
overrides the fetch pc register at t+1, and the correct-path instruction
is only on the imem bus at t+2. Total = ~164k of ~4.22M cycles (3.9%).
This is the predictor-category ceiling (perfect prediction = 3.9%), so
the hypothesis attacks both the count (-35%: 82k -> ~53k) and the cost per
mispredict (2 -> 1 cycle), for an estimated ~110k cycles (~2.6%) saved,
with every change kept off the EX critical cone (flop-driven muxes only).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three changes, all verified in EX exactly as today (pred_taken/pred_npc
ride the pipe, aliased/stale/partial-tag/wrong-path predictions are
merely mispredicts, so the formal flow's symbolic imem stays safe).
1. Redirect-cycle fetch bypass (penalty 2 -> 1). io_imemAddr = redir_q ?
   redir_target_q : pc, a 2:1 mux whose select and data are both flops.
   In the cycle redir_q is high the queue contents and the instruction
   in EX are dead; the incoming bundle for the corrected pc is treated as
   an empty-queue bypass head (head_valid = in_valid, not forced 0 by
   flush) and goes straight into ID/EX, so the correct-path op reaches EX

   target gets its own prediction). pc <= next_pc(target) when the bundle

title: Insert an operand-select (OF) stage so EX starts at operand flops: 6-stage IF-ID-OF-EX-MEM-WB with forwarding captured at the end of the previous cycle
motivation:
The champion (158.99 = 67.1 MHz x 2.37 CoreMark/MHz) is Fmax-limited, not cycle-limited:
CPI is 1.437 against a hard fetch floor of ~1.28 (1 word/cycle at 78% imem ready), so at
most ~10% is left on the cycle side, while Fmax is half of the 135 MHz target. Every
recent timing report (r4s0 breakdown, r4s1 worst path 20.58 ns / 14 LUT levels) shows the
same shape: EX is doing the work of two stages. Before the adder even starts, the EX path
spends ~8 ns on operand preparation:
  BSRAM regfile tC2Q (2.3) + write-first bypass/x0 LUTs (2.5) + forward-select compare
  from MEM/WB.rd / EX/MEM.rd (u_mem reg_q.rd -> u_fwd, ~2-3 LUTs) + 3:1 forward mux (1.8)
  + alu_a/alu_b select with fanout ~80 (1.6)
and after the adder ~5 LUTs / 4.9 ns of ALU-result mux tail. Five single-cone trims (r2s1,
r3s0, r3s1, r4s0, r4s1) each captured only 5-10% because the operand prefix is shared by
every EX cone (ALU result, dmem address, mispredict compare, redir_target, BTB training),
and r4s0 (ID-registered forward selects + one-hot result select) was cycle-identical but
worth only +4.7%. Trimming the prefix is capped; removing it from EX is not.

The regfile BSRAM already behaves as a pipeline break: the read address is captured at
the end of ID and the data arrives (after tC2Q) in the next stage. Today that next stage
is EX, so BSRAM output, bypass, forwarding, operand select, ALU and result mux are all
one cycle. Splitting that into (BSRAM + forward + operand select) and (ALU + result mux)
is the classic fix, and it is nearly free in cycles here because (a) back-to-back ALU
dependencies stay bubble-free if the forward from the EX result is done as a late 2:1
mux into the operand flops, (b) load-use stays at exactly 1 bubble because load data
from the MEM-stage dmem BSRAM is forwarded straight into the operand flops at the end
of MEM instead of into a MEM/WB flop that EX then re-reads, and (c) only the mispredict
penalty grows by one cycle (~82k mispredicts of 4.22M cycles = +1.9% CPI).

1. ID (id_stage.sv) keeps decoder, imm_gen and the regfile read exactly as today (same
   reg_file.sv, same rs addresses from the fetch-queue head, same BSRAM-absorbed rs1_val
   / rs2_val register with the same stall/flush rules, so BSRAM inference is unchanged).
   Its register (the D/O register, keep the id_ex_t name/fields to limit churn) holds
   pc, instr, valid, ctrl, rd, rs addrs, imm, rs1_val, rs2_val and the prediction bits.
   The ID-time btgt / pc4 / mp_seq / mp_btgt precompute added by r4s1 is MOVED out of ID
   into OF: it sits behind imem BSRAM -> queue bypass -> imm_gen -> 32-bit add -> 32-bit
   compare, which would become the new critical path at ~100 MHz; in OF it starts at flops.

2. New rtl/of_stage.sv (operand fetch / forward) owns the O/X register (new type ox_t in
   core_pkg.sv). From the D/O register it computes btgt = pc + imm, pc4 = pc + 4,
   mp_seq / mp_btgt (vs pred_full) and the forwarded operands, and registers:
     rs1_v, rs2_v   post-forward rs1/rs2 (branch compare, jalr_sum, store data, muldiv,
                    RVFI rs1_rdata / rs2_rdata)
     opa, opb       ALU operands with the select folded in: opa = is_auipc ? pc : rs1_fwd,
                    opb = alu_src ? imm : rs2_fwd (separate flops, ~64 FFs, so EX has no
                    operand-select LUT)
     pc, instr, valid, ctrl, rd, rs addrs, imm, btgt, pc4, mp_seq, mp_btgt, pred_*.
   Forward sources, priority high to low, with 5-bit compares on FLOP-fed fields only:
     dist 1  instruction in EX: the EX result `x_result` = is_muldiv ? md_result :
             is_jump ? pc4 : alu_result (combinational, late). Qualify with the POST-TRAP
             reg_write (misalign_jump clears reg_write for JAL/JALR; use jalr_sum[1] /
             btgt[1], both early) and rd != 0.
     dist 2  instruction in MEM: m_result = mem_to_reg ? load_data : alu_result, taken
             combinationally from mem_stage (so a load's data goes directly into the
             operand flops at the end of MEM). Qualify with mem_stage's post-misalign-trap
             reg_write and rd != 0.
     dist 3  instruction in WB: the MEM/WB wb_data flop (qualify with its reg_write, NOT
             valid, so the held-data-after-dmem-stall behaviour of hold_mem_wb still
             forwards correctly).
     else    the D/O register's rs?_val (regfile read with its existing write-first
             bypass, which covers the producer in WB while the consumer was in ID).
   Structure the mux so the late EX result crosses exactly ONE LUT: operand_d = sel1 ?
   x_result : early_mux(sel2, sel3, rs_val), where sel1..3 come from flop-only compares
   and the early mux (including the late-ish m_result) is built in parallel.

3. ex_stage.sv: takes ox_t. Deletes the fwd_rs1/rs2 muxes, fwd inputs and the alu_a /
   alu_b select; alu gets opa/opb directly (alu.sv interface and ALTOPS arms untouched);
   branch compare uses rs1_v/rs2_v; jalr_sum = rs1_v + imm (still the load/store address
   adder feeding the dedicated mem_addr EX/MEM register from r4s1); btgt / pc4 / mp_seq /
   mp_btgt come from ox_t flops; muldiv.a/b come from rs1_v/rs2_v (stable while busy
   because O/X holds), so the md_a/md_b RVFI patch-up can stay as is or be dropped.
   Redirect / BTB-training / registered redir_q logic is otherwise unchanged. It also
   exports x_result and the post-trap reg_write for OF's dist-1 forward.

4. Hazard / forward control moves to flop-fed compares in OF:
     load_use = x.mem_read && x.rd != 0 && (x.rd == of.rs1 || x.rd == of.rs2)
     stall_id (hold D/O + pop nothing) = dmem_stall || load_use || ex_busy
     hold O/X = dmem_stall || ex_busy; bubble into O/X on load_use or redirect (when not
     held), exactly mirroring today's flush_id/stall_id rules one stage later; D/O flushes
     on redirect as today. This also removes today's longest hazard cone (imem BSRAM ->
     queue bypass -> rs compare -> stall_id -> consume -> queue pointers) because the
     load-use compare no longer reads the queue head instruction.
   redir_q stays sticky while stall as today; every upstream register (queue, D/O, O/X)
   is flushed in the first non-stalled redir_q cycle and the instruction in EX during
   redir_q is killed by ex_valid as before.

5. mem_stage.sv exposes m_result (and the post-trap reg_write) combinationally, and
   MEM/WB stores a single wb_data flop (mem_to_reg ? load_data : alu_result) in place of
   read_data / alu_result; wb_stage passes it through. RVFI rd_wdata comes from wb_data.
   RVFI-only payload (instr, pc, rs addrs, rs vals, mem info) is carried through the new
   stage; it is pruned from the timed netlist so it costs nothing in Fmax.

Cycle model: dependent ALU->ALU, ALU->branch, ALU->store, load->use (1 bubble) and
muldiv timing are unchanged versus today; the only added latency is +1 cycle on every
branch/JALR mispredict (EX resolves one stage later) and +1 stage of pipeline fill, so
CPI goes ~1.437 -> ~1.465 (+1.9%).

Path accounting after the change (all start at flops or the BSRAM output):
  EX loop   opa/opb flop -> 32b add/sub -> result mux tail -> late forward LUT -> operand
            flop: ~0.7 + 0.8 + 3.5 + ~3-4.9 + 1.2 + 0.4 = 9.6-11.5 ns (87-104 MHz),
            no change needed to the ALU tail; r4s0's one-hot tail would take it to ~8.5 ns.
  EX branch rs1_v/rs2_v flop -> 32b eq/lt -> mispredict select (2-3 LUTs) -> redir_q /
            redir_target_q / BTB write: ~8-9 ns.
  OF        BSRAM (2.3) + bypass/x0 (2.5) + fwd (1.8) + opb select (1.0) + setup: ~8.6 ns;
            dmem BSRAM (2.3-3) + load align/sext (3.6) + fwd LUT (1.2) + setup: ~9-10 ns.
  ID        queue head -> decoder / imm_gen -> D/O flops (no adder/compare now): ~7.5 ns.
Expected Fmax 80-95 MHz at ~+1.9% CPI, i.e. fitness ~175-205 (+10% to +30%); even the
pessimistic 76 MHz case clears the +4.6% acceptance bar (needs >71.5 MHz at the new CPI).

Risks and mitigations. (a) Formal: adds ~500 FFs and one stage of BMC depth but no new
memory/bypass structure (unlike the r4s2 timeout, which bundled a fetch bypass, 64-entry
BTB and RAS); retirement latency from reset grows by one cycle, well inside the check
depths. (b) Forwarding correctness under dmem_stall, ex_busy (muldiv) and sticky redirect:
O/X and D/O capture only when they advance, forwards from MEM use post-trap reg_write,
and cocotb/cosim exercise it (test_pipeline.py already covers EX->EX, MEM->EX, load-use,
traps, random i/d stalls). (c) If the dmem-data -> align -> forward LUT -> operand flop
path ends up co-critical, the fallback is to forward only the aligned word case from MEM
and take byte/half loads through MEM/WB one cycle later with a 2-bubble load-use for
sub-word loads only.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-002-r5s1 (improvement, +31.32%): After five single-cone trims of the shared EX operand prefix (BSRAM tC2Q -> write-first bypass -> forward compare/mux -> alu_a/alu_b select) each stalled at ~5-10%, adding an OF stage so EX starts at operand flops (post-forward `rs1_v`/`rs2_v` plus pre-selected `opa`/`opb`, the EX result crossing exactly one late 2:1 LUT into them, MEM load data forwarded combinationally into the operand flops so load-use stays 1 bubble, forward compares on flop-fed rd/rs fields only, and the r4s1 `btgt`/`pc4`/`mp_*` precompute moved from ID to OF) reached 208.78 and landed at the top of its +10-30% projection for a ~+1.9% CPI cost (mispredict penalty +1), so when a prefix is shared by every cone and trimming it is capped, move it into its own stage rather than shortening it, and keep the cycle cost near zero by forwarding into the new stage's input flops instead of through a new pipeline register.

title: One-cycle mispredict recovery: one-shot redirect pulse fetches the target in the redirect cycle
motivation:
Predictor accuracy work is capped: replaying the CoreMark ISS trace (see
LESSONS r3s2 / r4s2) the champion's 16-entry BTB has ~82k mispredicts
(54.7k cond. branches, 13.5k JAL, 13.8k never-trained returns), each costing
2 bubbles = ~164k of 4.22M cycles (3.9%). A perfect predictor is therefore
worth < 3.9% (below the 4.6% bar), and larger/associative BTBs, RAS or
history tables each recover only ~0.5-1% while growing the state that the
riscv-formal BMC must unroll (r4s2 timed out in formal). The remaining
lever in this category is the COST per mispredict, which hits every one of
the 82k mispredicts (and every future one, whatever the predictor), and
needs no new predictor state at all.
Today: EX detects the mispredict in cycle t, redir_q is set for t+1, in
t+1 only the flush happens and fpc <= redirect_target, and the correct-path
instruction is first on the imem bus in t+2 (EX at t+3 instead of t+1).
The registered redirect was a big Fmax win (r2s2) and must stay registered;
but the *fetch* of the target does not have to wait for the pc register to
be loaded -- redir_target_q is already a flop in cycle t+1.
Fresh Gowin timing (65.4 MHz option 0, 14 logic levels) shows the ID cone
redir_q -> fetch_queue head -> decoder/imm_gen -> mp_btgt and the EX->BTB
training cone are co-critical with the ALU cone, so the change is shaped to
keep both neutral: everything new is flop-selected (no imem_ready /
dmem_ready / EX compare in the new muxes).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Split the registered redirect into two flops with different jobs, then let
fetch use the redirect target in the redirect cycle, saving 1 cycle per
mispredict (82k -> ~64k net cycles after the 22% chance that the imem bus is
not ready in that cycle, i.e. ~1.5-2% of cycles, with zero new predictor
state and no change to which instructions are predicted or verified).

1. ex_stage.sv: keep redir_q / redir_target_q exactly as they are for their
   existing duties (ex_valid kill of the wrong-path instruction in EX,
   EX/MEM bubble, sticky while a dmem stall holds EX). Add a one-shot flop
     redir_go <= !redir_q && mispredict && !stall && !ex_busy;
   (same condition that sets redir_q the first time; reset to 0). It is high
   for exactly the first redirect cycle even if redir_q then stays sticky
   because of a dmem stall. Export it (output redirect_go) next to
   redirect / redirect_target.

2. if_stage.sv: add input redirect_go. Fetch address becomes
     fetch_pc = redirect_go ? redirect_target : pc;   // two flops + flop select
     imem_addr = fetch_pc;
   The BTB lookup (core.sv already feeds it io_imemAddr[19:2]), in_e.pc,
   next_pc and pc+4 all use fetch_pc. pc update priority becomes
     reset -> RESET_PC; fire -> next_pc (from fetch_pc);
     else if redirect_go -> redirect_target;
   (If imem_ready is low in the redirect cycle we simply fall back to
   today's behaviour: pc <= redirect_target and fetch next cycle.)
   The old sticky `redirect` input is no longer used by the fetch side; fetch
   runs normally during sticky dmem-stall cycles (ID is held by stall_id so
   nothing is consumed and the queue just fills with correct-path entries).

3. fetch_queue.sv: flush input is now the one-shot redirect_go. In that cycle
   the queue is treated as empty with a fresh bypass:
     base pointers = 0 (wr_ptr/rd_ptr/count reset),
     head_e     = (empty || flush) ? in_e : mem[rd_ptr],
     head_valid = flush ? in_valid : (!empty || in_valid),
     fire       = in_valid && (flush || !full),
     mem write address = flush ? 0 : wr_ptr, and next pointers/count =
     base + fire - pop, so if ID consumes the bypassed target instruction
     the queue ends empty, and if ID is stalled (dmem_stall in the first
     redirect cycle) the entry is parked in slot 0 (wr_ptr=1,count=1).
   All selects are driven by flops (redir_go, count==0), never by an input
   pin or the EX compare.

4. hazard_unit.sv / core.sv: the instruction in EX during the redirect
   cycle is wrong-path, so mask the load-use compare with the sticky
   redirect (redir_q): load_use_hazard &= !redirect. Remove `redirect` from
   flush_id (the target instruction must be captured into ID/EX in the
   redirect cycle instead of being flushed):
     flush_id = load_use_hazard && !dmem_stall && !ex_busy.
   During sticky redirect cycles that follow a dmem stall nothing changes
   (stall_id holds ID/EX; ex_valid/EX-MEM bubble still use redir_q, the
   wrong-path instruction is overwritten when the stall releases).
   core.sv wires redirect_go to if_stage/fetch_queue and keeps redirect
   (redir_q) for hazard_unit.

Correctness: every instruction is still verified in EX against its own
prediction, rvfi order/pc continuity is unchanged (same architectural
instruction stream, just earlier), and the symbolic imem the formal flow
provides enters ID in the redirect cycle exactly like it already does in
the empty-queue bypass case. No BTB/RAS/queue growth, so BMC depth cost
should stay close to the champion's.

Why this slot: it attacks the same ~3.9% cycle pool as a better predictor
but multiplies every mispredict by 1 cycle instead of trying to remove
mispredicts that are mostly data-dependent. If it lands cycle-neutral on
Fmax (selects are flop-driven, fetch_pc mux adds one LUT level to the short
pc->BTB->next_pc loop, not to the 14-level EX cone), it is also a base for
later BTB/RAS growth because each remaining mispredict is half as costly.

Add redirect_go input; fetch_pc = redirect_go ? redirect_target : pc drives imem_addr, in_e.pc, BTB lookup, pc+4 and next_pc; pc update priority fire > redirect_go > hold; stop gating fetch with the sticky redirect.

Flush becomes the one-shot redirect_go with a fresh bypass: base pointers reset to 0, head_e/head_valid select the incoming entry in the flush cycle, fire allowed in the flush cycle, write slot 0 on flush so a stalled ID parks the target instruction.
Mask load_use_hazard with the sticky redirect (EX holds a wrong-path instruction) and drop redirect from flush_id so the target instruction is captured into ID/EX in the redirect cycle.
Wire redirect_go from ex_stage to if_stage; keep the sticky redirect for hazard_unit.

Flush becomes the one-shot redirect_go with a fresh bypass: base pointers reset to 0, head_e/head_valid select the incoming entry in the flush cycle, fire allowed in the flush cycle, write slot 0 on flush so a stalled ID parks the target instruction.
Mask load_use_hazard with the sticky redirect (EX holds a wrong-path instruction) and drop redirect from flush_id so the target instruction is captured into ID/EX in the redirect cycle.
Wire redirect_go from ex_stage to if_stage; keep the sticky redirect for hazard_unit.

title: Decode-into-flops for the three co-critical late-select cones: registered is_md (1-LUT ex_busy), one-hot load-lane selects (3-level m_result), jump/M result folded into the ALU
motivation:
`make timing` on the r5s1 champion (87.6/89.9/89.9 MHz) shows the top-5 paths all at 16.69-16.71 ns
(data path ~11.37 ns after the 5.33 ns clock-tree offset): the placer has balanced THREE cones,
so trimming any one alone is capped (the r2s1/r3s0 lesson). All three are made of decode work that
sits behind a late value and could be done a stage earlier in flops:
(A) path 1: O/X.ctrl.alu_op flop (fanout 128) -> muldiv is_muldiv range-compare LUT -> ex_stage
    req/ex_busy LUT (fanout 56) -> muldiv `start` LUT -> id_stage stall LUT (fanout 131) ->
    rs1_addr mux -> regfile LUT-RAM RAD -> 3 bypass/x0 LUTs -> rs1_val flop. 10 cells, the first
    three are pure "alu_op in [MUL..REMU]" decode and ex_busy fan-out.
(B) path 2: dmem BSRAM DO (tC2Q 2.26 ns) -> `shifted` 2 LUTs (addr[1:0]*8 barrel) -> sign/zero
    extend LUT (fanout 24) -> mem_to_reg mux 2 LUTs (= m_result, 5 levels) -> OF early1 / rs1_d /
    opa_d (3 more levels, because m_result is routed through the shared early1 mux) -> opa flop.
    9 cells. Every select here (addr[1:0], mem_width, mem_sext, mem_to_reg) is known in EX.
(C) paths 3-5: opa/opb flop -> ALU (adder carry / barrel shifter) -> alu result mux ->
    x_result = is_muldiv ? md_result : is_jump ? pc4 : alu_result -> OF forward LUT -> flops.
    The two x_result select levels do nothing but pick a source that is already a flop.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Cycle-identical re-timing of the three cones; no M-op / ALTOPS / RVFI semantics change.
(A) is_md flop. of_stage registers `is_md = in.valid && alu_op in [ALU_MUL..ALU_REMU]` in the O/X
    control block (cleared by reset/bubble with valid/ctrl/rd, loaded when !hold; tied 0 under
    RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS exactly as ex_stage's is_muldiv is today). ex_stage drops the range compare:
    is_muldiv = in.is_md, muldiv req = in.is_md && !redirect, so ex_busy = is_md_q & !redir_q &
    !done_q is ONE LUT of flops. That removes ~2 LUT levels (~3 ns incl. routing) from the
    ex_busy -> stall_id/hold_ox/bubble_ox/consume cones (O/X ~250-flop hold, D/O enable,
    regfile-address mux, fetch-queue pop, EX/MEM bubble, redir_q, BTB tr_en).
(B) one-hot load lanes + two-late-input forwarding. In EX compute, from in.ctrl.{mem_width,
    mem_sext,mem_to_reg} and jalr_sum[1:0] (2-bit add of flops), registered one-hot selects carried
    in ex_mem_t: sel_alu (=!mem_to_reg), d-lane selects for bits[7:0] (4: lane0..lane3 incl. half@2),
    for bits[15:8] (d[i] for word/half@0, d[i+16] for half@2, else fill), word-select for bits

    are left alone. In of_stage, restructure the operand muxes so BOTH late sources cross one LUT:
    opa_d = sel_x ? x_result : sel_m ? m_result : base_a, with base_a = (is_auipc|is_jump) ? pc

(C) fold x_result's source mux into the ALU. JAL/JALR: of_stage forces opa=pc, opb=4 when
    ctrl.is_jump (alu_op is already ADD for jumps; the target uses the separate jalr_sum/btgt
    adders), so alu_result IS pc+4 and the `is_jump ? pc4` level disappears. M ops: alu.sv with
    HAS_MULDIV=0 already outputs 0 for MUL..REMU, so x_result = alu_result | (is_md ? md_result : 0)

    output plus one OR instead of a 2-level priority mux, shaving ~1 level from the 3 ALU->operand
    paths.
Expected: A -2 levels, B -4 levels, C -1 level, so the new worst cone is the ALU shifter/adder
(previously 9-10 cells) minus one level: data path ~11.4 -> ~10.2 ns (~+10% Fmax), derated to ~+8%
for placement noise since the three cones were balanced by the placer. If time allows, also hoist
the (ox_mem_read && ox_rd != 0) term of the load-use compare into a registered O/X bit.
