title: Dual-bank regfile read (head bank + held bank) with registered bank select, taking the late stall off the regfile address; pre-decoded M-op flag
motivation:
The r5s1 champion (208.78 = 89.9 MHz x 2.32 CoreMark/MHz) reports its worst path as
O/X ctrl.alu_op flop -> u_muldiv (is_muldiv compare, req, busy) -> u_ex (ex_busy) ->
hazard stall_id -> u_id rs1_addr/rs2_addr 2:1 mux -> u_rf, 10 logic cells, 16.7 ns arrival,
roughly 1.4 ns per cell, i.e. dominated by fanout routing. This is the one remaining cone
where a late control signal (stall_id = dmem_stall | load_use | ex_busy, fanout in the
hundreds because it also drives every D/O clock enable) is used as a DATA-path select
in front of a memory address pin:
    rs1_addr = stall ? reg_q.rs1_addr : in.instr[19:15]
The mux exists only so a held D/O instruction can re-read the regfile every cycle it is
held and so pick up producers that retired from WB during the hold. The OF-stage forwards
cover only EX/MEM/WB, so a single extra forward leg cannot replace the re-read for
multi-cycle holds (dmem stall + load-use + a 35-cycle divide can all hold D/O). The address
select is therefore needed, but it does NOT need to be resolved before the memory: both
candidate reads can be issued every cycle and the choice made after the read from a
one-cycle-delayed copy of the same decision, which is a plain flop.
Lessons from r2s1/r3s0/r4s1/r5s1: single-cone trims stall at 5-10% when other cones sit
right behind, but removing a whole class of late-select -> memory-address dependence (r4s1
for dmem_addr, r5s1 for the operand prefix) paid off, and r5s1 left this stall -> regfile
cone as the limiter. The next-worst cones (ALU -> x_result -> late 2:1 into O/X operand
flops, EX compare -> redir_target_q, MEM load align -> m_result -> O/X) are one adder or
one BSRAM read plus 3-5 LUTs deep from flops and should sit around 14-15 ns arrival.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the regfile read address a pure function of flops/queue-head bits with no dependence
on stall_id, by splitting the read into two banks and selecting after the read.
(1) reg_file.sv: add a second pair of read ports (bank B) with its own address inputs and
    data outputs. Bank A is addressed by the fetch-queue head (in.instr[19:15] / [24:20]),
    exactly as today minus the stall mux. Bank B is addressed by the D/O register's own
    rs1_addr/rs2_addr flops (the held instruction). Both banks share the single write port
    and both keep the same write-first bypass and x0 gate, each against its own address
    (bank B's compare is flop-fed). Storage is duplicated (the array is declared once per
    bank so each maps to its own memory) and written identically, so both banks always
    hold the same architectural state; reset clears both.
(2) id_stage.sv: drop the `stall ? reg_q.rsX_addr : in.instr` mux. Register both banks'
    read data into separate rs?_val_a / rs?_val_b registers next to the read (kept
    directly at the memory output so the output register is still absorbed into the
    BSRAM), and register stall into a one-bit stall_q flop. D/O's effective rs1_val /
    rs2_val seen by OF is `stall_q ? rs?_val_b : rs?_val_a`, i.e. the held instruction's
    re-read when the previous cycle was a hold, otherwise the freshly captured head read.
    This is exactly the value the current mux-then-read scheme produces, so the
    architectural behaviour and the cycle count are unchanged (pure re-timing). A flush
    cannot coincide with a stall (flush_id already requires !dmem_stall && !ex_busy and a
    load-use bubble cannot be pending with redirect), so stall_q is 0 after a flush and
    bank A is selected for the NOP head.
(3) of_stage.sv / id_stage.sv: the extra 2:1 (stall_q select) sits on the BSRAM-output ->
    early1/early2 path, which starts at the BSRAM tC2Q and goes through only the 3:1
    forward mux and the opa/opb select before the O/X flops, so it has ample slack
    compared to the x_result late forward. Fold stall_q into the lowest-priority leg of
    the early1/early2 mux so it costs at most one LUT.
(4) Shave the other half of the old worst path: pre-decode `is_muldiv`
    (alu_op in [ALU_MUL, ALU_REMU], forced 0 under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS) in of_stage as a
    ctrl/O-X flop and use it in ex_stage and muldiv.req instead of the 5-bit range
    compare on in.ctrl.alu_op. ex_busy then becomes `ox.is_md && !redir_q && valid &&
    !done_q`: one LUT from flops instead of ~3, and the stall cone feeding the D/O/O-X
    clock enables gets shorter too.
Expected effect: the 10-cell stall -> regfile-address path disappears (stall now ends at
D/O CE pins and one stall_q flop), worth roughly 1.5-2.5 ns on the critical path; the
next cones (ALU forward loop, redirect target, MEM load-align forward) bound the gain at
about 8-12% Fmax. IPC is unchanged. Cost: +2 regfile memories (bank B copies), +~70
flops/LUTs for bank outputs and the select; formal stays tractable because there is no new
control state beyond one flop (stall_q) and an extra memory read with the same write port.

title: Architectural return-address stack (is_ret BTB bit, EX-updated) plus 32-entry BTB to cut ret/JAL/aliasing mispredicts
motivation:
Mispredict recovery is now 3 cycles (registered redir_q + ID/OF/EX refill) and,
because fetch is bandwidth-bound by the ~22% imem stalls, each mispredict wastes
three fetch slots. The champion BTB still takes ~82k mispredicts on the 10-iteration
CoreMark trace (log.jsonl r3s2 finding: 54.7k cond. branches, 13.8k returns,
13.5k JAL, 21 other JALR), i.e. ~246k of ~4.3M cycles (~5.7%). Two classes are
purely structural, not data-dependent, and therefore removable:
  * 13.8k returns: JALR is never trained into the BTB, so every `ret` falls through
    to pc+4 and pays the full 3-cycle penalty (~41k cycles, ~1.0%).
  * 13.5k JAL (+ a share of the cond-branch misses): a 16-entry direct-mapped BTB
    indexed by pc[5:2] thrashes on CoreMark's hot code spread over many 64B windows;
    capacity/alias evictions force re-learning (~40k cycles for JAL alone, ~0.9%).
The remaining cond-branch mispredicts are mostly data-dependent (CRC bit tests, list
compares, state machine) and no predictor of this size fixes them, so this
hypothesis targets only the removable classes and does it without touching the
Fmax-critical EX/OF cones: the RAS is updated in EX from flop-fed fields only and
read at fetch, so it is a pure function of registered state.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
1) Return-address stack. Add a 4-entry, 18-bit (pc[19:2]) *architectural* RAS inside
   btb.sv (or a small ras.sv), updated only from EX when the instruction advances
   (ex_valid && !stall && !ex_busy): push pc4[19:2] when a JAL/JALR has rd==x1
   (instr[11:7]==1, or x5), pop when a return retires (JALR, rd==x0, rs1==x1/x5,
   taken from in.instr, flop-fed). Because only correct-path instructions advance
   out of EX (ex_valid already excludes the wrong-path leftover while redir_q is
   set), the stack never needs speculative-checkpoint/repair. Depth counter
   saturates; pop on empty is a no-op. Fetch reads `ras_top` (a register mux).
2) is_ret BTB flag. One extra bit per BTB entry (flop vector next to valid_q).
   JALR returns are allocated into the BTB when they advance from EX (tr_en gains an
   `is_ret` term; tag written, counter set to 3, is_ret=1; target field is don't-care).
   At fetch, hit && is_ret => pred_taken = 1 and pred_target = ras_top (one extra 2:1
   on the BTB read path, still pc-register-only: no imem_data dependence). Ordinary
   branch/JAL training rewrites is_ret=0. The existing EX verify-everything check
   (mp_jalr compares the full JALR sum against pred_full) is unchanged, so a stale RAS
   top (call not yet advanced when the ret was fetched, nested back-to-back rets,
   aliased BTB hit, the formal flow's symbolic imem) just costs a redirect, never
   correctness. Ret allocation/pop do NOT need jalr_sum (the target is not stored), so
   the JALR adder stays out of the BTB-training cone, which earlier lessons say must
   be preserved.
3) 32-entry direct-mapped BTB: index pc[6:2], tag pc[19:7] (13b), same
   tt/ctr LUT-RAM arrays doubled and valid/is_ret as 32 flops. Direct-mapped only (no
   2-way) so the fetch-side lookup depth is unchanged (single tag compare). The lesson
   from r4s2 (64-entry BTB + RAS + redirect-cycle fetch bypass broke formal wall-clock)
   is respected by NOT bundling the redirect bypass and by keeping the BTB at 32
   entries with the tag/target storage as memories; if formal wall-clock is a concern
   the implementer may keep BTB at 16 entries and ship only the RAS (the RAS alone
   is the bulk of the structural win) -- fall back, do not drop the RAS.
Expected cycle effect: returns ~13.8k x 3 cycles * ~80% hit (shallow call/ret pairs
and leaf calls that return before the call leaves EX miss) ~ -33k cycles (~0.8%),
JAL/cond capacity misses from the 2x BTB ~ -40..60k cycles (~1-1.4%), total ~2-3%.
Fmax should be neutral: the new logic is one extra mux on the BTB read -> next_pc
path (not near the 16.7 ns muldiv/hazard/regfile limiter) and an extra 2x BTB
LUT-RAM (+~100 LUT4, +~40 FF, well inside the 10k budget).
Honest caveat: predictor-only gains are capped (perfect prediction is ~5.7% of
cycles), so acceptance likely depends on this landing at the top of range or on
placement luck; it is cycle-only, low-risk, and formal-safe by construction.

Decode call (JAL/JALR rd==x1/x5) and return (JALR rd==x0, rs1==x1/x5, from in.instr) once, gate with ex_valid && !stall && !ex_busy, export ras_push/ras_pop/ras_push_addr (pc4[19:2]) and tr_is_ret; extend tr_en so returns train the BTB without depending on jalr_sum or the late branch compare.
Wire the new RAS push/pop/tr_is_ret signals between ex_stage and btb; no change to the top-level IO or RVFI.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-003-r6s2 (improvement, +11.36%): A 4-entry architectural RAS (pushed/popped only by instructions advancing out of EX, `is_ret` BTB flag, ret target read from the `ras_q[0]` flop) plus a 32-entry direct-mapped BTB passed formal and scored +11.36%, which exceeds the ~5.7% perfect-predictor cycle ceiling, so most of the gain must be Fmax from registering the BTB training request (`tr_en_q`/`tr_*_q`, write lands one cycle after the CTI leaves EX) that took the late EX branch compare off the 32-entry write-decode fan-out (the EX->BTB training cone r6s0 flagged as co-critical); this also suggests r4s2's formal timeout came from the redirect-cycle fetch bypass rather than the RAS or BTB size, so when a "cycle-only" predictor change beats its cycle ceiling, credit the timing side-effect and re-use the register-the-late-update trick before projecting predictor gains.

title: Stall-free regfile read address: recirculate dist-3 forward into D/O rs vals on hold, plus pre-decoded is_md flop for ex_busy
motivation:
The champion's reported worst path (r6s2, arrival 17.5 ns, 10 cells) is
O/X.ctrl.alu_op -> is_muldiv range decode -> muldiv busy -> hazard stall_id ->
id_stage rs1_addr/rs2_addr hold mux -> regfile async read -> write-first bypass
compare/mux -> D/O rs?_val flops. Every term of that cone is downstream of the late
`stall`: the stall selects the regfile *address*, and the write-first bypass compare
(w_addr == rs1_addr) and x0 check are computed on that muxed address, so the stall
sits in front of the LUT-RAM read, a 5-bit compare and two select muxes (~4-5 LUT
levels after stall). Earlier single-cone trims (r6s1 dual-bank read: +1.9%) paid
regfile area for a registered select; the other co-critical cones (EX->BTB training,

levels after stall). Earlier single-cone trims (r6s1 dual-bank read: +1.9%) paid
regfile area for a registered select; the other co-critical cones (EX->BTB training,
which r6s2 already cut by registering the training request) are no longer the

hypothesis.hypothesis:
1) Make the regfile read addresses unconditional: rs1_addr = in.instr[19:15],
   rs2_addr = in.instr[24:20] (no `stall ? reg_q.rs?_addr : ...` mux). The write-first
   bypass compare and x0 check then depend only on the queue-head instruction, never on
   stall_id.
2) Replace the "re-read with the held address" refresh by a recirculation of the one
   forward source that ages out: while D/O is held, the rs?_val flops capture
     stall ? (wb_fwd_rs? ? mem_wb.wb_data : reg_q.rs?_val) : regfile_read_data
   where wb_fwd_rs? = the forward_unit dist-3 flag for the held instruction
   (w_reg_write && w_rd != 0 && w_rd == reg_q.rs?_addr; flop-fed). Only flop sources
   (wb_data, the existing rs?_val) are recirculated, never m_result/x_result, so the
   MEM load-align cone is not lengthened. Correctness: a producer P that is in
   EX/MEM/WB when the consumer C is captured is forwarded at dist 1/2/3 while C waits in
   OF; the only way P is lost is leaving WB (regfile written, no longer forwarded) while
   C is still held, and in that exact held cycle P is at dist 3 and its wb_data is
   recirculated into rs?_val. Producers pass WB in program order, so rs?_val only ever
   takes progressively younger values and the dist-1/2/3 > rs_val priority in OF is

title: Word-granular direct-mapped instruction cache in front of the imem bus (break the 0.78 word/cycle fetch floor)
motivation:
CPI on CoreMark is ~1.44 (4.226M timed cycles / 2.92M instructions) against
a hard fetch floor of ~1.28: imem is one 32-bit port and ~22% of fetch
cycles return nothing regardless of the address (LESSONS r5s1). The
decoupled fetch queue (r3s2) already overlaps those bubbles with backend
stalls and the BTB/RAS (r6s2) already removed most mispredict loss, so
every remaining front-end lever is capped by the bus itself. The only way
under the floor is to stop asking the bus for words the core has already
fetched. Four previous structural/timing attempts since r5s1 all targeted
Fmax cones and stalled at the co-critical EX/OF/regfile cones (~16.7-17.5
ns); this hypothesis is orthogonal: it adds cycles-per-iteration headroom
on the fetch side, away from those cones.

Measured before proposing (Verilator cosim of the real RTL, CoreMark 2K,
--istall --dstall, timed bracket only; CRCs + "Correct operation
validated" all pass with the cache in place):
  baseline (r6s2 RTL)              4,225,873 cycles
  perfect imem (no istall) bound   3,768,252  (+12.1% ceiling)
  128-entry word cache (IW=7)      3,879,957  (+8.9%)
  256-entry word cache (IW=8)      3,805,587  (+11.0%)   <- proposed
  512-entry word cache (IW=9)      3,789,353  (+11.5%)
Trace replay of the ISS stream: 1670 unique code words, direct-mapped hit
rate 83% @128, 94% @256, 97% @512. So a 256-entry cache already captures
~91% of everything an infinitely good imem could give.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add rtl/icache.sv: a word-granular direct-mapped instruction cache,
256 entries indexed by pc[9:2] (parameter IW=8), each entry {tag =
pc[19:IW+2] (10b), instr[31:0]} in an async-read / sync-write array (same
style as the BTB tt_arr), plus a flop valid vector reset to 0 (so the
array itself needs no reset). The lookup is a pure function of the fetch
pc register: independent of imem_data and of every ID/EX stall, the same
property that kept the BTB cheap in timing.

if_stage.sv changes only the definition of "the bus delivered an
instruction this cycle":
  ic_hit     = valid[idx] && tag match at pc
  in_e.instr = ic_hit ? ic_data : imem_data
  fetch_queue.in_valid = imem_ready || ic_hit
  icache write enable  = fire && !ic_hit   (data = imem_data, index/tag = pc)
fetch_queue, the BTB prediction that rides with each entry, the registered
redirect, EX verification and all hazard logic are untouched; pc/next_pc
already advance on `fire`, which already keys on in_valid. A miss behaves
exactly like today's fetch (wait for imem_ready, 22% stall chance); there
is no line fill, no refill FSM and no extra bus traffic. A hit ignores
imem_ready, so the queue refills after load-use / dmem / muldiv /
mispredict bubbles without re-rolling the stall dice. Stores never touch
the cache (CoreMark has no self-modifying code; FENCE.I is a NOP in this
core already).

Formal: the cache returns the exact bus word seen earlier for that pc, EX
still verifies every fetched instruction against its own prediction and
RVFI reports the instruction actually executed, so the symbolic-imem view
stays sound (a hit just supplies an older symbolic word; wrapper_si ties
imem_ready to 1 so only the hit path changes). To keep BMC tractable (r4s2:
formal wall-clock is a hard budget) shrink the entry count under
`ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS (the macro alu.sv/ex_stage.sv already rely on;
checks_si.cfg defines it) to IW=2 (4 entries), so the formal flow carries
only a few words of cache state while synthesis/cosim get 256 entries.

Timing/area expectation: the new cone is pc flop -> array read -> 10-bit
tag compare -> 2:1 instr select / in_valid (~5-6 ns) feeding the fetch
queue write data, head bypass and regfile address mux; today that input
arrives from an early flop. This sits well below the 17 ns EX-side cones,
so Fmax should be roughly unchanged (budget a few percent loss for placer
noise / extra fan-in on head_valid). Area: roughly +600-900 LUT4 if mapped
to LUT-RAM (or 1-2 BSRAM if Gowin absorbs the pc register), no DSP. If the
front-end cone turns out to be critical, fall back to IW=7 (+8.9% cycles,
one mux level less) rather than adding pipeline stages.

lesson: - 2026-10-01 hyp-20261001-002-r7s1 (regression, -6.29%): The 256-entry word-granular icache delivered its cosim cycle gain (4.226M -> 3.806M, CRCs pass, ~+11% CoreMark/MHz) yet scored 217.88 vs 232.5, which implies Fmax fell ~15% (98 -> ~83 MHz) instead of the "few percent" budgeted, most likely because `ic_hit` (256x42b async array read + 10b tag compare off the pc flop) now gates `in_valid`/`fire` and so fans out into the queue push, pc/next_pc advance and the cache write enable as a late control signal rather than just fetch-queue data; imem-independence is what kept the BTB cheap but does not make a large async-read array timing-free, so before adding fetch-side storage whose hit signal feeds `fire`, run `make timing` on the cone (none was run here) and weigh the cycle-only upside against a double-digit Fmax risk.

title: Per-BTB-entry local branch history + shared 2-bit PHT (replaces the per-entry counter), 64-entry BTB
motivation:
Trace-driven model (RV32IM ISS on coremark.elf, 2.94M insns, 532k conditional branches, BTB
model identical to btb.sv incl. a 3-4 instruction training delay) shows where the remaining
predictor loss is: ~58k mispredicts total, of which ~48k are conditional branches, ~8.4k JAL
(BTB capacity/aliasing), ~1.2k returns. Each costs 3 cycles (registered redir_q + refill) so
the whole predictor-addressable pool is ~4% of the 4.23M cycles. Findings that pick the design:
  * gshare / global history does NOT help (gshare h=2..8 on 512-4096 entries: 42k-58k, no better
    than bimodal 40k): CoreMark's hard branches are data-dependent, but its loop/state branches
    are strongly *per-branch periodic*.
  * per-branch LOCAL history helps a lot: an ideal local-history predictor with h=8 drops cond
    mispredicts 48k -> 21k. Realisable form (history kept in the BTB entry, shared 1024x2b PHT
    indexed by {hist[7:0], pc[3:2]} xor-folded): 32.4k at 32 BTB entries, 28.4k at 64 entries,
    27.7k at 128; adding a 3-4 instruction update delay (training lands after EX) changes it by
    <0.1k, so no speculative-history repair is needed.
  * BTB growth 32 -> 64 entries removes another ~1.7k JAL + ~0.7k ret mispredicts.
Net: ~48.2k+8.4k+1.2k -> ~28.4k+6.7k+0.5k, i.e. ~22k fewer mispredicts = ~66k cycles (~1.5%)
at unchanged Fmax. The gain is modest because the ceiling is low (a perfect predictor is only
~4%), so this is proposed as the highest-yield *predictor-only* angle, not a large step.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
In btb.sv replace the 2-bit saturating counter array (ctr_arr) by an 8-bit local history array
(hist_arr, same async-read/sync-write LUT-RAM style, indexed by pc[IW+1:2]) and add a shared
pattern-history table pht_arr[1024] of 2-bit counters (LUT-RAM, async read, sync write).
Fetch: pht index = {hist[7:0], pc[3:2]} folded to 10 bits ({hist, 2b pc} -> 10 bits, no hash
logic needed); pred_taken = hit && (is_ret || pht[idx][1]). The lookup is still a pure
function of the pc register (BTB LUT-RAM -> PHT LUT-RAM -> pred_taken -> next_pc mux), never of
imem_data. Entries allocate (taken CTI, history <- 1 or all-ones for JAL so JAL always
predicts taken via a dedicated is_jal/always-taken bit, kept in the existing is_ret-style flop
array) exactly as today. Training reuses the registered tr_*_q request: the history observed at
fetch (pred_ctr widens from 2 to 8 bits and rides down fetch_queue / D/O / O/X like the
existing pred_ctr) is handed back, the PHT counter at {hist, pc[3:2]} is updated with the
outcome, and the BTB entry history becomes {hist[6:0], taken}; not-taken CTIs that hit still
update (existing wr_ctr condition). Grow the BTB from 32 to 64 entries (IW=6, tag 12 bits);
formal tractability is guarded by keeping RAS at 4 and not adding any fetch-bypass (the r4s2
timeout came from the redirect-cycle bypass). EX still verifies every instruction against its
own prediction, so aliased/stale PHT or BTB entries only cost a redirect, never correctness;
the EX compare cone, redir_q and the training registers are untouched. Cycle-model estimate:
~22k fewer mispredicts x 3 cycles = ~66k of 4.23M cycles (+1.5%); the second-level PHT read adds
one LUT-RAM stage to the fetch cone (~1-1.5 ns) which currently has slack versus the
stall->regfile and ALU->x_result cones that set Fmax, so Fmax should be unchanged.

title: Cycle-identical co-cone cut: post-flop redirect-target select, pre-decoded is_md, jump PC+4 folded into the ALU
motivation:
Fmax (98.25 MHz, ~10.2 ns period) is the only lever left for micro_opt: the
perfect-predictor, mul-latency and load-use ceilings are all low-single-digit
cycle gains, below the 4.6% acceptance bar. Prior single-cone trims (r2s1, r3s0,
r6s1, r7s0) each landed at +2..7% because the top-N endpoints are bunched
(r6s2 worst path 17.5 ns on O/X ctrl.alu_op -> muldiv busy -> stall_id -> regfile
BSRAM address; r7s0, with that cone gone, only reached 100.4 MHz because the next
path, O/X rs2_v -> 32-bit branch compare carry chain -> 30-bit select -> redir_target_q,
sat at 16.3 ns with 37 cells). The branch-compare cone is currently shaped as
carry chain -> late 2:1 select fanned out to ~30 redir_target_q flops, and the
EX result cone as ALU case mux -> is_jump ? pc4 -> is_muldiv ? md_result -> OF forward
LUT. These are shaped by late-signal fan-out and extra mux levels, not by
irreducible arithmetic, so cutting them in the same change is cycle-identical and
should move the median Fmax rather than just one placement's worst path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three cycle-identical edits that each remove a LUT level / a wide fan-out from a
co-critical cone, bundled so the Fmax floor moves instead of one endpoint:
(1) Redirect target select after the flop. Today redir_target_q <= pc_next_w, where
pc_next_w = (is_branch && branch_cond) ? tgt_b : pc_nt, so the 32-bit branch compare
(carry chain) drives a 30-way select fan-out into the flops. Instead register the
two candidates and the compare result separately (redir_tgt_b_q <= tgt_b,
redir_tgt_nt_q <= pc_nt, redir_br_q <= is_branch && branch_cond, all written only
while !redir_q, as today) and form redirect_target = redir_br_q ? redir_tgt_b_q :
redir_tgt_nt_q combinationally after the flops. The compare now ends at one flop (plus
the existing redir_q / tr_taken_q endpoints); the extra LUT lands on the

title: Sync-read BSRAM instruction cache pre-read at pc_d: registered hit/data fill the ~22% imem-stall slots without a LUT-RAM array on the fetch cone
motivation:
The core is fetch-bandwidth-bound. The imem bus delivers at most 0.78 words/cycle
(~22% random imem stalls, bench_stall_gen), and CoreMark's 4.226M cycles for ~3.3M
retired instructions (IPC ~0.78) suggest nearly every remaining cycle is a fetch slot lost
to the bus: the fetch queue only overlaps bus bubbles with downstream stalls, it cannot
raise fetch throughput above the bus rate. Predictor work is capped at <~5% cycles
(LESSONS r5s2/r6s2), and the Fmax cones (EX compare -> redir_target_q, stall -> regfile
address, load-align -> m_result, ALU -> x_result) are balanced at ~16-17 ns so
single-cone trims stall at +2%. The only structural lever left that is worth >10% cycles
is to stop depending on the bus for instructions we have already fetched.
r7s1 proved the cycle side: a 256-word direct-mapped icache cut cycles 4.226M -> 3.806M
(-10%, CRCs pass, formal pass) but scored 217.88 because its hit signal came out of an
async-read 256x42b LUT-RAM + tag compare off the pc flop and gated `fire`, costing ~15%
Fmax. That failure was about HOW the cache was read (async LUT-RAM on the pc->fire cone),
not about having a cache. The BTB works because its lookup is a single parallel read of
the pc flop; this proposal gives the cache a similar property by making the cache read
synchronous and one cycle early, so the hit and the data are flops when they are used.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add rtl/icache.sv and instantiate it in if_stage.sv. It is a bus-stall *supplement*, not
a replacement: the bus is still used whenever imem_ready=1; the cache only supplies the
instruction on cycles where imem_ready=0 and the cache hits.

1) Storage (parameter IC_AW, default 10 => 1024 words = 4 KB, tag = pc[19:IW+2]):
   - data array  logic [31:0] data_arr[0:N-1]  (sync write, SYNC read -> 2 BSRAM)
   - tag  array  logic [TW:0] tag_arr[0:N-1]   ({valid, tag}, sync write, sync read -> 1 BSRAM)
   Both are written in always_ff and read into registers in the same always_ff
   (`data_q <= data_arr[rd_idx]; tag_q <= tag_arr[rd_idx];`), the canonical Gowin
   BSRAM-inferable sync-read pattern. No async read, no LUT-RAM, no per-entry flops.
2) Early read address: rd_idx = idx bits of pc_d, where pc_d is exactly the value the
   fetch pc register loads this cycle (redirect ? redirect_target : fire ? next_pc : pc).
   So data_q/tag_q always hold the entry for the CURRENT pc register. A redirect or a
   BTB-predicted-taken target is covered because it is part of pc_d; the BTB lookup itself
   is untouched (still one parallel read of the pc flop, never of imem_data or the cache).
3) Hit: ic_hit = ic_en && tag_q.valid && (tag_q.tag == pc[19:IW+2]) -- flop-vs-flop
   compare, ~2 LUT levels, no array read in the cycle. in_valid (the fetch-queue push) =
   imem_ready || ic_hit, so fire = (imem_ready || ic_hit) && !redirect && !full.
   Fetched instr = imem_ready ? imem_data : data_q (one 2:1 LUT on the instr data path;
   the prediction fields are unchanged and pc-only).
4) Fill: on fire && imem_ready (the bus really delivered) write data_arr/tag_arr at
   idx(pc) with {1, pc tag} / imem_data. Wrong-path and aliased fills are harmless: the
   entry is tagged with the full address and EX still verifies every prediction. A
   same-cycle read/write of the same index is only possible when the pc has not moved
   (hit is then re-evaluated next cycle); the RTL (Verilator) semantics are read-old and
   the tag/data arrays use the same style so they stay mutually consistent.
5) Invalidation without per-entry reset flops: a post-reset sweep counter walks idx
   0..N-1 writing {valid=0} into tag_arr (shared write port, mux on sweep), then sets
   ic_en=1. While ic_en=0 ic_hit is forced 0 so the core runs from the bus exactly like
   today. The sweep (1024 cycles) finishes long before the CoreMark start marker, so it
   does not count; under riscv-formal (BMC depth 20) ic_en never rises, so the cache is
   dead logic there and the solver cost is unchanged. The cosim/ISS diff (every retired
   instruction compared field-by-field) is what proves the hit path, and the CoreMark
   CRCs must still match (invariant 7).
6) Nothing else changes: fetch_queue, btb, hazard_unit, ex_stage, RVFI and all IO stay as
   they are. No change to core.sv is required (the cache is inside if_stage).

Expected effect: with a 4 KB direct-mapped cache covering most of CoreMark's hot code the
stalled-bus slots (22% of fetch cycles) become hits most of the time, raising the
effective fetch rate from 0.78 toward ~0.95 words/cycle. r7s1's 256-word cache already
gave -10.0% cycles; 4x the capacity should give more (-12..-16%). Fmax cost is
budgeted at <=5%: the only new logic on timed paths is a flop-vs-flop 9-bit compare into
`fire`, one 2:1 on the instruction data, and the BSRAM address fanout from pc_d. If
`make timing` shows the compare->fire->pc_d->BSRAM-addr path becoming critical, the
fallback is to compare against pc_d one cycle earlier into a registered hit flop.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261001-002-r8s1 (regression, +6.25%): Reading the 1024-word icache as a sync BSRAM one cycle early from the pc_d index (flop-fed `ic_hit`/`ic_data`, bus-stall supplement only) recovered most of what the async-array icache lost (r7s1 217.88 -> 247.02), so the async 256x42b read was the main Fmax cost there, but 247.02 is +6.25% only against the pre-r8s0 232.5 baseline and lands ~1% below r8s0's ~249.6, so the cache still nets roughly break-even; likely residual costs are that `imem_ready || ic_hit` still gates `fire` (queue push, pc advance, BSRAM index fanout from `redirect`/`fire`) and that cache hits cannot use the empty-queue bypass (push-then-pop adds a cycle) while `ic_rd_ok` drops the hit after every predicted-taken advance, which eat into the cycle gain, but no cycle count or `make timing` arrival was recorded, so before another icache attempt measure cycles and the `ic_hit` -> `fire` arrival separately and keep hit latency equal to bus latency rather than growing the array.

title: One-cycle-shorter mispredict recovery: one-shot redirect_go fetches the target in the redirect cycle (OF-stage pipeline)
motivation:
Predictor *accuracy* is exhausted, measured on the full CoreMark ISS trace
(2.94M instructions, model of the champion: 32-entry direct-mapped BTB,
pc[6:2] index, 2-bit ctr, 4-entry RAS): 56,967 mispredicts = 47.3k cond
branches + 8.4k JAL (BTB conflicts) + 1.3k returns, ~5.8% of the 4.226M
cycles at ~4.3 cycles each (3 dead fetch slots, amplified by the ~22% imem
stalls because fetch is bandwidth-bound). Alternatives checked and rejected
with numbers: (a) short-forward-branch predication - only 5.9k dynamic SFBs,
666 taken, i.e. 1% of the mispredicts; (b) gshare (3-5 history bits, 128-256
counters) is WORSE than bimodal here (63-65k vs 57k mispredicts); (c) BTB
64/128 entries cut mispredicts by 11%/21% (-6k/-12k, ~0.6%/1.2% of cycles)
but grow the state riscv-formal must unroll (r4s2 timed out) - and 8 RAS
entries change nothing; (d) the top mispredicting branches (3280 each = 328
per iteration at 0x191c/0x1a44/0x2568, ...) are ~50% data-dependent CRC/list
tests that no history predictor fixes (r7s2 lost a third of Fmax trying).
The only lever left in this category that hits ALL 57k mispredicts is the
cost per mispredict. Today: EX detects at t, redir_q is set for t+1, in t+1
only the flush happens and pc <= redir_target_q, and the correct-path
instruction is first on the imem bus in t+2. redir_target_q is already a
flop in t+1, so the target can be fetched in t+1 without un-registering the
redirect (which was the big Fmax win of r2s2).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Re-do r5s2 (one-shot redirect_go fetch, measured 4.22M -> 4.14M cycles,
~1.9%, but it lost ~5% Fmax through the then-critical BTB-training cone) on
the current pipeline, where that cone is already cut by the registered BTB
training request (r6s2) and EX starts at operand flops (OF stage). Keep every
new mux flop-selected; nothing late (imem_ready, dmem_ready, EX compare)
enters the new muxes.

1. ex_stage.sv: keep redir_q / redir_target_q exactly as they are (they keep
   killing the wrong-path instruction in EX, bubbling EX/MEM, and stay sticky
   across a dmem stall). Add a one-shot flop
     redirect_go <= !redir_q && mispredict && !stall && !ex_busy;  (reset 0)
   i.e. high for exactly the first redirect cycle. Export it next to redirect.
2. if_stage.sv: new input redirect_go. fetch_pc = redirect_go ? redirect_target
   : pc (flop-select between two flops); imem_addr, the BTB lookup index
   (core.sv already feeds the BTB from io_imemAddr), in_e.pc, pc+4 and
   next_pc all use fetch_pc. pc priority: reset -> RESET_PC; fire -> next_pc
   (computed from fetch_pc); else redirect_go -> redirect_target. If the bus
   is not ready in the redirect cycle (~22%) behaviour falls back to today's
   (pc <= target, fetch next cycle), so the worst case equals the champion.
   The fetch side no longer keys off the sticky redirect (ID is held by
   stall_id during a sticky dmem-stall redirect, so the queue just fills with
   correct-path entries).
3. fetch_queue.sv: flush becomes the one-shot redirect_go. In that cycle the
   queue is reset with a fresh bypass: head_e/head_valid select the incoming
   entry (not the stale mem[rd_ptr]), fire is allowed in the flush cycle and
   writes slot 0 with wr_ptr<=1 (or rd_ptr/count adjusted so that a stalled ID
   parks the target instruction), so ID/D-O captures the target instruction in
   the redirect cycle instead of a bubble.
4. hazard_unit.sv / core.sv: wire redirect_go; flush_id (D/O capture of a
   bubble) is dropped in the redirect_go cycle so the target is captured, but
   bubble_ox still kills the wrong-path instruction in OF (flop-fed redirect)
   and load_use_hazard is masked while the held EX instruction is wrong-path.
   Wrong-path instructions never retire, so rvfi_order / pc_wdata are
   unchanged; every fetched instruction is still verified in EX against its

title: Pre-decode MEM byte-lane controls in EX: flat AND-OR load-align into m_result
motivation:
Cycles are fetch-bound (22% random imem stalls, ~5.8% mispredict, all below the
4.6% bar), so micro_opt can only pay through Fmax. The champion's worst logged
path (r8s0, 15.941 ns, 9 cells) is clock_ibuf > u_mem > u_of: the dmem BSRAM
read data (io_dmemRData) -> load-align shifter (dmem_rdata >> addr[1:0]*8) ->
byte/half/word sign-extend case mux -> mem_to_reg ? load_data : alu_result ->
forward mux (fwd[1] ? m_result) -> opa/opb/rs1_v/rs2_v operand flops in OF.
Every select on that cone (addr[1:0], mem_width, mem_sext, mem_to_reg, and the
misalign gate on reg_write that feeds the forward-select compares) is a pure
function of EX/MEM flops, but today it is decoded AFTER the late BSRAM data is
already in flight, so the data crosses a 4:1 byte mux, a width case mux, a
sign-fill AND, and a mem_to_reg 2:1 before it reaches the forward mux.
BSRAM data is the single latest arrival on the MEM side, so every level that can
be moved ahead of it (into EX, where the O/X flops give a full cycle and
jalr_sum[1:0] are the earliest bits of the adder) is a direct cut of this cone.
Note: a fresh `make timing` was not obtained for this proposal (the background
run did not survive the session); the path above is from the logged r8s0 result.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move all MEM-stage byte-lane decoding into EX and register it in EX/MEM, so the
dmem read-data cone becomes a flat flop-selected AND-OR and the dmem control
outputs come straight from flops. Cycle-identical (retire stream and RVFI values
unchanged; cosim CRCs and cycle count must match the champion exactly).

1. core_pkg.sv, ex_mem_t: add pre-decoded fields (RVFI-only consumers keep using
   the existing fields): misalign (1b), ld_sel_pass (per-byte-lane "pass rdata"
   flags), ld_alt (half-word upper-half select), ld_fill[3:1] (sign/zero-fill
   enables per upper byte), sgn_sel[3:0] (one-hot: which rdata MSB is the sign
   bit, all-zero when zero-extending or word load), lo_sel[1:0] (effective byte
   index for result bits [7:0]: word->0, half->{a[1],0}, byte->a[1:0]),
   ld_en (mem_to_reg, i.e. load result vs ALU result), wen_q[3:0], ren_q (dmem
   write-enable / read-enable already misalign-gated), and write_data replaced
   by the byte-replicated store word (wdata_rep).
2. ex_stage.sv: compute the above from in.ctrl (mem_width, mem_sext, mem_read,
   mem_write, mem_to_reg) and jalr_sum[1:0] (the low two adder bits arrive well
   before the upper carry chain, so this adds no depth to the EX critical cone;
   they only feed EX/MEM flops, never x_result, redirect or BTB training), and
   store them into reg_q under the existing stall / ex_busy / redir_q hold-or-
   bubble rules (bubble -> all-zero => dmem_wen=0, dmem_ren=0).
3. mem_stage.sv: drop the shifter, the width/sext case muxes and the
   byte_mask/misalign logic from the dmem path. Drive dmem_wen = wen_q,
   dmem_ren = ren_q, dmem_wdata = write_data (already replicated) straight from
   flops. Form load data as a flat AND-OR, one term per source with flop-only
   selects:
     sign       = |(sgn_sel & {r[31], r[23], r[15], r[7]})
     m_result[7:0]   = ld_en ? r[8*lo_sel +: 8] : alu_result[7:0]   (4:1 flop-selected)
     m_result[15:8]  = (pass1 & r[15:8]) | (alt & r[31:24]) | (fill1 & sign) | alu term
     m_result[23:16] = (pass2 & r[23:16]) | (fill2 & sign) | alu term
     m_result[31:24] = (pass3 & r[31:24]) | (fill3 & sign) | alu term
   where every `alu term` is (!ld_en & alu_result[i]) and is computed from flops in
   parallel with the late rdata, so rdata crosses: (a) one LUT/MUX level for
   sign-less bits, (b) two levels for sign-extended bits, then straight into the
   OF forward mux -- versus ~5 levels today (4:1 shift mux, width case, sext AND,
   mem_to_reg mux). m_reg_write = ctrl.reg_write & !misalign becomes a 1-gate
   function of two flops (shortens the forward_unit compare -> select cone too).
   reg_q.mem_rmask/mem_wmask/mem_addr/mem_rdata/mem_wdata for RVFI are derived
   from the registered fields and are RVFI-only (pruned from the timed netlist).
4. If `make timing` shows the ALU -> x_result -> OF operand-flop cone is now the
   co-critical limiter (r6s1/r8s0 lesson: top-N endpoints are bunched), the
   implementer may additionally decode alu_op to a one-hot in OF (O/X flops) and
   express the ALU result mux as an AND-OR; otherwise keep the change confined to
   the MEM path. Verification: test_alu.py unaffected; cosim (CRCs and cycle
   count identical), riscv-formal ALIGNED_MEM / misaligned-trap checks must still
   pass (misalign trap and reg_write clearing semantics are preserved bit for bit).
Expected: 2-3 LUT levels (~1.0-1.8 ns) off the BSRAM-data -> OF-operand-flop path,
and the BSRAM write-enable/write-data path becomes flop -> pin; area +~15 flops,
-~60 LUTs (shifter removed). Gain is limited by the next co-critical cones
(ALU -> x_result, branch compare), so expect low-to-mid single digits.

title: Re-land the sync-BSRAM bus-stall-filling icache on the r8s0 champion (single {valid,tag,data} array, pc_d early read)
motivation:
The core is fetch-bandwidth-bound by construction. The imem bus delivers at most
~0.78 words/cycle (22% random stalls independent of the address), the champion
retires ~2.94M instructions in 4.226M cycles (IPC 0.70) and the fetch queue only
overlaps a bus bubble with some downstream stall; it cannot raise fetch throughput
above the bus rate. The cycle floor from the remaining stall sources (mispredicts
~57k x ~4, dmem stalls, load-use, muldiv) is ~3.6-3.8M, so ~9-10% of the cycles are
pure imem-bus bubbles and are the single biggest remaining structural loss.
History: r7s1 (async 256x42b LUT-RAM icache) cut cycles 4.226M -> 3.806M but lost
~15% Fmax because the async array read + tag compare sat on the pc->fire cone.
r8s1 (1024-word SYNC BSRAM cache read one cycle early from pc_d, bus-stall
supplement only) kept the cycle gain (3.830M cycles, CRCs/formal/cosim pass) and
limited the Fmax loss to 98.25 -> 94.6 MHz (-3.7%) for a net +6.25% -- but it was
evaluated against the pre-r8s0 base and its worst path was ALU -> u_of opa
(16.43 ns), i.e. exactly the x_result/is_jump cone that r8s0 has since cut (and
r8s0 moved the champion to 105.482 MHz / 249.61). r8s1 was never merged, so the
champion still pays the full bus-bubble cost. Stacking the two should give
~3.83M cycles at ~100-105 MHz = ~261-275 iter/s (+4.6..+10%).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add rtl/icache.sv and wire it into rtl/if_stage.sv as a pure bus-stall filler:
when imem_ready=1 the bus word is used exactly as today; when imem_ready=0 and the
cache holds the word for the current fetch pc, the cached word is delivered
instead, so the fetch queue still gets an entry that cycle. Everything downstream
(fetch_queue, BTB, per-entry predictions verified in EX, redirect) is untouched.

Design (keep it structurally identical to what already worked in r8s1, with the
fixes below):
1. ONE synchronous-read array icache_mem[0:IC_N-1] of {valid, tag, data}
   (IC_N = 1024 words, parameter IC_AW; width = 1 + (18-IC_AW) + 32). A single
   array (not separate tag and data arrays) guarantees that a read-during-write
   collision returns a consistent {tag,data} pair (both old or both new), so a
   stale-tag/new-data false hit is impossible. Read and write in the same
   always_ff template so Gowin infers BSRAM (1024x40 -> 3 x 1Kx18 blocks).
2. Early read: the read address is pc_d[IC_AW+1:2], where pc_d is EXACTLY the
   next-state value of the pc flop (reset ? RESET_PC : redirect ? redirect_target :
   fire ? next_pc : pc) -- the hold case is included, so ic_q at cycle t+1 is
   always cache[pc(t+1)] and no "read-ok" qualifier or CE gating is needed (r8s1's
   ic_rd_ok dropping the hit after every predicted-taken advance is not needed:
   the address already follows the BTB-predicted next pc). Compute pc_d once in
   if_stage and use it for both the pc flop D input and the BSRAM address.
3. Hit = ic_en && ic_q.valid && (ic_q.tag == pc[19:IC_AW+2]) -- compare of the
   BSRAM output against the pc FLOP (not against imem_data or any late signal).
   in_valid to fetch_queue = imem_ready || ic_hit; in_e.instr = imem_ready ?
   imem_data : ic_q.data. fire still comes out of fetch_queue (in_valid && !flush
   && !full) so the pc advance / queue push structure is unchanged, and the
   empty-queue zero-latency bypass still applies to cache-supplied entries (the
   muxed instr is simply in_e.instr), so a hit never costs an extra cycle vs a
   bus delivery (hit latency == bus latency).
4. Fill: on fire && imem_ready write {1, pc tag, imem_data} at pc index (write
   address is the pc flop, data is the bus word: all flop/bus fed). Collision of
   the fill with the same-cycle early read of the same index (single-instruction
   BTB self-loop) is harmless because of the single-array consistency above.
   Instruction memory is ROM-like in CoreMark (no stores to code), so no snooping.
5. Reset: a post-reset invalidation sweep (IC_AW-bit counter writes {valid=0,..}
   to every index through the same write port, write port muxed with the fill
   under sweep_busy) sets ic_en when it wraps; hit is forced 0 until then. The
   sweep takes ~1024 cycles before the timed region; it also means riscv-formal
   (BMC depth << 1024) never sees a cache hit, so the formal unroll sees the
   same fetch behaviour as the champion plus a memory the solver never reads
   through a hit (r8s1 passed the formal flow with this exact structure; keep
   the array at 1024 words for formal tractability).
6. Optional tuning knob (decide by cosim cycle count, not by guess): IC_AW=11
   (2048 words, 5 BSRAM) if it cuts cycles by >=1.5% vs 1024; otherwise keep 1024.

Why it should beat r8s1's net: (a) same +10% cycle gain (3.83M), (b) the r8s0 cuts
remove the ALU->OF opa cone that was r8s1's worst path, so the base Fmax the cache
is added to is ~7% higher, (c) the cache read adds only flop-fed logic (BSRAM
output -> 8-bit compare -> in_valid) and a pc_d fan-out to 10 BSRAM address pins
rather than any async LUT-RAM on the pc cone. Required verification before
handing back: run cosim and record the cycle count (expect ~3.8M), run
`make timing TARGET=bench` and read the arrivals of ic_hit -> fire -> pc_d ->
BSRAM address and of the top-N distinct endpoints. If ic_hit -> fire -> pc_d ->
BSRAM address is the worst path, break it by making the BSRAM address depend on
`fire` only through the final 2:1 (addr = fire ? next_pc_idx : pc_idx, with
redirect handled before the flop) or by reading the cache with the sequential
candidate pc+4 / pc and accepting a miss (bus fallback) after predicted-taken
advances, rather than growing the array or the hit logic.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-002-r9s1 (regression, -3.17%): Re-landing the sync-BSRAM bus-stall icache on the faster r8s0 base scored 241.69, below both the champion (249.61) and r8s1's 247.02 on the slower pre-r8s0 base, so the cache's Fmax cost is not offset by the EX-cone cuts: it sits in the fetch cone r8s0 never touched (BSRAM tCO -> tag compare -> `imem_ready || ic_hit` -> `fire` -> `pc_d` -> 10 BSRAM address pins, with `fire` now a late select on the early-read address), and fitness = 10*Fmax/Mcycles means the expected ~3.83M cycles would imply only ~92.6 MHz (-12% vs 105.5); the diff also routed cache hits through `byp_valid = imem_ready` (push-then-pop, no empty-queue bypass) to keep BSRAM tCO off decode, contradicting the spec's "hit latency == bus latency" and likely giving back part of the cycle gain, so this is the second icache that nets break-even-or-worse, and the next attempt must first take `fire`/`ic_hit` out of the BSRAM address (e.g. read pc+4/pc sequentially off flops and accept a bus fallback after predicted-taken advances) and log cycles plus the `ic_hit` -> `fire` -> `pc_d` arrival, rather than assuming Fmax gains on the base are additive with the cache's cost.

title: BTB branch-target-instruction folding: predicted-taken hits supply the target word from the BTB so it skips the 22% imem stall dice and a bus slot
motivation:
Predictor accuracy is exhausted (r8s2 measured on the full CoreMark ISS trace:
57k mispredicts = 47k data-dependent cond branches + 8.4k JAL conflicts + 1.3k
returns; gshare is worse than bimodal, 64/128-entry BTB only buys 0.6%/1.2%).
Accuracy work is capped at ~1% and cannot clear the 4.6% acceptance bar.
What is NOT exhausted is fetch *bandwidth*: the champion runs at IPC ~0.70
(2.94M instr / 4.226M cycles) against an imem cap of 0.78 words/cycle (22%
random not-ready), i.e. the machine is ~90% fetch-bound. A 256-entry icache
(r7s1, 4.226M -> 3.806M cycles, -10%) proved the bandwidth is worth ~10%, but
it lost Fmax because a big async-array `ic_hit` gated `fire`. The same
bandwidth can be harvested for the ~10% of dynamic instructions that are
*taken-branch targets* with a classic branch-target-instruction cache that
rides on the structure we already have: the BTB is read once per fetch from
the registered pc, so a 32-bit target-instruction word stored beside
{tag,target} costs one more parallel LUT-RAM read (no serial array stage, no
`fire` dependence), unlike the icache or the r7s2 PHT.
Dynamic predicted-taken BTB hits are ~300k+ (taken cond branches ~275k, JAL,
returns excluded), each currently costs one bus slot for the target word (1/0.78
= 1.28 fetch-bound cycles including the stall dice). Folding that word away
lifts the fetch cap from 0.78 to ~0.85 IPC; with the remaining stalls
(mispredicts 5.8%, dmem/load-use) absorbing about half, ~3-6% cycles.

   and `tw_valid_q` (32 flops, reset 0). New outputs `pred_tw[31:0]` and
   `pred_fold = pred_hit && ctr_rd[1] && !ret_rd && tw_valid_q[idx]` (all pure
   functions of the pc flop, same cone depth as pred_hit; imem_data is never
   read). Only direct branch/JAL entries fold; is_ret entries never fold.
2. Learning is fetch-side and EX-independent. When a predicted-taken hit with
   tw_valid=0 is pushed (fire), set `learn_pend_q`/`learn_idx_q`. When the next
   fetch entry (pc == that predicted target, i.e. fpc just advanced to T) is
   pushed, write its imem word into tw_arr[learn_idx_q] and set tw_valid_q
   iff the word's opcode is not a CTI (BRANCH 1100011 / JAL 1101111 / JALR
   1100111 -> do not fold: the folded word would carry no prediction of its
   own). `learn_pend_q` is dropped by redirect and by ANY BTB training write
   (`wr_tt` from the registered tr_en_q) landing between the two fetches, so
   the word can never be filed under an entry whose owner changed. A training
   write that changes the entry (allocation, !tr_hit_q, or target mismatch)
   clears tw_valid_q[tr_idx]; a pure refresh of an unchanged, correct,
   counter-saturated hit is suppressed so hot loops do not keep invalidating
   their own word. (Direct branch / JAL targets are fixed by the instruction
   and the tag is the full pc[19:2], so tw word is correct for (tag,target)
   as long as the owner is unchanged; CoreMark has no self-modifying code.)
3. fetch_queue.sv: second write port ("fold"). With fire && fold, push entry A
   = {pc, bus instr, prediction as today} AND entry B = {pc = predicted target
   T, instr = pred_tw, pred_taken=0, pred_npc=don't-care, pred_hit=0,
   pred_ctr=0}; count += 2, wr_ptr += 2. Fold requires room for two (count <=
   DEPTH-2) else behaves as a normal fire (fold only costs the optimization).
   Entry B has pred_taken=0 so EX verifies it against pc+4 = T+4, which is
   exactly where fetch continues. Raise DEPTH to 8 (AW=3) if the extra
   head-of-line pressure shows in cosim cycles; storage becomes flop-based
   (second write port), area is a few hundred LUT/FF, well inside budget.
   Empty-queue bypass is kept for entry A (the head); entry B always goes
   through storage (it is consumed the cycle after), so the registered
   mispredict path gains no cycle and loses none.
4. if_stage.sv: when fire && pred_fold, `pc <= pred_target + 4` (T+4) instead
   of T. The pc+4 adder already exists; the fold value is a second
   {pred_target,2'b00}+4 on the flop-fed BTB output (one extra carry chain on
   the pred_target -> pc path, in parallel with the existing next_pc mux).
   BTB lookup for T+4 happens next cycle as usual. A BTB hit at the folded
   branch's *target word* is never needed because CTI words are not folded.
5. core.sv: wire the new btb outputs through if_stage (pred_fold, pred_tw) and
   the btb learn interface; no IO / RVFI change.

Correctness argument (formal + cosim): every instruction (including folded
entry B) is still verified in EX against its own prediction, so a wrong fold
target PC is only a redirect. What is NOT covered by verify-everything is the
folded instruction *word*, hence rule 2 (word filed only under an unchanged
owner, cleared on any owner-changing write, CTI words excluded); the word is
taken from the bus at pc==T in the same program-visible state, so it equals
what a normal fetch of T would return. riscv-formal's symbolic imem can feed
different words for repeated fetches of the same pc, so the formal-flow build
must keep the fold rule sound without assuming imem is a ROM: the wrapper's
`rvfi_insn` check compares against the symbolic insn seen by the *core*, which
is the folded word, so it is consistent by construction; if formal still
rejects the stale-word case, the implementer must gate folding off under
`ifdef RISCV_FORMAL` (fold disabled; cycle gain only measured in cosim/FPGA).
This is the escape hatch that keeps the formal unroll at champion size (lesson
r4s2/r8s2: do not grow the redirect or BTB-state cone).

Expected cycle effect: ~300k predicted-taken hits x fold-eligible share (~70%,
non-CTI target words, entries warmed) x ~1.28 fetch-bound cycles x ~50% still
fetch-limited after the change = ~130-190k cycles, i.e. ~3-4.5% of 4.226M,
plus a smaller win from removing the dice on predicted-taken heavy loops. Fmax:
the new read is a parallel LUT-RAM read off the same pc flop and feeds queue
write data only (no `fire`/`in_valid` dependence); the `pred_fold` AND-term
adds one LUT input to the `fire`-side count/wr_ptr update and a (T+4) adder to
the pc mux, both well off the 15.9 ns MEM->OF cone. Run `make timing` and check
the pc/next_pc and wr_ptr/count endpoints; if they approach the top-N, drop
DEPTH back to 4 or fold only when queue count <= 1.

title: Co-cut MEM load-align and ALU result cones: EX-predecoded byte lanes + OF one-hot ALU select with shared sub/slt adder
motivation:
Cycles are fetch-bound (22% random imem stalls, ~5.8% mispredict, load-use
and mul latency are all low-single-digit ceilings below the 4.6% bar), so
micro_opt can only pay through Fmax. LESSONS.md is consistent on one point:
with the top-N endpoints bunched at ~16-17.5 ns, a single-cone trim stalls at
+2..7% (r2s1, r3s0, r6s1, r7s0), and only bundles that cut every co-critical
cone together move the median Fmax (r8s0 +7.36%). The latest data point is
r9s0: pre-decoding the MEM byte-lane controls in EX (cycle-identical, flat
flop-selected AND-OR load-align into m_result) measured a real +4.08%
(249.6 -> 259.80), but was explicitly noted to be capped by the next cone
behind it, ALU -> x_result -> OF operand flops (O/X ctrl.alu_op / opb[0] ->
u_alu 11-way encoded result mux -> x_result -> forward LUT -> opa/opb/rs1_v/
rs2_v + EX/MEM alu_result flops, ~16-17.4 ns in the r5s1/r8s0 reports), and
the r9s0 notes say to land the two together. This hypothesis is exactly that
bundle; both halves are cycle-identical and fanout/level cuts, not new state
machines, so the retire stream, CRCs and cycle count must stay bit-identical.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two cycle-identical edits aimed at the two cones that sit at the top of the
champion's endpoint list (MEM load data -> m_result -> OF operand flops, and
O/X operand -> ALU -> x_result -> OF operand flops / EX/MEM alu_result).

(A) MEM byte-lane pre-decode in EX (re-land of the measured r9s0 idea).
Every select on the load-align cone (addr[1:0], mem_width, mem_sext,
mem_to_reg, misalign gate on reg_write) is a pure function of EX/MEM flops
but is decoded AFTER the late dmem BSRAM read data is already in flight.
Compute them in EX from in.ctrl and jalr_sum[1:0] (the low two adder bits,
early; they feed only EX/MEM flops, never x_result/redirect/BTB) and register
them in ex_mem_t: misalign, per-byte-lane pass flags, half-word-alt select,
upper-byte fill enables, one-hot sign-bit select (sgn_sel[3:0], all-zero for
zero-extend/word), lo_sel[1:0] for result bits [7:0], ld_en (mem_to_reg),
pre-gated wen_q[3:0] / ren_q, and the byte-replicated store word in
write_data. mem_stage then drives dmem_wen/ren/wdata straight from flops and
forms m_result as a flat AND-OR (rdata crosses 1 level for sign-less bits,
2 for sign-extended bits; the ALU-result term (!ld_en & alu_result) is early).
m_reg_write = ctrl.reg_write & !misalign (one gate of two flops) which also
shortens the forward_unit compare -> select cone. RVFI-only fields (mem_addr,
rmask/wmask, rdata/wdata) are derived from the registered fields and are
pruned from the timed netlist. Bubble (ex_busy / redir_q / reset) zeros all
of them so dmem_wen/ren are 0; stall holds them (existing reg_q rules).

(B) ALU result cone: one-hot select decoded in OF + shared adder.
(B1) of_stage decodes alu_op into a one-hot select bus (s_add, s_sub, s_and,
s_or, s_xor, s_slt, s_sltu, s_sll, s_srl, s_sra, plus s_md for the muldiv
result) registered in the O/X register next to ctrl (cleared by bubble/reset
like ctrl; the encoded alu_op stays in ctrl for muldiv and RVFI). The ALU
result then becomes a flat AND-OR of flop-gated terms (a LUT4 absorbs two
sel&data terms, so ~11 terms resolve in 3 LUT levels with no encoded-op
decode tree), and md_result (a flop, res_q) joins as one more gated term so
x_result = OR(terms) with no separate is_muldiv ? md_result : alu_result
2:1 level in front of the OF forward LUT.
(B2) Fold LUI into ADD: OF already builds opa/opb with the is_auipc/is_jump
select, so for is_lui force early_a = 0 (sel_a excludes is_lui so the late
x_result forward never lands in it) and set the decoder's LUI alu_op to ADD
semantics in the one-hot (s_add). That deletes the LUI arm.
(B3) Share one subtract-capable adder between ADD, SUB, SLT and SLTU:
sum = a + (b ^ {32{sub|slt|sltu}}) + (sub|slt|sltu); SLTU = !carry_out,
SLT = (a[31]^b[31]) ? a[31] : sum[31] (equivalently overflow-corrected sign),
so the two separate 32-bit comparators (and their fanout on opa/opb) leave the
ALU. Fewer loads on opa/opb[*] (which today feed adder + 2 comparators + 3
barrel shifters + logic ops) is a routing-delay cut, and the r8s0 report
showed these paths are ~1.7 ns/cell (routing dominated), not logic dominated.
The ALTOPS stand-ins for MUL/MULH/.../REMU stay as extra one-hot terms
generated under the same `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` (in OF, keyed off the
decoded alu_op) so the formal view keeps the same one-hot structure and still
proves routing/trap behavior; the real-arithmetic HAS_MULDIV=1 reference
(and the encoded `op` port) stay in alu.sv so test_alu.py keeps passing
unchanged; add a cocotb test that drives the one-hot path against the same
vectors.
Verification: cosim CRCs and cycle count must equal the champion exactly
(bit-identical retire stream); riscv-formal insn/ALIGNED_MEM/misaligned-trap
checks must pass; test_alu.py and the new one-hot test pass.

Expected: (A) alone measured +4.08%; (B) removes the next bunched cone so
the floor moves instead of one endpoint (r8s0 pattern), for ~+6..9% total,
with the 4.6% acceptance bar being the main risk (placement noise is several
percent). If `make timing` shows (B3) hurts (the inverted-b XOR in front of
the carry chain), drop B3 and keep A + B1 + B2.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-001-r10s0 (regression, -0.18%): Landing r9s0's EX-predecoded MEM byte-lane controls together with a registered one-hot ALU result select (`alu_sel_t` in the O/X flops, flat AND-OR `alu_oh` with `md_result` as one more gated term, LUI folded into ADD; the shared sub/slt adder was dropped after it measured slower, so SUB/SLT/SLTU kept separate units) scored 249.17, flat against the 249.61 champion and ~4% below the 259.80 that the MEM pre-decode earned alone in r9s0, so the "next bunched cone is the ALU encoded-op decode" premise is wrong: the one-hot select adds ~11 flops that each fan out across 32 result bits and removes only a shallow decode, while the ALU -> `x_result` path is routing/fanout-dominated (operand flops feeding adder, comparators, shifters and logic ops), so cutting LUT levels there does not move Fmax and may cost it; no `make timing` was run to name the true next cone, so do not retry the one-hot ALU select, and re-land the r9s0 MEM pre-decode alone (or with a cut aimed at a cone a fresh report actually shows) and check the +4% survives placement noise.

title: Resolve-after-flop split: registered mispredict select + thin pre-decoded MEM + one-hot EX result, all co-critical cones cut together
motivation:
Fetch is the cycle floor (~0.78 word/cycle from the 22% imem stalls; cycles 4.226M are essentially
instr_count/0.78), and three icache attempts (r7s1, r8s1, r9s1) each lost ~10-15% Fmax for ~10% cycles,
so Fmax is the only lever left that is not cancelled by its own cost. The log shows the top-N
endpoints bunched at ~15.4-16 ns across three cones: MEM load-align -> m_result -> OF operand
flops (r8s0 critical path), the EX branch compare -> mispredict select -> redir_q (r9s0 critical
path, rs2_v -> redir_q, 13 levels / 38 cells), and ALU -> x_result -> OF operand flops. r9s0 cut
only the MEM cone and measured a real +4.08% (259.80, 109.8 MHz) but missed the 4.6% bar because the
branch cone was exposed right behind it; r8s0's recipe (end the late compare at a flop and do the
select after the flop) is what produced its +7.36%. The lessons say these cones only move when
they are cut in the same change, and no attempt has yet landed the MEM cut and the branch cut
together. Everything proposed is cycle-identical (4,225,873 cycles) and adds no formal-hostile
structure (no fetch bypass, no BTB/RAS growth).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Re-partition the EX/redirect/MEM boundaries so every late cone ends at a flop after one or two
LUT levels, with zero cycle cost:

(1) Mispredict decision after the flop (ex_stage). Today redir_q <= mispredict && !stall && !ex_busy,
where mispredict = ex_valid && (jalr ? mp_jr : (jal || br&&cond) ? mp_tgt : mp_seq) sits behind the
32-bit branch compare (carry chain) and is the r9s0 critical path. Instead register, at the
end of EX when the instruction advances (pend = ex_valid && !stall && !ex_busy):
  cond_q = is_branch && branch_cond                                (late, one flop; already exists as redir_br_q)
  mpt_q  = pend && mp_tgt                                          (mispredict if the branch is taken; early)
  mpn_q  = pend && (is_jalr ? mp_jr : is_jal ? mp_tgt : mp_seq)    (mispredict if not taken / jump / non-CTI)
and make `redirect` the single-LUT combinational function  redirect = cond_q ? mpt_q : mpn_q  of
those flops (one LUT3 from flops, so it is timing-equivalent to the old redir_q flop for the
IF/hazard/fetch-queue consumers). The one-cycle redirect latency is unchanged (redirect is
asserted in the cycle after the mispredicting instruction leaves EX, exactly when redir_q was).
Sticky-while-dmem-stall behaviour is preserved by holding {cond_q, mpt_q, mpn_q, redir_tgt_b_q,
redir_tgt_nt_q} while (redirect && stall) and clearing them otherwise (ex_valid = in.valid &&
!redirect is 0 in the redirect cycle, so a recapture yields pend=0 automatically). Target flops keep
their existing `if (!redirect)` capture. The compare now ends at one flop (cond_q), the JALR
adder+!= pred_full ends at one flop (mpn_q), and the 2-3 level mispredict mux plus the
ex_valid/stall/busy ANDs leave the compare cone.

(2) Thin MEM stage (mem_stage / ex_stage / core_pkg), the r9s0 change that measured +4.08%:
EX registers the pre-decoded byte-lane controls into EX/MEM (misalign, wen/ren, byte-replicated
store word, load lane select, sign-fill one-hots, folded misalign reg_write), so the dmem BSRAM read
data crosses one flat flop-selected AND-OR into m_result and the OF forward muxes; no shifter, no
width/sext case muxes. misalign comes from jalr_sum[1:0] (already early in EX).

(3) One-hot EX result select (alu.sv / of_stage / core_pkg, secondary, keep only if it stays
cycle-identical): OF decodes alu_op into a registered one-hot (add/sub-arith, logic, slt, shift,
lui) so the ALU output is an AND-OR instead of the 19-way case, and pre-inverts opb for SUB/SLT/SLTU
in OF (opb_d = sel_b ? x_result ^ inv : early_b_inv is still one LUT4 for the late x_result; rs2_v
stays un-inverted for compare/store data) so one shared adder serves ADD/SUB/SLT/SLTU. The ALTOPS
branch and the HAS_MULDIV=0 arms are kept so riscv-formal and test_alu.py still pass.

Expected: (2) alone gave ~+4% at 109.8 MHz with the branch cone at 15.45 ns as the new worst path;
(1) removes ~2-3 levels (~1.5-2 ns) from exactly that cone and (3) trims the ALU -> x_result sibling,
so the bunched cones all fall to ~13.5-14.5 ns -> ~115-120 MHz at the same 4.226M cycles, i.e. ~+7% over
the 249.61 champion with enough margin over the 4.6% acceptance bar and the ~±3% P&R noise.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-002-r10s1 (regression, -4.42%): Bundling r9s0's EX-predecoded MEM controls with a post-flop mispredict select (`cond_q`/`mpt_q`/`mpn_q` flops, `redirect = cond_q ? mpt_q : mpn_q` as one LUT3) and a one-hot ALU result select was cycle-identical but scored 238.58, ~8% below the 259.80 the MEM pre-decode earned alone in r9s0 (and below r10s0's 249.17 with the one-hot ALU), so adding cone cuts on top of the MEM cut is not additive and here subtracted; the most likely culprit is that `redirect` stopped being a flop, so a LUT3 now sits ahead of its high-fanout consumers (IF NOP mux, hazard flush, fetch-queue flush, ~170-flop ID/EX reset net, `ex_valid`), which is the same net r2s1/r2s2 found worth ending at a flop, and "one LUT off flops is timing-equivalent to a flop" ignores that fanout routing, not LUT depth, dominates these cones; no `make timing` was run to confirm, so keep `redirect`/`redir_q` a true flop (move the late-compare select into the flop's D side or duplicate the flop per consumer group), and land the r9s0 MEM pre-decode alone before stacking further cuts on it.

title: EX-trained BTB target-word folding with in-queue phase bit: one bus slot feeds a taken branch and its target instruction
motivation:
Predictor accuracy is exhausted (r9s2 trace study: ~57k mispredicts, 47k of them
data-dependent conditional branches; gshare/64-128-entry BTBs buy <=1.2%), and the
machine is ~90% fetch-bound: IPC ~0.70 vs an imem cap of 0.78 words/cycle from the
~22% random not-ready bus. The only lever left inside the predictor category is to
supply instructions without spending a bus slot. r9s2 proved the idea (BTB stores the
predicted-taken target's instruction word, cycles 4.226M -> 4.072M = -3.6%) but lost
~10% Fmax (94.7 MHz) because (a) a predicted-taken hit pushed TWO entries into the fetch
queue in one cycle (second write port, 2-slot full check, count += 2, all gated by the
late BTB hit/fold signal), and (b) the word was learned fetch-side with a pending/learn
FSM that sat on fire/in_valid. This hypothesis keeps the cycle win but moves every
fold decision off the fetch cone: the fold word rides in the SAME single queue entry
as the branch (one write port, one pointer bump, exactly as today), the "second
instruction" is produced at the queue READ side by a phase flop, and the word is learned
from flops in OF/EX one training cycle later, never from the live bus.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
1) btb.sv: add three per-entry arrays next to tt_arr/ctr_arr (all async-read LUT-RAM,
   read with the same pc-flop index, so no serial stage and no imem_data dependence):
     tw_arr[32]  : 32b target-instruction word
     fn_arr[18]  : fetch-next word address = tw_valid ? target+1 : target
                   (pre-added at training time from tr_target_q, so the fetch next_pc
                   mux input is a plain array read, same depth as today's pred_target)
     tw_valid_q  : 32 flops, reset 0
   pred_target (T, used for EX verification, queue pred_npc) is unchanged; a new output
   pred_fnext = ret_rd ? ras_q[0] : fn_rd feeds if_stage.next_pc, and
   pred_fold = pred_taken && tw_valid_q[idx] && !ret_rd, pred_tw = tw_rd.
   Returns never fold (their target is the RAS).
2) Training (EX, flop-fed, registered through the existing tr_*_q stage). In ex_stage a
   new `tr_tw_ok` = adv && in.pred_taken && !in.mp_btgt && !is_ret && D/O.valid &&
   D/O.pc[19:2]==in.pred_npc && D/O.instr is not a CTI (opcode not BRANCH/JAL/JALR) -
   i.e. the instruction sitting in OF is exactly the predicted target of the branch/JAL
   in EX, and the actual branch outcome (registered tr_taken_q) will confirm it.
   core.sv routes D/O.{valid,pc,instr} into ex_stage; tr_tw_q <= D/O.instr (32 flops).
   The BTB writes tag/target/tw/fn/tw_valid/valid/is_ret ATOMICALLY and only when
   tr_en_q && tr_taken_q && (!tr_hit_q || tr_tw_ok_q); tw_valid <= tr_tw_ok_q. Plain
   taken-hit refreshes with no word available write nothing but the counter, so a word
   filed under (tag,target) can never end up under a different owner (the stale-owner
   race the r9s2 learn FSM needed extra invalidation logic for). Learning therefore
   happens on the 2nd+ dynamic occurrence of each hot taken branch; the first
   occurrence allocates with tw_valid=0 exactly as today.
3) if_stage.sv: next_pc = pred_taken ? {pred_fnext,2'b00} : pc+4 (unchanged shape);
   in_e additionally carries pred_fold and pred_tw into the fetch queue.
4) fetch_queue.sv (the key difference from r9s2): entry gains {fold, tw[31:0]} (33 more
   LUT-RAM bits, written by the existing single fire write). A `phase` flop marks
   "head entry's branch already popped, its folded target word is now the head".
     head (phase=0): as today.   head (phase=1): pc={pred_npc,2'b00}, instr=tw,
     pred_taken=0, pred_hit=0 (a non-CTI, so EX predicts pc+4 and never mispredicts it).
     pop_eff = pop && !(head.fold && !phase); rd_ptr/count move on pop_eff only.
     phase <= flush/reset ? 0 : pop && head.fold && !phase ? 1 : pop && phase ? 0 : phase.
   With an empty queue and a folding branch arriving on the bus, the branch is still
   bypassed to ID this cycle, but also written (fire) with count staying 1, so the
   target word is the head next cycle without any bus slot. The phase mux only touches
   the EARLY (flop/LUT-RAM-fed) side of the head mux; the late imem_data still crosses
   the same single `empty ? in : mem` mux as today. flush (redir_q) clears phase.
   Wrong-path safety is unchanged: the branch carries pred_npc=T and is verified in EX
   as today; the folded word is younger than it, so a mispredict kills it exactly like
   any wrong-path instruction; the folded word is non-CTI so EX has nothing to verify
   for it. Correctness does not rely on the folded word matching memory except under
   self-modifying code (none in CoreMark; formal's symbolic imem only requires that
   rvfi_insn is the instruction actually executed, which it is).
Expected effect: ~4.0-4.1M cycles (-3.5..-4.5%, in line with r9s2's measured -3.6%
with the slightly later 2nd-occurrence learning offset by dropping the learn-pend
invalidations), with the Fmax cost cut to the extra 33-bit queue-entry width and an
18-bit fn_arr read on the pc->next_pc cone (the same depth as pred_target today).
Before landing, the implementer should run `make timing` and compare the u_btb ->
u_if/u_fq arrivals against the champion; if the fold path costs more than ~2% Fmax,
fall back to fold-eligible entries only in the lower 16 BTB indices (smaller tw/fn
arrays, same queue-side phase logic) rather than re-adding a second queue write port.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-003-r10s2 (regression, -6.19%): Moving BTB target-word folding to a single-write-port fetch queue (33-bit `{fold,tw}` entry, read-side `phase` flop, EX/OF-trained `tw_arr`/`fn_arr`/`tw_valid_q` written atomically with tag/target, no learn FSM) scored 234.17, essentially the same as r9s2's second-write-port/learn-FSM version (232.61: 4.072M cycles, only ~-3.6%, 94.7 MHz, worst path `u_if/pc` -> `u_btb` -> `u_fq` -> `u_if/pc`), so the ~10% Fmax loss does not come from the double queue push or the fetch-side learning but from what both share (a 32x32b word array plus 18b `fn_arr` read off the pc flop, `pred_fold`/`pred_fnext` fanning into `next_pc` and the queue entry write, wider queue entries); since fitness = 10*Fmax/Mcycles and the ~3.6% cycle ceiling of folding is far below that cost, don't retry BTB-resident instruction words in any queue arrangement, and note no `make timing` was recorded for r10s2 to confirm its worst path, so the cone attribution is inferred from r9s2.

title: Re-land MEM byte-lane pre-decode + single-chain branch compare with D-side redirect select + 2-busy-cycle MUL
motivation:
The only micro_opt that has measurably moved Fmax on the champion is r9s0
(EX-pre-decoded MEM byte-lane controls, flat flop-selected AND-OR load
align): 259.80 vs 249.61 = +4.08%, cycle-identical (4,225,873 cycles), seeds
[98.5, 109.8, 109.8] MHz. It missed the 4.6% bar by ~0.5%, and r9s0's own
logged critical path after the cut is no longer the MEM cone: it is
u_of/rs2_v flop -> u_ex branch compare -> mispredict -> redir_q (13 logic
levels, 38 cells, arrival 15.4 ns). Two later bundles (r10s0 one-hot ALU
select, r10s1 post-flop registered mispredict select) LOST 4-8% against r9s0:
the one-hot ALU select adds high-fanout flops without removing real depth,
and r10s1 turned `redirect` into a LUT in front of its ~170-flop fan-out.
So the recipe is: keep r9s0, do NOT touch the ALU result select, keep
`redir_q` a true flop, and add only cuts that (a) shorten the branch-compare
-> redir_q D-input cone r9s0 exposed and (b) buy a few tenths of a percent
of real cycles at zero timing cost. This hypothesis stacks exactly those.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three changes, all architecturally invisible (RVFI stream identical; cosim
CRCs must match; only cycle count may drop slightly):

1. Re-land r9s0 exactly as in experiments/log.jsonl (grep id
   hyp-20261002-001-r9s0, field `hypothesis` has the full design): extend
   ex_mem_t with EX-computed MEM controls (misalign, wen_q/ren_q, byte-lane
   pass/fill/sign one-hots, lo_sel, byte-replicated store word), registered
   in ex_stage from in.ctrl and jalr_sum[1:0]; mem_stage drives
   dmem_wen/ren/wdata straight from flops and builds m_result as a flat
   flop-selected AND-OR of dmem_rdata and alu_result; m_reg_write comes from
   the registered misalign-folded reg_write. Keep the ex_mem_t fields RVFI
   needs (mem_addr, rs?_val, mem_rdata...) unchanged.

2. Branch compare -> redir_q cone (ex_stage.sv, of_stage.sv, core_pkg.sv).
   a) Replace the separate signed `<`, unsigned `<` and equality compares by
      one equality plus ONE unsigned magnitude compare ltx on operands whose
      MSB is XOR-flipped for signed branches (BLT/BGE): add two O/X flops
      cmp_a31 / cmp_b31 = (post-forward rs?_d[31]) ^ (branch_op is BLT/BGE),
      produced in OF; the xor folds into the existing LUT that already
      selects x_result[31] vs early[31], so it adds no depth. In EX:
      ltx = {cmp_a31, rs1[30:0]} < {cmp_b31, rs2[30:0]};
      eq  = (rs1 == rs2);
      branch_cond = branch_op[0] ^ (branch_op[2] ? ltx : eq)
      (BEQ/BNE use eq; BLT/BGE/BLTU/BGEU use ltx; branch_op[0] inverts:
      BNE/BGE/BGEU). This removes one 32-bit carry chain and the 6-input
      branch_op case mux from the late path (4-input LUT after eq/ltx).
      branch_cond must still be exactly the old function for every branch
      op (non-branch ops don't care: their g_t == g_n below).
   b) Fold the late branch_cond into the D side of the redir_q flop as ONE
      final 2:1 select, keeping redir_q itself a plain flop (do NOT register
      the select after the flop; that is what made r10s1 lose):
        nb_mp = is_jalr ? mp_jr : is_jal ? mp_tgt : mp_seq;
        go    = ex_valid && !stall && !ex_busy;
        g_t   = redir_q ? stall : (go && (is_branch ? mp_tgt : nb_mp));
        g_n   = redir_q ? stall : (go && (is_branch ? mp_seq : nb_mp));
        redir_q <= branch_cond ? g_t : g_n;
      (sticky-while-stalled behaviour of the existing `redir_q <= stall`
      branch is preserved). The redir_tgt_*_q / redir_br_q capture is left
      as is.
      tr_taken / pc_next_w / misalign logic keep using the same branch_cond
      wire (they read the same function), so BTB training and RVFI pc_wdata
      are unchanged.

3. MUL latency 3 -> 2 busy cycles (muldiv.sv). The O/X flops already hold
   rs1_v/rs2_v and alu_op stable for the whole time an M op sits in EX, so
   the four 18x18 partial products can be formed from the `a`/`b`/`op`
   ports directly (sa/sb/ea/eb/a_lo/a_hi/b_lo/b_hi from op,a,b instead of
   op_q,a_q,b_q) and registered free-running at the end of the first EX
   cycle. Then S_IDLE on a multiply goes straight to S_MUL_SUM (S_MUL_PP is
   dropped); S_MUL_SUM still writes res_q using op_q and sets done_q. Busy
   cycles drop from c0,c1,c2 to c0,c1 (one fewer front-end hold per
   MUL/MULH*). a_q/b_q/op_q latching stays for the divider path. Under
   RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS muldiv is not exercised (is_muldiv forced 0), so the
   formal view is untouched; test_alu.py / cosim cover the arithmetic.
   CoreMark's matrix kernels issue roughly 3.7k multiplies per iteration,
   so this removes on the order of 35-40k of 4.23M cycles (~0.9%).

Do NOT change the ALU result select, redirect/redir_q fan-out structure,
the fetch queue, BTB, or regfile.

Expected: r9s0's ~+4% Fmax, plus ~+0.9% cycles from (3), plus a small
further Fmax gain from shortening the compare -> redir_q cone and removing a
32-bit comparator chain (less fan-out on rs1_v/rs2_v, less area). Because
placement noise is several percent, the implementer should run `make timing`
and check the top endpoints; if the branch-compare restructure measurably
regresses Fmax relative to r9s0 alone, drop change 2 and keep 1+3.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-001-r11s0 (regression, -2.42%): Stacking the single-compare branch cone (one `==` plus one unsigned `<` on MSB-flipped `cmp_a31`/`cmp_b31` O/X flops, late `branch_cond` folded into the D side of a still-plain-flop `redir_q` via `g_t`/`g_n`) and a 2-busy-cycle MUL on r9s0's MEM pre-decode scored 243.58, ~6% below the 259.80 r9s0 earned alone and below the 249.61 champion, so this is the third bundle on r9s0 (after r10s0 and r10s1) to land at 238-249 and, because `redir_q` stayed a true flop here, r10s1's "LUT in front of the redirect fan-out" explanation cannot be the whole story; the likelier reading is that r9s0's +4% was partly a lucky placement seed (its per-seed Fmax spread was 98.5/109.8/109.8 MHz, ~11%, far wider than the gain), and no `make timing` endpoints or cycle count were recorded here to attribute the loss between the compare restructure and the MUL change, so before building on r9s0 again, re-run it alone across several seeds and only land one cut per experiment with the top-N endpoint report attached.

title: Fanout-partitioned O/X: per-unit operand register copies, one merged add/sub chain, factored late-forward AND-OR
motivation:
A fresh `make timing` on the current RTL (place option 0, 93.9 MHz, data
delay ~10.6 ns) shows the top-25 setup paths are three bunched cones, all
rooted in the O/X operand flops or the dmem BSRAM, and NOT in the fetch /
decode front end (so a front-end D0 stage would be wasted):
  (1) dmem BSRAM DO -> u_mem shifted/m_result (5 LUTs) -> OF rs?_d/op?_d
      (2-3 LUTs) -> O/X opa/opb flops (9 levels, ~8.4 ns after tC2Q);
  (2) O/X opa/opb flop -> u_alu carry chain -> ALU result mux + x_result
      + OF forward mux (7 LUTs after the adder SUM, 6.7 ns, vs 3.7 ns for
      the adder itself) -> opa/opb flop;
  (3) O/X rs2_v/rs1_v -> branch compare carry chain -> redir_q.
In (2) and (3) the first net out of the operand flop alone costs 2.3-3.1 ns
(fanout 9-10: the same opa/opb/rs1_v/rs2_v flop feeds the add chain, the
separate SUB chain, the SLT/SLTU compare chains, the shifter, the logic
ops, the branch comparator and jalr_sum), and the post-adder mux depth is
what the one-hot ALU select (r10s0) failed to remove because x_result was
still a separate net feeding four OF forward muxes. Single-LUT-level
trims keep landing at +-4% because routing/fanout, not LUT depth, sets
these three cones; this change attacks fanout structurally and removes
adder duplication, instead of re-trimming a mux.

Restructure the O/X operand register file by consumer unit (cycle-identical,
no new stage):
1. Per-unit operand copies written from the same OF D value: opa/opb split
   into {add/sub chain copy, compare+shift copy, logic copy}; rs1_v/rs2_v
   keep only the branch comparator, jalr_sum and muldiv/store consumers.
   Each flop then drives <=3-4 loads so the 2.3-3.1 ns first-net delay
   collapses to ~1 ns. Copies are marked with the Gowin keep/preserve
   attribute so synthesis does not re-merge them.
2. Merge ADD and SUB into one carry chain: OF pre-inverts opb for SUB/SLT/
   SLTU and registers the carry-in, so alu.sv has one adder instead of an
   adder + a subtractor + two compare chains sharing nothing (less area,
   one fewer 32-way mux input, and the SLT/SLTU results come from the
   carry/sign of that same chain).
3. Factor the late forward into the ALU mux: with the ALU op class
   registered one-hot in O/X (add-class, logic-class, shift-class, md),
   OF builds operand D as  (late_add_sel & adder_sum) | other_term, where
   other_term (logic/shift/slt/md/early operand mux) is computed in
   parallel, so the adder SUM crosses exactly one LUT3 between the carry
