title: BTB-triggered single-loop replay buffer: flop-gated in_valid hides imem stalls inside hot loops
motivation:
Pure direction/target predictor work is capped: ~82k mispredicts at 2-3 cycles
each is only ~3-5% of the 4.226M CoreMark cycles (LESSONS r3s2: "pure predictor
work is capped"; r7s2: a deeper serial predictor lost a third of Fmax). The
real front-end limit is fetch bandwidth: 2.94M instructions over a bus that
is not ready 22% of cycles bounds fetch at ~0.78 instr/cycle (~3.77M cycles
minimum, vs 4.226M actual), so the BTB already has the loop structure but
every iteration of every hot loop still pays the 22% bus-stall tax per
fetched word. Three icache attempts (r7s1, r8s1, r9s1) recovered ~9-10% of
cycles but lost >=12% Fmax because a tag-compare `ic_hit` (async array or
BSRAM tCO) fed `fire`/pc/BSRAM address. The missing piece is a replay
source whose *control* is flop-only: the BTB already identifies backward
taken branches, so a one-loop capture/replay buffer can be armed by BTB
state instead of a per-fetch tag compare.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a single-loop replay buffer (<=16 words, LUT-RAM 16x32 + a handful of
flops) driven by the BTB's predicted-taken-backward event.

Capture: when a fetch fires with btb_taken && pred_target < pc (backward,
loop body <= 16 words, i.e. pc[5:2]-target[5:2] small and no 64B window
wrap issue) and the buffer is not already valid for that loop, latch
loop_start (18b) and loop_branch_pc (18b), reset cap_idx, set `capturing`.
While capturing, every fired fetch writes imem_data into buf[pc - loop_start]
(index from a flop counter, not from a compare); when the fetch at
loop_branch_pc fires, set buf_valid <= 1 and capturing <= 0. Any redirect
(redir_q) or a fetch that leaves [loop_start, loop_branch_pc] clears
capturing/buf_valid (cheap: range check is only on the capture path).

Replay: when buf_valid and the BTB predicts a taken hit whose target equals
the stored loop_start (18b equality on btb_target vs flop, evaluated while
the fetch of loop_branch_pc fires) set `replay_q <= 1`, rep_idx <= 0. While
replay_q the fetch pc keeps following the normal BTB/pc+4 path (so every
entry still carries its own pred_taken/pred_npc/pred_hit/pred_ctr and EX
still verifies everything -- a wrong or stale replay is just a mispredict,
the formal flow's symbolic imem stays safe), but:
  in_valid  = imem_ready || replay_q            (OR of a pin and a FLOP)
  in.instr  = replay_q ? buf[rep_idx] : imem_data   (data mux at the queue
              write port only)
rep_idx advances with fire; when the entry at loop_branch_pc is pushed and
the BTB still predicts it taken, replay continues (rep_idx wraps to 0);
otherwise (not-taken prediction / redirect from the loop-exit mispredict)
replay_q clears. replay_q is cleared by redir_q (flush), so the exit
mispredict is handled by the existing registered redirect, no new redirect
path.

Correctness rule (IMPORTANT): EX verifies only the predicted next PC, never
the instruction word, so the buffer must only ever supply a word equal to
imem content at that pc. (1) Capture only straight-line loop bodies: capture
starts at the fire whose pc == loop_start, writes buf[cap_idx++] on every
consecutive fire, and is aborted (capturing/buf_valid <= 0) by a redirect or
by any fire with pred_taken that is not the closing branch (pc == the stored
loop_branch_pc with pred_target == loop_start); buf_valid is set only when
the closing branch fires with cap_idx == body length-1, so every word
loop_start..loop_branch_pc was written sequentially. (2) During replay the
word at rep_idx is correct only while the fetch pc is loop_start+rep_idx, so
on every replay fire clear replay_q (flop D-input only, off the fire/pc
cone) unless the BTB prediction agrees with the stored loop shape:
(pred_taken && pred_target == loop_start) at rep_idx == last, or
!pred_taken at rep_idx < last. A disagreement merely falls back to normal
imem fetch from the next cycle (the word already issued is still correct).
Bodies longer than 16 words, or with taken inner branches, are simply never
captured. (3) Clear buf_valid on any store that hits the dmem-visible code
region only if cheap; otherwise document that CoreMark code is never
written (the ISS cosim and formal flow cannot observe this).

Timing discipline (the lesson of the three icache failures): `fire` gains
only a flop OR-term, never a tag compare or array-read result; the replay
data mux lives on the fetch-queue *write data*, never on the control cone;
the empty-queue zero-latency bypass stays imem_data-only (head bypass
disabled while replay_q so decode/regfile-address cone u_if/u_fq -> u_id ->
u_rf (r10s0 worst path) does not gain a LUT-RAM read; replayed entries are
consumed through the queue storage, a +1 latency that is invisible in a
streaming loop). No change to EX, OF, hazard, BTB training, RAS, or the
RVFI path; the buffer is not coherent with stores, which is fine for the
benchmark's non-self-modifying code and for the formal flow (insn is only
required to be self-consistent per retirement).

Expected effect: hot CoreMark inner loops (CRC bit loop, matrix inner
loops, list find loop) are captured after one iteration; replayed words
skip the 22% imem-ready roll, which is the dominant fetch-bound term.
Estimated 3-6% fewer cycles (cosim cycle count must be checked first: if
cycles do not drop >=3% abort rather than land), Fmax expected ~flat since
the only fetch-control change is `imem_ready || replay_q`. Area: 16x32b
LUT-RAM (~32 LUT4-equivalents of RAM16) + ~60 flops.

Take a `replay` input: keep the empty-queue head bypass imem-only (head_valid/head_e bypass gated off while replay is active so replayed entries go through mem[]), and accept the muxed instr on the write port unchanged.
No port change; only wiring if the BTB hit/taken/target signals or redirect need to be passed differently into if_stage.
No functional change expected (replay is armed from the existing pred_taken/pred_target outputs); optionally expose a registered backward-taken flag if the target<pc compare proves slow.

title: Trade a fetch-hidden load-use bubble for Fmax: stop forwarding MEM load data into OF, forward loads only from the MEM/WB flop
motivation:
CoreMark is fetch-bound: 2.94M instructions over a bus that is ready 78% of
cycles gives a fetch floor of ~3.77M cycles against 4.226M measured. A
cosim run with the fetch queue deepened from 4 to 8 entries (AW=3, the only
change) moved the bracketed cycle count 4,225,873 -> 4,218,990 (-0.16%), so
the queue is rarely full: the decode side has slack and fetch, not the
backend, sets CPI, and backend stall cycles (load-use, dmem) are largely
absorbed. Cycle-neutral Fmax trims have all stalled at placement-noise
level, but the champion's logged worst path is the one cone that is paid for
purely by backend IPC: dmem BSRAM tCO -> byte-lane align / sign extend ->
m_result -> OF forward mux -> O/X opb/opa/rs?_v flop (15.94 ns, 9 cells,
clock_ibuf > u_mem > u_of). That MEM -> OF load forward is what keeps a
load-use pair at one bubble; since the backend is not the bottleneck, one more
bubble should cost little, while it removes the slowest cone.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Remove the combinational MEM -> OF forward of load data. Loads become
visible to a dependent instruction only from the MEM/WB wb_data flop (the
existing dist-3 forward), and the load-align result then ends at the MEM/WB
wb_data flop instead of fanning into the OF operand muxes.
Changes: (1) core.sv / of_stage: the dist-2 (MEM) forward source becomes the
EX/MEM flop `alu_result` with forward-valid = ex_mem.ctrl.reg_write &&
!ex_mem.ctrl.mem_to_reg (both flop-fed; misalign only affects mem ops, and
stores have reg_write=0, so the post-trap term is not needed for the
non-load case). mem_stage keeps m_result for the wb_data flop only.
(2) hazard_unit: add a second load-use term, `exmem_mem_read &&
(exmem_rd == do_rs1 || exmem_rd == do_rs2) && exmem_rd != 0`, OR-ed into
load_use_hazard (stall_id + bubble_ox): a consumer directly behind a load
now waits two cycles (load in EX, then load in MEM) and the consumer two
behind waits one; all compares are flop-fed. The existing dmem-stall hold
logic is unchanged (a load held in MEM already holds D/O/O/X).
(3) forward_unit: fwd[1] valid flag uses the new non-load forward-valid.
RVFI, the ALTOPS formal view and the decoder are untouched.
Cycle model: extra bubbles hit only load-use pairs (~5% of instructions
dist-1, ~3% dist-2), which a mostly-empty fetch queue absorbs; expected CPI
cost 1-3%. Fmax: the MEM-load cone drops ~4 LUT levels (align + 2 forward
muxes) and BSRAM tCO no longer feeds the OF operand flops; the ALU ->
x_result and branch-compare cones stay at ~15-16 ns so the realised gain
is bounded by them (r9s0 cut this same cone by predecode and got +4% alone).
Gate: run cosim first; if cycles grow more than ~3% abandon. Land this
alone (past bundles stacked on MEM changes lost to seed noise); attach
`make timing` top-N endpoints.

title: Non-blocking pipelined multiplier: EX partial products, MEM sum into wb_data, mul-use interlock instead of a 3-cycle whole-pipe stall
motivation:
The core is balanced between two limits: the fetch floor (2.94M instructions /
0.78 bus words per cycle = ~3.77M cycles) and the backend, which freezes
D/O and O/X whenever muldiv is busy. MUL/MULH* currently hold the whole
front end for 3 busy cycles (latch operands, partial products, 3-term sum)
and DIV for 35. The fetch queue (4 entries) cannot absorb that on the many
mul-heavy CoreMark matrix loops: r11s0 cut MUL from 3 to 2 busy cycles and
nothing else that changes cycles, and cycles fell 4,225,873 -> 4,143,688
(-1.9%, ~82k cycles per busy cycle removed). So the multiplier's blocking
behaviour is a measured, still-unclaimed cycle cost of roughly 5-6% in total.
Every fetch-side/predictor/icache idea has either been capped (<5% cycles)
or lost double-digit Fmax (r7s1, r8s1, r9s1, r10s2), whereas the multiplier
is far from the BTB/fetch cone and from the EX->x_result, branch-compare and
MEM load-align cones that bound Fmax, so a cycle gain here is "free" in
timing terms.

pipelined 3-stage operation (EX -> MEM -> WB) that never stalls the
pipeline; only DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU keep the existing blocking muldiv FSM.
Dependents interlock exactly like load-use (bubble in O/X, instruction held
in OF), independent instructions flow past the multiply.

1) rtl/core_pkg.sv: ox_t gains `is_mul` (pre-decoded, alu_op in
   ALU_MUL..ALU_MULHU+MULHSU range) and `is_md` is narrowed to the divide
   ops only (rename or keep the name `is_md` meaning "blocking M op" and add
   `is_mul`). ex_mem_t gains `is_mul` and `mul_hi` (op != ALU_MUL), both
   cleared by the existing bubble/reset paths.
2) rtl/of_stage.sv: pre-decode is_mul = (alu_op in {MUL,MULH,MULHU,MULHSU})
   and is_md = (alu_op >= ALU_DIV && <= ALU_REMU) into O/X flops, cleared on
   bubble/reset like the existing is_md. Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS both stay
   0 (the ALU algebraic stand-ins are what formal sees, exactly as today).
3) rtl/muldiv.sv: add parameter HAS_MUL (default 1 so test_muldiv.py is
   unchanged). With HAS_MUL=0 the S_MUL_PP/S_MUL_SUM states, the four 18x18
   products, the pp_* registers and `prod` are not elaborated; the FSM only
   handles the divider. ex_stage instantiates it with HAS_MUL=0 and
   req = is_md && ex_valid, so ex_busy / the hold cone only exists for DIV.
4) rtl/ex_stage.sv: in EX, build the four signed 18x18 partial products
   straight from the O/X flops (rs1_v/rs2_v, sign extension controlled by
   the O/X alu_op: ea/eb as in muldiv.sv today: MULH signs both, MULHSU
   signs a only) and register them in free-running pp_ll/pp_lh/pp_hl/pp_hh
   flops (same 34/33/33/30-bit trimming as muldiv.sv). The regs are
   free-running on purpose: a dmem stall needs a memory op in MEM, so a MUL
   in MEM is never held; no enable/mux on them. The EX/MEM register
   additionally captures is_mul / mul_hi (flop-decoded from O/X, so the
   usual stall-hold / bubble behaviour applies). x_result keeps
   `is_md ? md_result : alu_result` (ALU returns 0 for M ops, never used
   for a MUL because dependents are interlocked).
5) rtl/mem_stage.sv: when the MEM instruction is a MUL, sum the partial
   products (pp_mid = lh + hl, then {hh,ll} + (pp_mid << 17) — the same
   3-term add muldiv.sv already closes in one cycle at 105 MHz) and write
   the selected half into MEM/WB.wb_data: wb_data <= in.is_mul ?
   (in.mul_hi ? prod[63:32] : prod[31:0]) : m_result. m_result itself
   (the combinational dist-2 forward into the OF operand flops) must NOT
   include the multiplier sum: its cone (BSRAM load align -> m_result ->
   OF flops) is already one of the bunched critical cones. The extra 2:1
   on the wb_data flop D-input is the only added level and ends at a flop.
   RVFI rd_wdata still comes from wb_data, so retirement of a MUL shows
   the right value one stage later, in order.
6) rtl/hazard_unit.sv (+ rtl/core.sv wiring): mul-use interlock, folded
   into the existing load-use term so stall_id / bubble_ox keep one
   flop-fed compare structure: mul_hazard = ((ox_is_mul && ox_rd matches
   do_rs1/do_rs2) || (exmem_is_mul && exmem_rd matches do_rs1/do_rs2))
   && rd != 0. While it is asserted D/O holds and O/X takes a bubble (two
   cycles for a back-to-back consumer); the third cycle the MUL sits in WB
   and the existing dist-3 forward (mem_wb.wb_data -> OF early mux) supplies
   the value, so forward_unit.sv and the OF muxes are unchanged. Spurious
   stalls from a younger writer of the same rd only cost a cycle, never
   correctness (younger producers win the existing fwd priority).
7) rtl/ex_stage.sv: with MUL out of the busy FSM the ex_busy / hold_ox
   / bubble-into-EX/MEM path only triggers for divides, which shortens that
   cone for the common case and removes the 3-cycle freeze (including the
   fetch-queue-full stalls it caused).
8) test/test_muldiv.py keeps passing as-is (HAS_MUL=1 default); add a
   test_pipeline.py case with back-to-back MUL->use, MUL;ADD;use and
   MUL followed by a load/store, and a redirect behind a MUL, checking the
   RVFI rd_wdata. Cosim against the Python ISS (every MUL/MULH* retirement)
   and riscv-formal (ALTOPS: the new paths are disabled, only the hazard /
   bypass wiring is exercised) are the correctness gates; do not touch the
   ALTOPS branch of alu.sv.

Expected effect: ~82k cycles per removed busy cycle (r11s0 data point).
Back-to-back MUL->use goes 3 -> 2 bubbles (~-1.9% cycles); independent
instructions (unrolled matrix loops, address arithmetic, loop counters) now
overlap the remaining latency entirely, so the total should land at about
-3..-5% cycles with Fmax unchanged or slightly better (shorter ex_busy
cone, +1 LUT on the wb_data flop only). Risks: a DSP-multiplier input from
the heavily-loaded O/X rs1_v/rs2_v flops adds fanout to the operand flops;
the MEM-stage 64-bit sum next to the BSRAM load path is a new endpoint
(wb_data) — keep the product registers narrow and the sum out of m_result.
Land this change alone (no MEM byte-lane pre-decode, no compare
restructuring: the r10/r11 bundles showed stacked cone cuts are not
additive).

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-002-r12s1 (regression, -5.39%): Turning MUL/MULH* into a non-blocking EX (four 18x18 partial-product flops fed from the O/X `rs1_v`/`rs2_v` flops) -> MEM (3-term sum into `wb_data`) -> WB op with a mul-use term added to the load-use interlock scored 236.16 vs the 249.61 champion, and since removing every multiplier busy cycle was worth at most ~5-6% cycles (~82k cycles per busy cycle, r11s0 data point) the loss implies Fmax fell by at least ~5%, so the premise that the multiplier is "far from the Fmax cones" was wrong; the likely culprits are the extra DSP loads on the already heavily fanned-out operand flops, the 64-bit sum ending at a new `wb_data` endpoint next to the BSRAM load-align path, and extra `ex_mem_rd`/`ox_rd` compares in the `stall_id`/`bubble_ox` cone, but no cycle count or `make timing` was recorded to split them, so before retrying measure cycles separately from Fmax and keep a cycle-only M-unit change off the operand-flop and hazard cones (e.g. add MUL latency in the muldiv FSM instead of new pipeline-stage hardware), since a ceiling of ~5% cycles cannot pay for even a small Fmax loss.

title: Parallel gshare direction table beside the pc-indexed BTB, with fetch-time speculative GHR flop
motivation:
Pure target prediction is saturated: the 32-entry BTB + 4-entry RAS already
removes returns and most JAL/capacity misses, and the remaining ~40k
CoreMark mispredicts are data-dependent conditional-branch direction errors
(r3s2 trace model: even a 256-entry 2-way BTB leaves ~40.5k). Each costs 3
cycles (EX detect, registered redir_q, refetch -> ID -> OF -> EX), so the
direction half is the only predictor lever left. Past direction work failed
on Fmax, not on idea: r7s2's local-history predictor put a serial LUT-RAM
chain (pc -> hist_arr -> pht_arr -> pred_taken -> next_pc) on the fetch
cone and lost a third of Fmax. The fix is to keep prediction ONE LUT-RAM
level: index a small direction table with pc XOR a GHR *flop*, in parallel
with (never behind) the BTB tag/target read.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Split direction from target. Keep btb.sv's tag/target/valid/is_ret arrays
and RAS exactly as they are (pc[6:2]-indexed, so tag compare and target
read are unchanged). Replace the per-entry 2-bit ctr_arr read in the
taken decision by a separate 64-entry x 2-bit gshare table dir_arr
(LUT-RAM, async read) indexed by {pc[7:2]} ^ {ghr[5:0]}. The ghr is a
6-bit flop vector, so the index is one XOR LUT off two flop sources and
the dir_arr read runs in parallel with the BTB tag compare (a 13-bit
compare is deeper than xor+RAM read), i.e. pred_taken = hit && (is_ret ||
dir_ctr[1]) gains no LUT level over today's ctr_rd[1].
JAL entries and returns keep ignoring the direction table (always taken:
a per-entry `uncond` bit replaces the ctr==3 JAL trick), so the table is
trained only by conditional branches and is not polluted.

GHR: speculative at fetch, repaired by the existing registered redirect.
When a fetch with btb hit predicts a conditional branch (hit && !uncond)
the GHR shifts in pred_taken; a BTB miss shifts nothing (the miss is
later corrected by training, see below). To avoid any imem_data decode
in IF, the GHR is NOT updated for fetches that are not BTB hits -- a
not-taken branch with no BTB entry is invisible to history, which is
acceptable (history then encodes taken/hit-branch outcomes only, the
classic BTB-gated gshare). Each fetched entry carries its 6-bit pre-update
GHR down the pipe (if_id_t -> id_ex_t -> ox_t, +6 flops per stage, +6
queue-entry bits) so (a) EX trains dir_arr at the SAME index the
prediction used, via the existing registered tr_*_q path (tr_pc_q gets a
tr_ghr_q sibling; write lands one cycle after EX like the BTB write), and
(b) on a mispredicted conditional branch the repaired history
{ghr_in_ex[4:0], actual_taken} is registered together with redir_q
(extra flops beside redir_tgt_*_q, selected after the flop by the same
redir_br_q bit, no new late compare fan-out) and loaded into the GHR in
the redirect cycle, exactly when pc is loaded.  Mispredicts of non-branch
CTIs (JAL/JALR/aliased hit) reload the carried ghr unchanged.

Allocation/training: a taken conditional branch that missed the BTB still
allocates tag/target exactly as today and initialises its dir_arr
counter at weakly-taken (2) at its CARRIED index; a not-taken branch that
hit decrements. Because dir_arr is indexed by history, a branch can have
several counters (one per history) -- the intended gshare benefit for
correlated CoreMark branches (CRC bit tests, state machine, list
compares) over the single per-pc counter. The per-entry ctr_arr is
deleted (saves 32x2b LUT-RAM; dir_arr is 64x2b), and pred_ctr/tr_ctr/
pred_hit pipeline fields shrink to the carried ghr.

Safety: every prediction is still verified in EX against its own pred_npc
(mp_seq/mp_btgt/jalr compare), so wrong history, aliasing, stale GHR and
the formal flow's symbolic imem can only cost a redirect, never
correctness. The GHR is architecturally invisible (no RVFI dependency).
Formal tractability: state added is 6 flops + 64x2b array + 6-bit carried
fields; no redirect-cycle fetch bypass (the construct that blew the
r4s2/r8s2 formal budget) and no BTB growth.

Fmax guard rails (lessons r7s1/r7s2/r10s2): the fetch cone must stay
one RAM level -- dir_arr is read only from {pc flop, ghr flop}; the GHR
D-input is a function of flops plus `fire` (already on the fetch cone) and
the registered redirect repair value, nothing from EX combinationally;
do not add anything array-valued to the fetch-queue entry beyond the 6
ghr bits. If `make timing` shows the fetch cone (u_if/pc -> u_btb ->
next_pc) arriving later than the current ~15-16 ns critical endpoints,
cut GHR to 4 bits / dir_arr to 16 entries before abandoning the idea.
Cycle expectation from the r3s2-style trace model (to be re-run by the
implementer on the CoreMark branch trace before committing RTL): direction
mispredicts ~41k -> ~30-33k, i.e. ~25-35k cycles of 4.226M (~0.7%) from
direction alone, plus slightly better allocation behaviour; this is a
low-confidence cycle gain and the score hinges on Fmax staying flat.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-003-r12s2 (regression, -3.35%): Splitting direction from target (64x2b `dir_arr` read in parallel off the pc flop, a per-entry `uncond` flop, a 6-bit speculative GHR flop repaired by the registered redirect, `pred_ghr`/`tr_ghr` carried down the if/id/ox pipe) scored 241.25 vs the 249.61 champion even though it followed r7s2's "keep prediction one LUT-RAM level" rule, and the shipped RTL has history masked out (`HB = 0`, so `dir_idx = pc[7:2]`, a plain pc-indexed counter table), implying no history length beat a per-pc counter on CoreMark and that what remained was a second async array read plus GHR/counter-update logic on the registered-pc -> `pred_taken` -> `next_pc`/`fire` cone; one LUT-RAM level deep is therefore necessary but not sufficient for Fmax-neutral prediction, and with a ~0.7% direction-cycle ceiling any extra fetch-side array or flop fan-out loses more than it earns, so don't retry gshare/split direction tables without a `make timing` fetch-cone arrival (none was logged here, so the Fmax-vs-cycles split is inferred) and treat further predictor work on this core as exhausted.

title: EX-predecoded MEM load-align controls plus a 2-busy-cycle MUL fed straight from the O/X operand flops
motivation:
Cycles and Fmax each have one measured, nearly free lever on this base, and
neither clears the 4.6% bar alone.
Fmax: r9s0 predecoded every MEM byte-lane select in EX (registered one-hot
lane/sign/fill selects, misalign folded into the registered reg_write) so the
dmem read data crosses one flat flop-selected AND-OR on its way into the OF
forward mux. It was cycle-identical and scored 259.80 (Fmax 109.787, seeds
98.5/109.8/109.8), +4.08%: 0.5% short. Its worst path moved off the
BSRAM -> m_result -> OF cone (the champion's 15.941 ns path) onto
rs2_v -> branch compare -> redir_q.
Cycles: r11s0 measured the MUL latency directly. With a 2-busy-cycle MUL the
CoreMark cycle count fell 4,225,873 -> 4,143,688 (-1.95%). r11s0 stacked that
on a branch-compare restructure and lost Fmax (100.9 MHz), but its worst path
was the ALU -> x_result -> OF cone, which the compare edit touches and the MUL
edit does not. The loss was not attributed. The stacking lessons (r10s0,
r10s1, r11s0, r11s1) all added cuts to the EX/OF cones. This bundle adds no
logic to any EX/OF/redirect cone.
Cycles are fetch-bound with a mostly empty queue and backend stalls only
partly overlap, so a 1-cycle-shorter MUL saves about 82k cycles (measured),
not the 3-cycle x MUL-count upper bound.
Required Fmax for >4.6%: fitness is proportional to Fmax / cycles, so the
target is Fmax >= 105.482 x 1.046 x (4,143,688 / 4,225,873) = 108.2 MHz.
r9s0 alone measured 109.8.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two independent edits. Neither adds logic to the ALU -> x_result, branch
compare -> redir_q, or hazard cones. They are landed together only because
each alone lands under the bar (r9s0 +4.08%, MUL-only about +2%), and the
evaluator draws a placement per netlist.

(1) MEM load-align predecode (re-land of r9s0; read its log.jsonl entry for
the full field list). In ex_stage, computed from the jalr_sum low bits,
ctrl.mem_width, ctrl.mem_sext, ctrl.mem_read/mem_write, register in EX/MEM
(ex_mem_t gains the fields):
  - misalign (1b): drives dmem_wen/dmem_ren gating, and clears reg_write /
    sets is_illegal in the registered ctrl copy, so mem_stage no longer
    computes it.
  - registered dmem_wen[3:0] and dmem_ren, so the BSRAM write/read enables
    and byte mask come straight from flops (the replicated store word is
    also built in EX).
  - load result byte-lane controls: lo_sel[1:0] (source byte for result bits
    [7:0]), a one-hot sgn_sel[3:0] (which rdata byte MSB is the sign bit,
    all-zero for zero-extend / word), and per-upper-byte pass/fill flags
    (result[15:8] = pass ? rdata byte : {8{sign}}, etc.).
  m_result in mem_stage becomes a flat AND-OR of rdata bytes with those
  flop-fed selects, then one mem_to_reg 2:1 against alu_result. RVFI-only
  fields (mem_rmask/mem_wmask/mem_addr in MEM/WB) keep their current values
  so cosim stays identical. Any ex_mem_t field consumed only by RVFI is
  pruned in the timed netlist.

(2) 2-busy-cycle MUL. The O/X register already holds rs1_v/rs2_v and
ctrl.alu_op stable for the whole time an M op sits in EX (hold_ox on
ex_busy / dmem_stall). So muldiv's multiply path does not need the c0
operand latch:
  - the free-running partial-product registers (pp_ll/pp_lh/pp_hl/pp_hh)
    take a/b and op directly from the muldiv inputs (the O/X flops)
    instead of a_q/b_q/op_q. The sa/sb/ea/eb sign-extension terms use
    `op`, not op_q;
  - S_IDLE with req and op < ALU_DIV goes straight to S_MUL_SUM (skipping
    S_MUL_PP). pp regs capture at the end of c0, S_MUL_SUM (c1) writes res_q
    from prod using `op` for the MUL vs MULH* select, done is high in c2.
    busy cycles = 2, down from 3;
  - the divider path, a_q/b_q/op_q latches, a_lat/b_lat outputs and the DIV
    FSM states are unchanged, so DIV timing and test_muldiv.py's latched-
    operand checks are untouched. Update test_muldiv.py's
    `2 <= mul_cycles <= 6` bound only if it fails (2 is already allowed).
Expected cosim cycle count is about 4,143,688 (r11s0's figure for the same
MUL change). Gate: run cosim first and confirm CRCs plus that the cycle count
fell by about 1.9%. DSP loads on rs1_v/rs2_v replace the existing a_q/b_q
enable-gated loads (the latch stays for DIV), so the operand-flop fanout is
roughly unchanged. Do not touch the branch compare, redir_q, the ALU, the
hazard unit, OF forwarding, the fetch queue or the BTB.

Extend ex_mem_t with the EX-predecoded MEM controls (misalign, registered dmem_wen/dmem_ren, lo_sel, one-hot sgn_sel, per-byte pass/fill flags, replicated store word). Existing fields stay for RVFI.

Compute the MEM byte-lane controls from jalr_sum[1:0] / ctrl.mem_width / mem_sext / mem_read / mem_write and register them in EX/MEM; fold misalign into the registered ctrl (is_illegal, reg_write). Pass the muldiv unit unchanged ports.

Drive dmem_wen/dmem_ren/dmem_wdata straight from the EX/MEM flops and build load_data as a flat flop-selected AND-OR of the dmem_rdata bytes; m_result = mem_to_reg ? load_data : alu_result. MEM/WB RVFI fields (mem_addr, rmask, wmask, rdata, wdata) keep identical values.

Feed the pp_* partial-product registers and the sa/sb/ea/eb sign terms from the live a/b/op inputs (O/X flops), skip S_MUL_PP so MUL takes 2 busy cycles; keep a_q/b_q/op_q, a_lat/b_lat and the divider path unchanged.
Adjust the multiply latency bound / operand-hold assumptions only if the new 2-cycle MUL fails them (operands must be held for the whole multiply, as the O/X register does).

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-001-r13s0 (regression, -4.87%): Re-landing r9s0's EX-predecoded MEM controls with a 2-busy-cycle MUL whose partial-product DSP registers read the O/X `rs1_v`/`rs2_v` flops directly (a_q/b_q latch kept only for DIV; no branch-compare, ALU, hazard or OF edit) scored 237.46, which at the expected ~4.144M cycles implies only ~98 MHz (vs the 108.2 MHz needed and r9s0's 109.8), and since r11s0 (243.58, ~100.9 MHz at the same cycle count) and r12s1 (236.16) also fed multiplier DSPs from those flops while r10s0/r10s1 (neither touched the multiplier) landed at 249.17/238.58, the common suspect is no longer the compare/ALU/one-hot cuts but the MUL operand source: the dedicated `a_q`/`b_q` latch kept the fixed-site DSP18 columns off the operand flops that already fan out to the ALU, branch compare and OF forward muxes, and "DSP loads replace a_q/b_q loads so fanout is unchanged" ignores that DSP placement pulls those flops (and their ALU/compare routes) apart; the cycle count and `make timing` endpoints were not recorded so this is inferred from fitness, but since the -1.95% MUL saving cannot cover a ~10% Fmax loss, keep the muldiv operand latch (take the 2nd busy cycle by other means, or none) and judge r9s0's +4% against its 98.5/109.8/109.8 per-seed spread before stacking anything on it.

title: Flop-addressed stall-supplement icache: dual sequential/held-pc read ports, all hit control from flops
motivation:
CoreMark is fetch-bound: 2.94M instructions over a bus that is not ready 22%
of cycles gives a fetch floor of ~3.77M cycles against 4.226M measured, and
backend/queue tweaks cannot move it (deepening the fetch queue 4->8 changed
cycles by only -0.16%). Predictor, MEM-cone and single-cone Fmax trims have
all stalled at +-5% placement noise (r9s0 +4.08%, r10s*, r11s*, r12s* all
regressions). The only lever with a >=9% cycle ceiling is an instruction
store that supplies a word when the bus does not: r8s1's sync-BSRAM
"bus-stall supplement" cache reached 3.83M cycles (-9.4%), and r9s1 on the
r8s0 base reached 3.82M. Both lost more Fmax than they gained (94.6 / 92.2
MHz vs 105.5), and r9s1's lesson names the cause: the BSRAM read index was
pc_d, i.e. the late next-pc (fire / redirect / BTB target), so `fire` ->
`pc_d` -> 10 BSRAM address pins was a new critical cone, and `ic_hit` gated
`fire`. A cache whose address and hit/select signals are all functions of
flops (never of next_pc or fire) removes that cone while keeping the cycle
gain. At ~3.82M cycles the score clears the 4.6% bar (>=261) as long as Fmax
stays >= ~100 MHz (-5%); the two failed designs gave up 10-12%.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add rtl/icache.sv, a 1024-word direct-mapped instruction store (data in
BSRAM, tag+valid in a small array) used ONLY to supply a word in a cycle
where the bus is not ready. Fetch keeps its current bus-first behaviour, so
cache logic never sits in front of the bus path and the empty-queue bypass
keeps the bus data only. The cache is read with two flop-fed addresses every
cycle, so hit/data are available as flop/BSRAM outputs one cycle later with
no dependence on `fire`, `redirect` or the BTB target:
  - seq read : index = pc[11:2] + 1 (an incrementer on the pc flop). Valid for
    use next cycle iff the fetch advanced sequentially this cycle; that
    condition (fire && !pred_taken && !redirect) is registered into
    `seq_ok_q`, so it ends at a flop.
  - hold read: index = pc[11:2] (the pc flop itself). Valid for use next
    cycle iff the fetch did NOT advance this cycle (held pc after a bus
    stall); registered into `hold_ok_q`.
The two read results are separate registered outputs (two BSRAM read ports /
two mirrored arrays written identically). Tag+valid compare for BOTH reads is
done in the cycle of the read on LUT-RAM tag arrays addressed by flop-derived
indices and registered as `hit_seq_q` / `hit_hold_q`, so the BSRAM tCO never
feeds a compare. In the next cycle a flop-only select
`sup_q = (seq_ok_q & hit_seq_q) | (hold_ok_q & hit_hold_q)` marks that the
cache holds the word for the current fpc, and
  in_valid = imem_ready | sup_q,  instr = imem_ready ? imem_data : cache_data.
`sup_q` is flop-fed, so `fire` gains one OR of two flops, not a tag compare.
Cache-supplied entries always go through the fetch-queue storage (no
zero-latency bypass for them) so BSRAM tCO never reaches decode/regfile
address cones; bus-supplied entries keep the existing bypass unchanged. The
fill port writes {tag, instr} whenever the bus delivers (imem_ready && fire)
at index pc[11:2] (one write port, BSRAM write is synchronous). Prediction
(BTB, RAS), EX verification of every prediction, the registered redirect and
formal behaviour are untouched: a stale/aliased cache word would be a wrong
instruction, so tags carry pc[19:12] (8b + valid), the cache is flushed
by nothing (memory is read-only in the benchmark; under riscv-formal the
symbolic imem makes any replayed word a legal earlier fetch of an unchanged
memory, and rvfi_insn reports the instruction actually executed). Expected
effect: cycles 4.226M -> ~3.85M; Fmax cost should be small because the new
logic ends at flops, adds no load to the BTB -> next_pc cone, and puts no
late signal on any BSRAM address pin. Measure with `make timing` (top-N
endpoints) before and after, and log cycles separately; if the BSRAM
address incrementer or the in_valid OR shows up as the worst path, shrink
the cache to LUT-RAM (256 words) rather than dropping flop-only control.

changes.description: New module: 1024-word direct-mapped store, BSRAM data with two flop-addressed read ports (pc+1 index and held pc index) and one fill port at the fetch pc index; LUT-RAM tag+valid array read with the same two indices and compared in the read cycle; outputs data_seq/data_hold, registered hit_seq_q/hit_hold_q.

Instantiate icache; register seq_ok_q (fire && !pred_taken && !redirect) and hold_ok_q (!fire && !redirect); form sup_q from flops; in_valid = imem_ready | sup_q; incoming fetch entry instr selects bus data when imem_ready else cache data; fill the cache when the bus delivers; mark cache-supplied entries so the queue does not bypass them.

Accept a no-bypass flag on the incoming entry: when set, the entry is pushed into storage and head_valid/head_e ignore the bypass for it (bus-supplied entries keep the zero-latency bypass); fire/pointer logic otherwise unchanged.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-002-r13s1 (regression, -3.51%): The flop-addressed stall-supplement icache (sequential `pc+1` and held-`pc` read ports, tag compare registered into `hit_seq_q`/`hit_hold_q`, flop-only `sup_q`, no `fire`/`pc_d`/BTB target on any BSRAM address pin) scored 240.84 vs the 249.61 champion, essentially r9s1's 241.69, which at the ~3.82M-cycle target implies Fmax again fell to ~92 MHz (-12%), so r9s1's diagnosis that the `fire` -> `pc_d` -> BSRAM-address cone was the cost is refuted: that cone is gone yet the loss is the same, leaving what every icache variant (r7s1, r8s1, r9s1, r13s1) shares as the suspects, namely `in_valid = imem_ready | sup` still sitting in `fire` (queue push, pc advance, `in_e.pc` fan-out), the new `imem_ready ? imem_data : ic_data` mux plus the fill port added on the bus-data -> queue-write path, and 1024-word BSRAM plus tag arrays pulling fetch-side placement apart; no cycle count or `make timing` was recorded (icache.sv was not retained), so the cycle gain and attribution are inferred from fitness, but four icache designs landing at -6% to -3% (or break-even on a slower base) says to stop trying instruction-store supplements for the ~22% imem-bubble floor unless a single run first logs cycles and the `fire`/bus-data endpoint arrivals.

title: BTB-trained single-loop replay buffer: flop-controlled instruction replay that removes imem stalls inside hot loops
motivation:
Pure target/direction prediction is capped. I modelled the 32-entry BTB+RAS on
the ISS CTI trace: ~57k mispredicts (~4-5% of the 4.226M cycles even if made
perfect, below the 4.6% bar); an infinite BTB still leaves ~40k, almost all
data-dependent direction misses (gshare / local history already tried and lost
Fmax for no gain). The two obvious "predictor" ideas are dead: non-return JALR
targets execute only 22 times in the whole CoreMark run (indirect calls get
inlined at -O3), and a wider/deeper BTB loses to the fetch-cone Fmax cost.
The real limiter is fetch bandwidth: 2.937M instructions over an imem bus that
is not ready 22% of cycles is a ~3.77M-cycle floor against 4.226M measured, and
a 4->8 entry fetch queue changes cycles by only -0.16% (queue is almost never
full, so decode starves on fetch). Measured on the ISS pc trace: 41.6% of all
dynamic fetches (1.22M of 2.94M) are inside straight-line backward-branch
loops of <=16 words once one iteration has been captured (27.5% for <=8 words;
no gain from longer bodies). Those fetches pay the 22% bus-stall tax every
iteration for words the core has just fetched. Three icaches (r7s1/r8s1/r9s1)
recovered cycles but lost >=12% Fmax because a tag-compare hit signal fed
fire/pc/BSRAM address. r11s2 proposed the flop-controlled loop buffer but its
logged run is bit-identical to the champion (cycles 4225873, empty
implementation notes), so the idea has never actually been built and measured.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add rtl/loop_buf.sv: ONE loop, <=16 words, captured and replayed under flop-only
control, armed by the BTB's own training bundle (this is a BTB-driven loop
predictor, not an address-tagged cache, so no per-fetch tag compare exists).

Arm: when the registered BTB training request (tr_en_q, tr_taken_q, tr_pc_q,
tr_target_q in btb.sv, already flops) is a BACKWARD taken branch with
0 < tr_pc_q-tr_target_q <= 15 words, latch lp_T (18b), lp_last = body_len-1
(4b, subtract done here off flops), state <= ARMED. Re-arming to a different
loop replaces the old one (state <= ARMED, replay_q <= 0).
Capture: in ARMED, when a fetch FIRES at pc == lp_T (18b equality of the pc flop
vs a flop, result goes only to state-flop D inputs) enter CAPTURE with
cap_idx <= 1 and write buf[0] <= imem_data. In CAPTURE every fired fetch writes
buf[cap_idx] (LUT-RAM 16x32, index from a flop counter) and cap_idx++. CAPTURE
aborts to IDLE on redir_q, or on any fire whose BTB prediction is taken
(pred_taken) other than the closing fire (cap_idx == lp_last with
pred_taken && pred_target == lp_T). The closing fire sets buf_valid,
state <= READY. So a word is only ever stored for a sequential straight-line
body that was fetched from imem at the matching pcs.
Replay: in READY, when a fire occurs at the closing branch with
pred_taken && pred_target == lp_T (the loop is going around again), set
replay_q <= 1 and rep_idx <= 0. While replay_q:
  in_valid  = imem_ready || replay_q        (an OR of a pin and a FLOP)
  in.instr  = replay_q ? buf[rep_idx] : imem_data  (mux on the fetch-queue
              WRITE data only; never on fire/pc/next_pc or the BTB lookup)
fpc / BTB lookup / pred_* bookkeeping run exactly as today, so every queue entry
still carries its own prediction and EX still verifies the predicted next PC
for every instruction. rep_idx++ on each replay fire. replay_q is cleared (flop
D-input terms only) by redir_q, by a fire at rep_idx==lp_last whose prediction is
not (pred_taken && pred_target==lp_T), and by any fire at rep_idx<lp_last with
pred_taken (the word already issued is still the correct one for that pc; the
next fetch just falls back to imem). The loop-exit mispredict is handled by the
existing registered redirect, so no new redirect path is added.
Decode-cone protection (the lesson of r10s0's worst path u_if/u_fq -> u_id ->
u_rf): fetch_queue's empty-queue bypass is disabled while replay_q (head_valid
for the bypass term uses imem_data only), so the buffer LUT-RAM read can never
reach the decoder/regfile-address cone combinationally; replayed entries go
through queue storage (+1 latency, invisible in a streaming loop).
Correctness/formal: EX never checks the instruction word, only the predicted
next PC, so the buffer must only hold words equal to imem at those pcs; CoreMark
never writes code, and in riscv-formal the executed word is what rvfi_insn
reports, so a stale replay word cannot violate a check (it is just an
instruction stream). The extra state is one 16x32 LUT-RAM, ~50 flops and a few
18b equalities that end at flops, so BMC unroll cost stays near the r6s2
baseline (the formal-blowup lessons were all about redirect-cycle fetch bypass
and 64-entry BTB, neither present here).
Expected: replayed fetches (~1.2M at <=16 words) stream at 1 instr/cycle rather
than 0.78, saving ~0.13-0.16 cycles per replayed instruction when the backend
(dmem stalls, load-use) is the remaining limiter: ~160-190k cycles = +3.8-4.5%
cycles, with Fmax required to hold at ~105 MHz. If the 16-word buffer costs Fmax,
the <=8-word variant (27.5% coverage, 8x32 LUT-RAM, 3b indices) is the fallback.
The implementer must run cosim first and record the bracketed cycle count; if
cycles fall by <3%, abandon.

Instantiate loop_buf; in_valid = imem_ready || replay_q; in_e.instr = replay_q ? loop_data : imem_data; pass replay_q to the fetch queue to disable the empty-queue bypass of replayed entries.
Add a no_bypass input (replay_q): head_e/head_valid use the stored entry path only when it is set, keeping the buffer read off the decode/regfile-address cone.
Export the already-registered training bundle (tr_en_q, tr_taken_q, tr_pc_q, tr_target_q) as outputs for loop arming; no change to lookup, arrays, RAS or training.
Wire the BTB training-bundle outputs and redirect into if_stage/loop_buf.

title: EX-predecoded MEM load-align with the OF forward select folded into a flat AND-OR (BSRAM data -> operand flops in 2 LUT levels)
motivation:
The champion's worst logged path (r8s0/r11s2, 15.941 ns, 9 cells) is the dmem BSRAM
read data -> u_mem load-align shifter / width / sign-extend / mem_to_reg mux -> u_of
forward mux -> opa/opb/rs1_v/rs2_v operand flops. The only prior attempt that cut
exactly this cone alone (r9s0, EX-predecoded byte-lane controls) improved ALL THREE
placement perturbations by 4-5% (champion 93.9/105.5/105.5 MHz -> r9s0
98.5/109.8/109.8 MHz, 259.80 vs 249.61, cycle count bit-identical at 4,225,873), i.e.
a real effect rather than a lucky seed, but landed at +4.08% against the +4.6%
acceptance bar. Every later attempt stacked r9s0 with an unrelated cone cut
(one-hot ALU select r10s0/r10s1, post-flop mispredict select r10s1, single-compare
branch r11s0, flop duplication r11s1, DSP-fed 2-cycle MUL r11s0/r13s0) and each landed
at 230-249, so stacking is the proven failure mode and the lesson is to keep the change
confined to the one cone. r9s0 still left the load data crossing two LUT levels in
mem_stage (align, then mem_to_reg/alu term merge) PLUS two more in of_stage (early
mux: fwd[1] ? m_result : fwd[2] ? w_data : rs_val, then fwd[0] ? x_result : early).
All selects on those later levels (fwd[1], fwd[2], ld_en, pass/fill selects) are
functions of flops only, so they can be merged ahead of the late BSRAM data.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Land r9s0's MEM pre-decode (kept confined to the MEM / forward cone, cycle-identical)
and go one step further on the SAME cone: fold the OF forward priority into the load
AND-OR so the dmem read data reaches each operand flop through ~2 LUT levels instead
of ~4-5, without touching the ALU, branch compare, hazard unit, muldiv, BTB or regfile.

1. core_pkg.sv ex_mem_t: add EX-predecoded MEM fields (RVFI-only consumers keep the old
   fields, which are pruned from the timed netlist): wen_q[3:0] and ren_q (dmem
   write/read enable, already misalign-gated), wdata_rep (byte-replicated store word,
   replaces write_data on the dmem_wdata path), ld_en (mem_to_reg), pass1/pass2/pass3
   (byte-lane pass-through flags), alt (halfword upper-half select for result[15:8]),
   fill1/fill2/fill3 (sign/zero-fill enables for result bytes 1..3), sgn_sel[3:0]
   (one-hot sign-bit source among rdata[31,23,15,7], all-zero for zero-extend / word),
   lo_sel[1:0] (source byte for result[7:0]), and mreg_w (= reg_write && !misalign).
2. ex_stage.sv: compute those from in.ctrl and jalr_sum[1:0] (the two earliest adder bits;
   they only feed EX/MEM flops, never x_result / redirect / BTB training) and store them
   under the existing stall / ex_busy / redir_q hold-or-bubble rules (a bubble clears
   them, so dmem_wen = dmem_ren = 0). Misalign trap semantics (is_illegal set,
   reg_write cleared, dmem port gated) must be preserved bit for bit.
3. mem_stage.sv: dmem_wen/dmem_ren/dmem_wdata straight from the EX/MEM flops; drop the
   shifter, width/sext case muxes and byte_mask logic from the dmem path. Export TWO
   terms instead of one m_result: m_alu_term = ld_en ? 0 : alu_result (early, flops
   only) and m_ld_term = flat AND-OR of rdata (late):
     sign          = |(sgn_sel & {r[31], r[23], r[15], r[7]})
     ld[7:0]       = ld_en ? r[8*lo_sel +: 8] : 0
     ld[15:8]      = (pass1 & r[15:8]) | (alt & r[31:24]) | (fill1 & sign)
     ld[23:16]     = (pass2 & r[23:16]) | (fill2 & sign)
     ld[31:24]     = (pass3 & r[31:24]) | (fill3 & sign)
   MEM/WB.wb_data <= m_alu_term | m_ld_term (RVFI/regfile path, unchanged values).
   m_reg_write = mreg_w (one flop instead of a 2-gate function).
4. of_stage.sv: rewrite the dist-2 / dist-3 / regfile early mux so the late load term
   enters as a single AND-gated OR term, with the other sources pre-merged from flops:
     pre1 = fwd1[1] ? m_alu_term : fwd1[2] ? w_data : rs1_val       (early, flop-only)
     e1   = (fwd1[1] & m_ld_term) | pre1                            (late term: 1 AND-OR)
     rs1_d = fwd1[0] ? x_result : e1                                (unchanged final 2:1)
   and the same for rs2 / opa / opb (fold the is_auipc/is_jump/alu_src early selects into

   ...) are flop-derived and may be pre-ANDed so each result bit costs a single LUT

title: Two-stage decoupled fetch: BTB stage hands a registered pc to a flop-addressed BSRAM instruction store; bus becomes a fill path
motivation:
The core is fetch-bound. 2.937M retired instructions over an imem bus that is
not ready 22% of cycles is a ~3.77M-cycle floor against 4.226M measured. The
decode-side stalls (mispredict ~57k x ~4, load-use, dmem stall, 3-cycle MUL)
total about 0.95M cycles. So fetch supply and decode demand are balanced at
roughly 3.8-3.9M. That is why every single-sided change has stalled: a
non-blocking MUL (r12s1) cut cycles 2.8% and the EX/MEM cone trims cut 0%,
while four stall-supplement icaches (r7s1/r8s1/r9s1/r13s1) cut cycles 8.5-10%
but each lost 5-12% Fmax. In r9s1 and r13s1 the worst path was not in the
cache, so the loss looks like placement drag from `imem_ready | sup` in
`fire` and from a bus/cache data mux in front of the queue write. All four
designs also share one shape: the cache is a *supplement* that only helps in
bubble cycles and that sits inside the single-stage fetch loop (pc flop ->
BTB -> next_pc -> fire -> pc). Cycle-identical edits on this base have landed
anywhere in 230-260 (placement noise ~5%), so the next acceptable change
needs about 10% fewer cycles and must not add logic to the pc/fire loop.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Split fetch into two registered stages so the instruction store is never on
the pc/fire loop, and make the store the primary instruction source.

Stage P (prediction), as today. The `pc` flop indexes the BTB (single-level
read, unchanged), and the predicted next pc is computed as before. The
difference is that P no longer touches imem. Each cycle P pushes
{pc, pred_taken, pred_npc, pred_hit, pred_ctr} into a small flop FIFO (2-4
entries, `pf_q`), and `pc` advances to the BTB target or pc+4 whenever the FIFO
has room. `fire`'s only inputs are flops (FIFO count, `redir_q`), and `imem_ready` is
removed from it.

Stage R (read). A new `icache.sv` holds a 1024-word direct-mapped BSRAM store
with a tag/valid array. Its read address is `pf_q` head's pc, which is a flop,
so no BTB, next_pc, fire or redirect signal reaches a BSRAM address pin. The tag
compare is registered. On the next cycle the entry is a hit, and its
{pc, instr, prediction} bundle is written into the existing fetch_queue
(`in_valid` is a registered hit flag).

Miss path. On a registered miss the head's pc is held and imem_addr is driven
from that flop. The first imem_ready cycle both delivers the word to the queue
(the existing path and bypass, with no extra mux on the hit side) and writes
the cache line, then the FIFO advances. The bus is the fill path only. Hits do
not need imem_ready, so the 22% bubbles disappear on hits. Cold misses cost
roughly the current ~1.28 cycles/word, and the 10 CoreMark iterations are
dominated by hits after iteration 1.

Redirect. `redir_q` flushes the FIFO, the R-stage registers and the fetch
queue, and sets `pc`. The mispredict penalty grows by one cycle (57k x 1 =
+1.3% cycles). The ISS-measured budget is cycles 4.226M -> ~3.75M (-11%) with
the remaining floor being the decode-side stalls. The BTB tag/target
arrays, RAS, EX verification of every instruction against its own prediction,
and the training path are untouched, so correctness and formal behaviour
carry over. The new state is a bounded 2-4 entry flop FIFO plus the tag
check, and there is no redirect-cycle bypass of imem into D/O, which is what
broke formal in r4s2 and r8s2.

Expected fitness: 10 * Fmax / 3.75M. At a pessimistic ~98 MHz that is ~261
(+4.6%). At 102-105 MHz it is 272-280.

changes.description: New module. 1024x32 BSRAM instruction store plus a tag/valid array, with a flop-only read address (head of the P-stage FIFO). The tag compare is registered into hit_q, and the module has a single fill write port driven by the bus. It exports {hit_q, instr} one cycle after the address.

Split fetch into stage P (pc flop + BTB lookup + pc advance, gated only by FIFO room and redir_q) and stage R (cache read, miss hold, bus fill). Drive imem_addr from the registered head pc only when the head is a miss. Remove imem_ready from the pc-advance path. Flush the FIFO and R registers on redirect. Instantiate/wire the icache and the P-stage FIFO inside if_stage. The BTB lookup input stays the pc flop. Keep io_imemAddr driven from a flop. Update the header comment for the 2-stage fetch.

title: Prediction-verify cone cut: OF-precomputed mispredict polarity (branch resolve = one 2:1 off eq/lt) on top of EX-predecoded MEM lanes, no MUL change
motivation:
Every cycle-side predictor idea on this core is capped: the perfect-predictor
ceiling is ~5.7% of cycles (r6s2), and the 32-entry BTB + RAS already take
most of it. The ~22% imem-stall fetch floor is not a predictor problem, and
every attempt to beat it (icache x4, BTB word folding x2, replay buffer x2)
or to deepen the predictor (local history r7s2, gshare r12s2) lost 3-33% to
Fmax. A predictor change therefore only pays through Fmax, and the only
predictor-side logic that is actually on a top path is the prediction-VERIFY
cone: O/X rs1_v/rs2_v flops -> branch compare (eq, signed lt, unsigned lt)
-> branch_op case mux -> is_branch&&cond -> mp_tgt/mp_seq select ->
mispredict -> redir_q (r9s0 and r12s2 both report rs2_v -> redir_q as the
worst path: 38 cells, 15.45-15.74 ns). The log gives a usable two-point
attribution. r9s0 (EX-predecoded MEM byte lanes alone) = 259.80 (109.8 MHz,
worst = rs2_v -> redir_q). r13s0 (r9s0 + 2-busy-cycle MUL fed straight from
the O/X flops) = 237.46. r11s0 (r13s0's MUL + single-chain compare cone) =
243.58 and its worst path MOVED off redir_q to ALU -> x_result -> OF
(16.18 ns). So the compare restructure bought ~+2.6% over its own
MUL-carrying baseline, and the MUL change (not the compare/MEM edits) is the
common cause of the 237-244 results. r10s1 differed in making `redirect` a
LUT3 off flops (not a flop) and adding the one-hot ALU select that r10s0
showed costs ~4% by itself. Nobody has landed MEM pre-decode + compare-cone
cut WITHOUT the MUL/one-hot/redirect-LUT edits. This hypothesis does exactly
that, with the predictor verify logic as the primary change.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep the r9s0 base and make the mispredict decision a function of two raw
compare flags plus flops that OF precomputes from the prediction, with
redir_q staying a plain flop (no logic between redir_q and its consumers).

(1) OF stage (flop-fed only, all in parallel with the forward muxes). For
the instruction in D/O compute and register in the O/X register:
  - sel_eq   = branch_op[2:1]==0 (BEQ/BNE use the equality, others use lt)
  - sgn      = branch_op[1]==0 for BLT/BGE (signed), 1 for BLTU/BGEU unsigned
  - cmp_a31 / cmp_b31 = rs1_d[31]/rs2_d[31] XOR sgn, so signed lt becomes
    one unsigned `<` on {cmp_a31,rs1_v[30:0]} < {cmp_b31,rs2_v[30:0]}. The
    XOR sits behind the dist-1 forward mux as ONE LUT4 (fwd0, x_result[31],
    early[31], sgn); do not add a level on the late x_result path.
  - the existing mp_seq / mp_btgt flops, plus mis_tgt = btgt[1:0]!=0,
    folded into A = mis_tgt ? mp_seq : mp_btgt (mispredict if the branch is
    taken) and B = mp_seq (mispredict if not taken).
  - inv = branch_op[0] (BNE/BGE/BGEU invert the base compare). Register
    T1 = inv ? B : A (mispredict iff base compare is TRUE) and
    T0 = inv ? A : B (mispredict iff base compare is FALSE).
  - class flops cls_br (is_branch), cls_jr (is_jalr) and stat_mp =
    is_jal ? A : (!is_branch && !is_jalr) ? mp_seq : 0, so non-branch,
    non-JALR instructions and JAL never touch the compare at all.
(2) EX stage. Replace the branch_cond case mux with
    eq = (rs1_v == rs2_v); lt = ({cmp_a31,rs1_v[30:0]} < {cmp_b31,rs2_v[30:0]});
    base = sel_eq ? eq : lt;  mp_br = base ? T1 : T0;
    mispredict = ex_valid && (stat_mp || (cls_br && mp_br) || (cls_jr && mp_jr));
with mp_jr unchanged (mis_jalr ? mp_seq : jalr_sum != pred_full; the JALR
adder path was not the reported worst). The late compare therefore ends in
a 5-input function (eq, lt, sel_eq, T1, T0) = two LUT levels, then the
existing `!stall && !ex_busy` gating into the D side of redir_q.
redir_q, redirect_target (redir_br_q select after the flops) and every
consumer of `redirect` stay exactly as in the champion. redir_br_q's D is
cls_br & (base ^ inv); tr_taken's D side uses the same base/inv so the BTB
training request registers (tr_*_q) see the same shallow cone.
RVFI pc_next (EX/MEM.pc_next) is RVFI-only and pruned from the timed
netlist; keep it correct for cosim/formal using the same base/inv form.

(3) The enabling co-cut (r9s0, re-landed unchanged in intent): EX
pre-decodes every MEM byte-lane control from jalr_sum[1:0], mem_width,
mem_sext and the load/store bits into EX/MEM flops: dmem wen[3:0]/ren
(misalign already folded in, so the timed dmem_wen/dmem_ren outputs come
straight from flops), lane-select / pass / fill / one-hot sign-select bits
for the load align, a byte-replicated write word, and the post-misalign
reg_write/is_illegal. mem_stage then does only a flat flop-selected AND-OR on
the dmem read data into m_result. Without this the MEM load-align -> OF
operand-flop cone (15.94 ns in the champion) is still the worst path and the
verify cut alone buys nothing (r2s1/r3s0 lesson).

Explicitly NOT changed (each was measured to lose): the multiplier/divider
and its a_q/b_q operand latch (r11s0/r13s0), the ALU result select (no
one-hot select, no shared adder: r10s0/r10s1/r11s1), the O/X operand flops
(no duplication: r11s1), the BTB/RAS/fetch queue/IF (no new fetch-side
array: r7s2/r12s2), and `redirect` must remain the output of a flop.
Cycle count is identical to the champion (4,225,873): this is a pure timing
restructure of the predictor's verify path, formal-safe because the same
mispredict function is computed, only factored.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-003-r14s2 (regression, -4.41%): Cutting the branch-verify cone with OF-precomputed polarity (`sel_eq`/`inv`/`cmp_a31`/`cmp_b31` plus `t1`/`t0`/`cls_br`/`cls_jr`/`stat_mp` O/X flops so EX resolves with one eq/lt 2:1, `redir_q` still a plain flop) on r9s0's MEM pre-decode with no multiplier change scored 238.60, which at the unchanged 4.226M cycles implies ~100.8 MHz vs ~105.5 for the 249.61 champion, so it refutes r13s0's reading that the MUL operand source was the common cause of the 237-244 results (r11s0 carried the same compare cut plus MUL and got a higher 243.58), and with r14s0 (MEM pre-decode alone, 247.22) it shows that nothing stacked on r9s0's MEM controls has beaten ~249 in six tries (r10s0, r10s1, r11s0, r13s0, r14s0, r14s2), so r9s0's 259.80 should be treated as an unreproducible seed outlier and the compare-cone restructure as unproven (it also added ~9 flops and a sign-XOR LUT4 on the OF forward path); no `make timing` endpoints were recorded to say whether the worst path moved, so stop re-landing r9s0 and branch-cone variants on the logged `rs2_v` -> `redir_q` path and require a multi-seed Fmax run plus top-N endpoint arrivals before the next EX-side cone cut.

title: Kill-bit-only reset/bubble/flush: take the wide sync-reset nets off D/O, EX/MEM and MEM/WB data flops
motivation:
Fetch is the cycle floor (cycles 4.226M ~ instr_count / 0.78 from the 22% imem stalls), four icache
variants and every predictor/MUL/branch-cone variant since r8s0 landed at -6%..+4% (noise-dominated),
so the remaining lever is Fmax and only cuts that remove a whole class of high-fanout nets, not LUT
levels, have ever moved it (r5s1 OF stage, r8s0 registered redirect select, r6s2 registered BTB train).
The one fanout class still untouched: three pipeline registers still clear their ENTIRE payload
(hundreds of flops) from late control nets.
  - id_stage D/O: `if (reset || flush) reg_q <= '0` — ~220 flops on a net that is
    flush_id = redir_q && !dmem_stall && !ex_busy, i.e. a function of the dmem_ready input,
    the EX/MEM ctrl flops and the muldiv done/valid chain (r2s0/r2s1 identified exactly this net, but it
    was only ever tried on a 50 MHz base and later rewrites put it back).
  - ex_stage EX/MEM: `reset` -> 0, `ex_busy || redir_q` -> 0 on ~330 flops (pc, alu_result,
    mem_addr, write_data, rs?_val, pc_next, branch_target, instr...) while `stall` (dmem_ready) is the
    hold/CE. The LSR of every one of those flops is reset | (!stall & (ex_busy | redir_q)), a 3-4 level
    cone from the dmem_ready input and the muldiv busy chain with ~330 sinks, sharing slices with the
    stall CE net.
  - mem_stage MEM/WB: `reset` clears ~300 flops (all RVFI-only except wb_data/rd/ctrl/valid).
Gowin LSR/CE are per-slice-pair shared control sets, so these wide clear nets both lengthen routing
of the nets themselves (ex_busy, redir_q, stall) and force the placer to pack data flops by control
set rather than by datapath locality. of_stage already proved the recipe works (only valid/ctrl/rd
are cleared by a bubble; the wide data path has no sync-reset net).
Fresh `make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion (place option 0: 93.9 MHz, 9 logic levels, 3285 LUT,
1159 FF) shows the top-25 setup endpoints bunched at 10.4-10.6 ns data delay in four cones: (a) 15 of
25 start at dmem_3 BSRAM DO[7] (the load sign bit, fanning out through load-align to opa/opb/rs1_v/
rs2_v), (b) OF opa/opb flops -> ALU -> alu_result / opa (forward), (c) rs2_v -> redir_q (branch
compare), (d) is_md -> regfile read-address register (ex_busy -> stall). The reset/flush/bubble nets
are NOT yet among the top endpoints, so this is a placement-pressure cut, not a level cut: ~700 flops
lose their LSR sinks, and the hot control nets feeding cones (c)/(d) (ex_busy, redir_q, stall) lose
~330+220 extra sinks each, which relieves routing around exactly those nets. It is deliberately the
one change that touches none of the four logic cones (every earlier cone-level cut was capped by the
other bunched cones), and it adds zero logic.

hypothesis.motivation:
Fetch is the cycle floor (cycles 4.226M ~ instr_count / 0.78 from the 22% imem stalls), four icache
variants and every predictor/MUL/branch-cone variant since r8s0 landed at -6%..+4% (noise-dominated),
so the remaining lever is Fmax and only cuts that remove a whole class of high-fanout nets, not LUT
levels, have ever moved it (r5s1 OF stage, r8s0 registered redirect select, r6s2 registered BTB train).
The one fanout class still untouched: three pipeline registers still clear their ENTIRE payload
(hundreds of flops) from late control nets.
  - id_stage D/O: `if (reset || flush) reg_q <= '0` — ~220 flops on a net that is
    flush_id = redir_q && !dmem_stall && !ex_busy, i.e. a function of the dmem_ready input,
    the EX/MEM ctrl flops and the muldiv done/valid chain (r2s0/r2s1 identified exactly this net, but it
    was only ever tried on a 50 MHz base and later rewrites put it back).
  - ex_stage EX/MEM: `reset` -> 0, `ex_busy || redir_q` -> 0 on ~330 flops (pc, alu_result,
    mem_addr, write_data, rs?_val, pc_next, branch_target, instr...) while `stall` (dmem_ready) is the
    hold/CE. The LSR of every one of those flops is reset | (!stall & (ex_busy | redir_q)), a 3-4 level
    cone from the dmem_ready input and the muldiv busy chain with ~330 sinks, sharing slices with the
    stall CE net.
  - mem_stage MEM/WB: `reset` clears ~300 flops (all RVFI-only except wb_data/rd/ctrl/valid).
Gowin LSR/CE are per-slice-pair shared control sets, so these wide clear nets both lengthen routing
of the nets themselves (ex_busy, redir_q, stall) and force the placer to pack data flops by control
set rather than by datapath locality. of_stage already proved the recipe works (only valid/ctrl/rd
are cleared by a bubble; the wide data path has no sync-reset net).
Fresh `make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion (place option 0: 93.9 MHz, 9 logic levels, 3285 LUT,
1159 FF) shows the top-25 setup endpoints bunched at 10.4-10.6 ns data delay in four cones: (a) 15 of
25 start at dmem_3 BSRAM DO[7] (the load sign bit, fanning out through load-align to opa/opb/rs1_v/
rs2_v), (b) OF opa/opb flops -> ALU -> alu_result / opa (forward), (c) rs2_v -> redir_q (branch
compare), (d) is_md -> regfile read-address register (ex_busy -> stall). The reset/flush/bubble nets
are NOT yet among the top endpoints, so this is a placement-pressure cut, not a level cut: ~700 flops
lose their LSR sinks, and the hot control nets feeding cones (c)/(d) (ex_busy, redir_q, stall) lose
~330+220 extra sinks each, which relieves routing around exactly those nets. It is deliberately the
one change that touches none of the four logic cones (every earlier cone-level cut was capped by the
other bunched cones), and it adds zero logic.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Apply the OF-stage recipe to the three remaining registers: ONLY valid, ctrl, rd (and, in D/O,
rs1_addr/rs2_addr so stale compares can never hit x0-gated hazard/forward logic) get the
reset/flush/bubble clear. Every data field becomes a plain enable flop (CE = !stall / !hold_wb) with
no reset and no clear — their value is don't-care whenever valid/ctrl are zero, because every consumer
is already gated by them: ex_valid (= in.valid && !redirect) gates muldiv req / adv / BTB train /
RAS / mispredict; m_reg_write / x_reg_write come from the cleared ctrl.reg_write so no forward fires;
dmem_wen / dmem_ren are ANDed with the cleared ctrl.mem_write / mem_read (so a stale mem_addr on the
dmem address bus is harmless; cosim oob only flags accesses with REn/WEn); wb_stage w_en =
ctrl.reg_write && valid; RVFI-only fields are only sampled when rvfi_valid=1 (and are pruned from the
timed netlist anyway).
Concretely:
  id_stage.sv: split the always_ff. Control group {valid, ctrl, rd, rs1_addr, rs2_addr}:
    `if (reset || flush) <= '0; else if (!stall) <= decoded`. Data group {pc, imm, instr, pred_*}:
    `if (!stall) <= in.*` (no reset/flush term). rs1_val/rs2_val: unconditional capture of the regfile
    read (no flush term). The regfile read address mux (stall ? reg_q.rs?_addr : in.instr[..]) is
    unchanged and reg_q.rs?_addr is still cleared by flush, so a dead D/O re-reads x0.
  ex_stage.sv: split reg_q. Control group {valid, ctrl, rd}: reset -> 0; else stall -> hold; else
    (ex_busy || redir_q) -> 0; else load. Data group {pc, alu_result, mem_addr, write_data, rs1_addr,
    rs2_addr, rs1_val, rs2_val, pc_next, branch_taken, branch_target, instr}: `if (!stall) <= in-derived`
    with no reset and no ex_busy/redir_q term. The late ex_busy / redir_q nets now fan out to ~40
    control flops instead of ~370; the data flops only see the stall CE.
  mem_stage.sv: control group {valid, ctrl, rd}: reset -> 0, hold_wb -> valid<=0 only (existing
    behaviour), else load. Data group (pc, wb_data, rs?_addr, rs?_val, pc_next, mem_*): no reset, CE =
    !hold_wb only.
Cycle count is identical by construction (no control decision changes); the load-use hazard compare
uses ox_rd (cleared by bubble) and D/O rs?_addr (cleared on flush), so no spurious stall is added.
Formal: all cleared fields are valid-gated for RVFI; riscv-formal only samples retired instructions,
and rvfi_order_q is still reset in core.sv. No decoder/ALU/muldiv logic is touched so ALTOPS and the
M-ext tests are unaffected. Expected effect is an Fmax effect only: shorter/less-congested stall,
ex_busy and flush nets and ~700 fewer flops on sync-reset LSR. Risk: the median-of-seeds Fmax is
noisy (~5%), so the true gain may be hidden; kept deliberately as a single cut (no other edits) so
it can be attributed, per r11s0/r14s2 lessons.

changes.description: Split the D/O register always_ff: reset/flush clear only valid, ctrl, rd, rs1_addr, rs2_addr; pc/imm/instr/pred_* are CE-only (!stall) with no reset/flush; rs1_val/rs2_val capture the regfile read unconditionally. Removes the ~220-flop flush/reset net.

Split the EX/MEM register: only valid/ctrl/rd get reset and the ex_busy||redir_q bubble clear (stall still holds everything); all data fields (pc, alu_result, mem_addr, write_data, rs/val fields, pc_next, branch_*, instr) load under !stall with no reset and no bubble clear, so ex_busy/redir_q stop fanning out to ~330 flop LSR pins.

Split the MEM/WB register: reset clears only valid/ctrl/rd; data fields (pc, wb_data, rs/val, pc_next, mem_addr/rdata/wdata/masks, instr) are CE-only on !hold_wb. hold_wb still clears just valid and keeps data for the dist-3 forward.

Split the D/O register always_ff: reset/flush clear only valid, ctrl, rd, rs1_addr, rs2_addr; pc/imm/instr/pred_* are CE-only (!stall) with no reset/flush; rs1_val/rs2_val capture the regfile read unconditionally. Removes the ~220-flop flush/reset net.

Split the MEM/WB register: reset clears only valid/ctrl/rd; data fields (pc, wb_data, rs/val, pc_next, mem_addr/rdata/wdata/masks, instr) are CE-only on !hold_wb. hold_wb still clears just valid and keeps data for the dist-3 forward.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-001-r15s0 (regression, -11.09%): Taking the wide sync-reset/bubble/flush clear off ~700 data flops in D/O, EX/MEM and MEM/WB (kill-bit-only: only valid/ctrl/rd, plus D/O rs?_addr, keep the late `flush`/`ex_busy || redir_q`/`reset` term, data fields become CE-only flops) added zero logic and is cycle-identical by construction yet scored 221.94, which at 4.226M cycles implies ~93.8 MHz vs ~105.5 for the 249.61 champion (and equal to the 93.9 MHz the champion's own fresh place-option-0 `make timing` reported, so seed spread may explain much of it), so reset-net fanout is not a binding Fmax limiter on this base: the proposal itself conceded none of the top-25 endpoints (load sign bit -> operand flops, ALU -> `alu_result`, `rs2_v` -> `redir_q`, `is_md` -> regfile address) touched those nets, and a "placement-pressure" cut justified by sink counts rather than endpoint arrivals cannot be told from noise, while splitting each register into a control group and a CE-only data group may also have fragmented Gowin LSR/CE control sets; no per-seed Fmax or post-change endpoints were recorded, so that mechanism is inferred, but don't retry kill-bit-only reset removal (the r2s1 +7% version is the same family) and require multi-seed Fmax against the champion before crediting any zero-logic fanout cut.

title: Registered-load WB-align stage: dmem BSRAM data ends at the MEM/WB flop, align moves to WB
motivation:
CoreMark here is fetch-bound: 2.94M instructions over an imem bus that is ready 78% of
cycles gives a ~3.77M-cycle floor against 4.226M measured, and a fetch queue deepened to
8 entries moved cycles only -0.16% (r12s0 notes), so decode/backend slack is real and a
bubble in the backend is largely absorbed by the queue. The champion's logged worst path
(15.94 ns, slack -5.65, 9 cells, clock_ibuf > u_mem > u_of) is dmem BSRAM tCO -> byte-lane
align / sign-extend -> m_result -> OF forward mux -> O/X operand flop. Every cycle-only
trim of this cone (r9s0 pre-decode +4%, r14s0 247.22, r10/r11 stacks) kept the BSRAM tCO
in front of the align and the OF forward fan-out, so they only moved Fmax inside
placement noise. r12s0 proposed removing the load forward but its result row is a
verbatim copy of the champion (249.61 / 105.482 / 4,225,873 cycles, same critical path),
i.e. the change was never actually timed. The structural fix is to give the load its own
stage boundary: raw BSRAM data goes into a flop and nothing else.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the pipeline IF-ID-OF-EX-MEM-WB with a load-data boundary at MEM/WB: the dmem read
data is captured RAW into the existing MEM/WB mem_rdata flops (BSRAM -> flop, zero logic
levels), and sign/zero-extension plus byte-lane shift moves to the WB stage, computed from
flops (mem_rdata, a new 2-bit ld_off flop, ctrl.mem_width/mem_sext/mem_to_reg).
wb_stage's w_data = mem_to_reg ? align(mem_rdata) : wb_data; it feeds the regfile write
port (and its write-first bypass into D/O rs?_val), the OF dist-3 forward (flop -> align
-> 2:1 -> O/X flop, ~4-5 ns shorter than BSRAM tCO -> align -> fwd -> flop) and RVFI.
The dist-2 (MEM) forward now takes only the EX/MEM alu_result flop with a flop-fed valid
(ex_mem.ctrl.reg_write && !ex_mem.ctrl.mem_to_reg; misalign traps only clear reg_write for
mem ops, so the post-trap term is not needed), so no load data crosses into OF in the MEM
cycle and the dmem BSRAM output fans out to exactly one place. hazard_unit gets one more
flop-fed load-use term (EX/MEM load rd vs D/O rs1/rs2, OR-ed into load_use_hazard ->
stall_id/bubble_ox), so a consumer directly behind a load waits 2 cycles (was 1) and the
one two behind waits 1 (was 0); the loaded value is then picked up by the dist-3 forward or
the regfile bypass. dmem-stall hold semantics are unchanged (hold_wb already retains all
MEM/WB data fields, mem_rdata/ld_off included, so w_data stays valid while held). Expected
cost: ~5% dist-1 + ~3% dist-2 load-use instructions each lose one slot, mostly absorbed by
the fetch-bound queue slack (net ~1.5-2.5% cycles). Expected gain: the logged worst
cone (BSRAM tCO + align + 2 mux levels) becomes flop -> align -> mux, moving the
limiter to the ALU -> x_result cone (~15.3 ns in r14s0), i.e. ~4-6% Fmax; to make the
trade pay, also drop the now-unneeded m_reg_write/m_result nets from mem_stage's port
list so no logic remains between EX/MEM and OF except the alu_result select. Land this
ALONE (no predecode, no MUL, no branch edits), run cosim first and abandon if cycles
exceed ~4.31M, and attach `make timing` top-N endpoints plus a multi-seed Fmax so the
result can be separated from placement noise. RVFI rd_wdata/mem_rdata fields and the
ALTOPS formal view are unchanged; nret stays 1.

Capture raw dmem_rdata and ld_off into MEM/WB (wb_data now holds only the non-load ALU result / alu_result); remove the load-align and m_result mux from the MEM cycle; export a flop-fed dist-2 forward (alu_result, valid = reg_write && !mem_to_reg). Compute w_data = mem_to_reg ? aligned/sign-extended mem_rdata (shift by ld_off*8, width, sext) : wb_data, from MEM/WB flops only; w_en/w_addr unchanged.
Add inputs ex_mem_load, ex_mem_rd and OR a flop-fed 'load in MEM matches D/O rs1/rs2' term into load_use_hazard so a consumer waits until the load reaches WB.

title: BTB capacity: 32 to 128 entries to kill JAL/branch conflict misses
motivation:
An ISS trace model of the timed CoreMark region (2.92M instrs, 529k branches,
49k JAL, 13.7k returns; same 2-bit counter / allocate-on-taken / 4-deep RAS
policy as btb.sv) shows 56.3k mispredicts with the current 32-entry
direct-mapped BTB: 46.8k branch, 8.3k JAL, 1.2k ret. JAL is allocated at ctr=3
and never changes direction, so its 8.3k mispredicts (17% of JAL executions)
are pure conflict/capacity misses. Sweeping only the entry count (same
policy): 64 entries -> 50.2k, 128 -> 44.5k, 1024 -> 39.9k (the last is the
2-bit-counter data-dependent floor). There are zero non-return JALRs in the
timed region (the mergesort comparator call is cloned/inlined), so indirect
targets are not a lever. At ~3.6 cycles per mispredict, 128 entries saves ~42k
cycles (~1.0%), so this is a small cycle-only gain and a low-confidence proposal;
it is the largest remaining capacity-side effect I could measure.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Grow the BTB from IW=5 to IW=7 (128 entries, tag = pc[19:9], 11 bits) by changing
the one localparam in btb.sv. Lookup stays a single LUT-RAM read off the pc flop
(one extra address bit, one more 2:1 level in the read mux), so the fetch cone
stays one-level deep per the r7s2/r12s2 rule. valid_q / is_ret_q grow to 128
flops each; the training path is already registered so the wider write decode
does not touch the late EX compare. No change to ex_stage, fetch_queue or
the redirect cone. The risk to watch is formal tractability (r4s2 timed out with a
64-entry BTB, but r8s2 showed the redirect-cycle bypass was the cause, not BTB
size) and Fmax from the larger LUT-RAM placement; if 128 is too costly fall
back to 64 (trace: -6k mispredicts, ~0.5%). Expected: -11.8k mispredicts of 56.3k,
~1% cycles, Fmax-neutral if placement is kind.

changes.description: IW 5 -> 7 (128-entry direct-mapped, tag pc[19:9]); update header comment. No other structural change.
IW 5 -> 7 (128-entry direct-mapped, tag pc[19:9]); update header comment. No other structural change.

lesson: - 2026-10-02 hyp-20261002-003-r15s2 (regression, -11.94%): Growing the pc-indexed BTB from 32 to 128 entries (one `IW` localparam, 11-bit tag, 128-flop `valid_q`/`is_ret_q`, still one LUT-RAM read off the pc flop) had only a ~1% cycle ceiling (-11.8k of 56.3k mispredicts; even 1024 entries only reaches the 39.9k 2-bit-counter floor) and scored 219.80 vs the 249.61 champion, which at ~4.18M cycles implies ~92 MHz vs ~105.5, so the extra index bit and read-mux level on the registered-pc -> BTB -> `next_pc`/`fire` cone cost far more Fmax than any capacity-side miss reduction can repay (it finished without a formal timeout, consistent with r8s2 blaming the redirect bypass, not BTB size, for r4s2); r15s0 saw the champion itself re-place at ~93.9 MHz so some of the gap may be seed noise and no `make timing` or cycle count was logged to split them, but either way keep the BTB at 32 entries and don't retry 64/128-entry scaling (~0.5-1% cycles) without a multi-seed Fmax comparison against the champion.
